en: [The Discourse on Discipline] For the homeless monk who is completely liberated from attachments, I shall explain the discipline; listen to me in due order. (Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1)
One who carries out the instructions, who performs services for the teachers, and who is endowed with the proper gestures and deportment—he is called "disciplined.
One who does not carry out the instructions, who does not perform services for the teachers... [Uttarādhyayana 2]

One who is hostile and lacks awakening is called undisciplined. (Uttarādhyayana 3) Just as a dog with pus-filled ears is driven out from every side, so too is the talkative person of evil conduct driven out. (Uttarādhyayana 4)
Just as a pig, having abandoned the grain and the fodder, eats what is found in the dung,
so too does a fool, having abandoned good conduct, delight in misconduct.
(Uttarādhyayana 5) Having heard the lack of self-restraint in the dog, the pig, and the man...
One who desires his own welfare should establish himself in discipline.
Therefore, O son of the Buddha, one who strives for liberation should seek discipline and attain virtuous conduct; such a person shall never be cast out from anywhere. (Uttarādhyayana 6–7)

One should be silent and not speak harshly; in the presence of the Buddhas, one should always learn what is meaningful and avoid what is meaningless. When instructed, one should not become angry; a wise person should practice patience.
One should avoid association with the young, as well as laughter and play. (Uttarādhyayana 9) One should not engage in harsh speech, nor should one talk excessively.
Having studied at the proper time, one should then meditate in solitude. (Uttarādhyayana 10)
Having committed a violent act, O Caṇḍālī, one should never conceal it;
one should say "it was done" if it was done, and "it was not done" if it was not done.
One should not desire repeated verbal correction, like a worn-out horse seeking the whip again and again.
One should avoid the wicked, who are like a lurking snake ready to bite.

(Uttarādhyayana 12) Those who are free from taints yet possess coarse speech and are of bad conduct, though mild, provoke fury in their disciples; for disciples who follow their own whims are difficult to manage.
However, those who are wise and endowed with self-control can win over even one who is hard to subdue. (Uttarādhyayana 13)

One should not say anything when unasked; when asked, one should not speak falsely. One should harbor what is pleasant and unpleasant [within]. The self alone must be subdued, for the self is indeed difficult to subdue.

One who has tamed oneself becomes happy both in this world and in the next. (Uttarādhyayana 15) It is better for me that I have tamed myself through self-restraint and austerity, rather than being tamed by others through bonds and beatings. (Uttarādhyayana 16)

One should never, at any time, act in opposition to the Buddhas, whether by word or by deed, openly or in secret. One should not [speak] from the side, nor from the front, nor even from behind those who are to be honored.
One should not place one thigh upon the other, nor should one stretch out the legs while lying down.
One should not cross the legs, nor should one clasp the knees together;
furthermore, one should not stand with the feet extended in the presence of the teacher. (Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18–19)
Urged on by his teachers, he remains silent; never seeking favor, but seeking only his own spiritual goal, he always attends upon the guru.
Whether they are speaking or remaining silent, he should never sit down [in a manner that implies defiance].
Having left his seat, the wise one should respectfully acknowledge what is said.
One should never ask a question while remaining on a seat or on a bed; rather, having approached and stood up, one should ask with palms joined in reverence. (Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 21.22)

Thus, to a student who is endowed with discipline and who asks about both the text and its meaning, one should explain it exactly as it was heard. A monk should avoid falsehood and should not speak disparagingly.
One should avoid defects in speech and always abandon deceit. (Uttarādhyayana 24) When questioned, one should not utter anything blameworthy, nor that which is meaningless, nor that which is vital;
whether for one's own sake, for another's sake, or for the sake of both. (Uttarādhyayana 25)
In battlefields, in houses, at the junctions of dwellings, or on great highways, one should neither stand nor converse with another person alone.

Thinking, "This is my gain," one should respectfully accept that instruction; the wise person considers beneficial that exhortation and the correction of misconduct, whereas for the wicked person, it becomes a source of resentment. (Uttarādhyayana 27.28)

The Buddhas, free from fear, are compassionate; though their instruction may be harsh, it is indeed pleasing to the deluded, for such speech brings about the purification of patience. One should remain seated on a seat that is not too high, not uneven, and firm.
Uninvited and unasked, he should sit with little agitation.
A mendicant should go out for alms at the proper time, and return at the proper time; avoiding the improper time, he should practice at the proper time. (Uttarādhyayana 30.31)
A monk should not stand in a line; he should wander for alms seeking what is given.
Having sought food with proper decorum, he should eat it in moderation at the proper time.
He should not stay too far away nor too close, nor within the range of sight of others.
I myself shall remain at the place for alms; having bypassed that [unfit] house, one should not step over it. (Utt.
33) Neither too high nor too low, neither too near nor too far, the self-restrained one should accept pure alms provided by others. (Utt. 34)
In a place with few living beings and few seeds, well-concealed and secluded, the self-controlled and restrained monk should eat with care, so as not to scatter [the food].
"Well-done! "Well-cooked! "Well-cut! "Well-fought!"—[such praise] regarding food is but vanity.

"Having completed [his task], the sage should say, 'Well gained! and avoid what is blameworthy. (Uttarādhyayana 36) "The wise man should delight in the instruction, just as a driver delights in a well-bred horse; instructing the fool with patience, he should guide him like one who guides a weary steed. (Uttarādhyayana 37)
"Blows with sticks are mine, lashes are mine, and insults and beatings are mine;

yet he who instructs me for my own welfare thinks, 'He has an evil view. A virtuous person considers him to be his son, brother, or kinsman, and regards him as one who brings about his welfare. (Uttarādhyayana 38)
One who has been instructed in the doctrine considers himself a slave;
he should not be angry with his teacher, nor should he be angry with himself.
He should not be one who harms the enlightened ones, nor should he be one who seeks out faults. (Uttarādhyayana 39–40)
Perceiving that the teacher is angry, one should appease him with humility;
with palms joined, one should propitiate him and say, "I shall not do it again.
This legal procedure, earned through righteousness, has always been practiced by the Buddhas.

One who conducts oneself according to that conduct does not incur reproach. (Uttarādhyayana 42) Having understood what has been thought by the teacher and what has been spoken, one should grasp it with speech and put it into practice through action. (Uttarādhyayana 43)
One who is never scorched by wealth quickly becomes well-scorched [of worldly attachment]; having always performed his duties as prescribed, he acts rightly.
Having understood this, the wise man bows down; thus his fame arises in the world.

It becomes a refuge for those who have performed their duties, just as the earth is for all living beings. (Uttarādhyayana 45) The Fully Awakened Ones, who were previously honored, will be pleased with him; being satisfied, they will bestow upon him vast, steadfast, and well-acquired knowledge. (Uttarādhyayana 46)

He is worthy of worship and praised for his excellent discipline; he dwells with a mind full of joy, endowed with the fruits of karma, restrained by austerity, right conduct, and meditative absorption.
Having observed the five great vows with great splendor, he—honored by gods, gandharvas, and humans—casts off this body which is like a mass of impure mire.
Or he becomes a perfected one, eternal, a god, self-luminous, and possessed of great majesty.
Thus I say. (Uttarādhyayana 48)
[The Analysis of the Parīṣahas]

I have heard, O venerable one, that it was thus declared by the Blessed One: "Indeed, here are twenty-two hardships (parīsaha) proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed Mahāvīra, the Kāśyapa. Having heard of them, having understood them, having conquered them, and having overcome them, a monk wandering for alms-food should not be overwhelmed when assailed. Which indeed are those twenty-two hardships proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed Mahāvīra, the Kāśyapa, which a monk—having heard of them, having understood them, having conquered them, and having overcome them—wandering for alms-food should not be overwhelmed when assailed?

These indeed are the twenty-two hardships (parīsaha) proclaimed by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, the Kāśyapa. Having heard of them, having understood them, having conquered them, and having mastered them, a monk wandering in the practice of alms-gathering should not be overwhelmed when assailed by them. They are as follows: the hardship of hunger, the hardship of thirst, the hardship of cold, the hardship of heat, the hardship of gadflies and mosquitoes, the hardship of nakedness, the hardship of discontent, the hardship of women, the hardship of wandering, the hardship of sitting, the hardship of lodging, the hardship of abuse, the hardship of assault, the hardship of begging, the hardship of non-acquisition, the hardship of illness, the hardship of the touch of grass, the hardship of dirt, the hardship of honor and reverence, the hardship of wisdom, the hardship of ignorance, and the hardship of right view.
The classification of the hardships (parīsaha) has been proclaimed by Kāśyapa;
I shall recite it to you—listen to me in due order.
(Uttarādhyayana 50) When the body is overcome by hunger, the ascetic monk, possessed of fortitude, [endures].

One should not cut [plants], nor cause them to be cut; one should not cook, nor cause them to be cooked. (Uttarādhyayana 51) Resembling the joints of a black antelope, emaciated and with veins showing, mindful of one’s food and drink, one should wander with an undaunted mind. (Uttarādhyayana 52)
Afflicted by thirst, even one who is disgusted with the world and has attained self-restraint should not resort to cold water; he should practice the careful examination of warm water.
On paths where water is cut off, being afflicted and extremely thirsty... [Uttarādhyayana 53]
With a face completely parched and free from dejection, he should endure that hardship.
Coldness touches the ascetic who wanders, practicing austerities and living on coarse food;
at times, the sage should not go out [at night], having heard the teaching of the Jina. (Uttarādhyayana 54–55)
"I have no shelter, no protection for my skin exists; yet I shall resort to fire"—thus a monk should not think.
[He may encounter] scorching heat and be tormented by a burning fever. (Uttarādhyayana 56)
Whether one suffers from cold or from fever, one should not lament at evening. (Uttarādhyayana 5.57) The wise man, even when afflicted by heat, should not desire a bath;
he should not sprinkle water on his body, nor should he fan himself. (Uttarādhyayana 5.58)
When bitten by gadflies and mosquitoes, like a great sage in battle or a hero at the head of the fray, he should overcome his adversary;
he should neither tremble nor ward them off, nor should he even give rise to anger in his mind. (Uttarādhyayana 5.9)
One should observe living beings but not kill them, even when they are consuming flesh and blood.
(Uttarādhyayana 60) Thinking, "I shall be one who wears worn-out clothes," or "I shall be unclothed," or "I shall be clothed"—a monk should not think such things. (Uttarādhyayana 61)
At one time he is without clothing, and at another time he is with clothing;
knowing this to be for the sake of the Dharma, the wise man should not lament.
[This applies to] the homeless one, possessing nothing, as he wanders from village to village.
One should not allow dissatisfaction to enter; one should endure that hardship.
Having cast aside dissatisfaction behind him, the sage—restrained, self-protecting, delighting in the Dharma, free from worldly undertakings, and tranquil—should wander. (Uttarādhyayana 6.3–4)
This is the attachment of men: women in this world.
For him who has fully understood this, his ascetic life is well-performed. Thus perceiving this, the wise man [should know] that women are indeed like mire.

One should not be struck down by them; one should wander seeking the self. (Uttarādhyayana 6.66) One should wander alone in the Lāḍha country, having overcome the hardships, whether in a village, a town, a market-town, or a capital city. (Uttarādhyayana 6.67)
A monk should wander without attachment and must not make any possessions;
unattached to householders, he should wander as one who is independent.
(Uttarādhyayana 6.8) Whether in a cemetery, an empty house, or at the foot of a tree, he should dwell alone.

One should sit without fidgeting and should not cause alarm to another. (Uttarādhyayana 69) While staying there, if an assault should be directed at him, he should not move away; rather, having risen, he should go to another seat. (Uttarādhyayana 70)
A steadfast ascetic monk should not neglect his practice on account of high or low beds; it is only one of evil views who neglects it.
Having obtained a secluded dwelling, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [he should remain there].
"What will he do for a single night?"—thus one should endure it there.
(Uttarādhyayana 72) If another reviles a monk, he should not retort to them;
such behavior is like that of fools. Therefore, a monk should not retort. (Uttarādhyayana 73)
Having heard harsh speech, cruel words that are thorns to the village, one should remain silent and not take them to heart.
A monk, when struck, should not cry out; he should not even harbor ill will in his mind.
Having understood that forbearance is supreme, a monk should practice the Dharma.
No one anywhere can kill a self-controlled ascetic; thus should the restrained one reflect: "There is no destruction of the life-force (jīva). (Uttarādhyayana 7.5–6)
"Indeed, O Lord, it is difficult for a homeless monk to always conquer everything;
there is nothing that remains unconquered.
For one who has entered the alms-round, his hand should not be stretched out [for anything other than food]. (Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.7)
"A householder"—thus a monk should not think.
He should seek his food among others when the meal is finished;
whether he obtains alms or does not obtain them, the wise man should not feel regret. (Uttarādhyayana 78–79)
"I cannot obtain [it] even today; perhaps there will be gain tomorrow.
He who reflects thus is not distressed by lack of gain. Having understood that suffering has arisen, and being afflicted by pain... (Uttarādhyayana 8.3)
One who is not dejected should maintain his wisdom; when questioned therein, he should endure it with composure.
(Uttarādhyayana 8.1) He should not take pleasure in medical treatment; he should remain reflective, seeking the self.
Indeed, this is his asceticism: that which he neither does nor causes to be done. (Uttarādhyayana 8.2)
For one who is unclothed, austere, self-restrained, and practicing penance, there may be injury to the body while sleeping on grass;
by the cessation of the heat [of the sun], there arises intense pain. (Uttarādhyayana 8.3)
Knowing this, those who have conquered craving do not indulge in what is woven from threads. (Utt.
84) The wise person, whose body is wet with mud or dust, or who suffers from exhaustion or heat, should not lament at evening. (Utt. 85)

Seeking the shedding of karma, he should practice the unsurpassed noble Dharma until the dissolution of the body, bearing the filth upon his person. (Uttarādhyayana 8.6) The master should offer salutation, rise from his seat in respect, and extend an invitation.

The sage should not envy those who indulge in such things. (Uttarādhyayana 8.7) One who is free from latent passions, moderate in desires, seeking no other [teacher], and devoid of greed, should not be attached to flavors; being wise, he should not feel remorse. (Uttarādhyayana 8.8)
Surely it must be that in the past I committed actions resulting from ignorance,
because of which I do not recognize anyone when questioned by anyone; later, those actions resulting from ignorance are brought to fruition.
Thus one should console oneself, having understood the ripening of karma:
"In this purposeless world, I am restrained from sexual intercourse and well-restrained;
yet I do not personally know the Dharma as being either auspicious or evil. (Uttarādhyayana 9.10–11)
"Having undertaken the practice of austerity and having entered the meditative posture (*pratimā*), even as I wander in this manner, my delusion does not cease.
Surely there is no other world, nor is there any power for ascetics. (Uttarādhyayana 9.2)
"Or perhaps I have been deceived by my friends"—thus a monk should not think. "The Jinas did not exist, there are no Jinas, or they will never exist;
those [others] speak falsely"—thus a monk should not think. (Uttarādhyayana 9.3–4)
All these hardships have been proclaimed by Kāśyapa; whichever monk, when touched by anyone anywhere, does not become distressed—thus I say. (Uttarādhyayana 9.5)
[The Discourse on the Fourfold Array] There are four supreme factors that are difficult for a living being to obtain in this world:
Human birth, hearing the Dharma, faith, and vigor in self-restraint—these are rare for those who have entered the cycle of saṃsāra.
Having performed various kinds of actions throughout diverse births and lineages, beings are born separately, each with distinct destinies. (Uttarādhyayana 96–97)
At one time in the worlds of the gods, at another even in the hells, and at another in the body of an asura— he goes according to his past actions (karma).
At one time he becomes a kṣatriya, and from there a caṇḍāla or a bukkasa.
Then there are insects and beetles, then ants and termites;
thus, in these revolving wombs, living beings who are defiled by their karma do not grow weary of *saṃsāra*, just as Kṣatriyas [do not tire] of all their various tasks. (Uttarādhyayana 9.99–100)
Deluded by their own karmic bonds, suffering and experiencing manifold pains, living beings are tormented within non-human wombs.
However, through the abandonment of karmas, a gradual sequence [toward liberation] is eventually achieved.
Living beings who have attained beauty come to the human state. (Utt.
102) Having obtained a human body, it is rare to hear the Dharma, hearing which they practice austerity, patience, and non-violence. (Utt. 103)
Having attained the opportunity to hear [the Dharma], faith is extremely difficult to find;
having heard the path leading to the end of existence, many fall away from it.
Having attained both hearing and faith, vigor, moreover, is difficult to find.
Even though many weep, one does not attain it.
Having attained human birth, he who, having heard the Dharma, places his faith in it, being an ascetic, having gained vigor, restrained, shall shake off the dust [of passion]. (Uttarādhyayana 10.5–6)
For one who has become upright, purity arises; for the pure, the Dharma abides.
One attains supreme Nirvana, like a fire fed with ghee.
Having discerned the cause of karma, accumulate glory through patience.
Having cast off the earthly body, he ascends toward the upper direction. (Utt.
108) By means of expansive virtues, the Yakṣas—shining like the Mahāsukkas, each higher than the next—consider themselves not to be subject to rebirth. (Utt. 109)
Unpleasant to the gods, yet able to assume any form at will and to transform themselves, they dwell in the celestial realms for many hundreds of previous years.
Having remained there in their respective places, those yakṣas fall when their lifespan is exhausted.
Having entered a human womb, he is born with tenfold wealth:
fields, land, gold, livestock, male and female slaves—therein he is reborn among these four categories of desirable things. (Uttarādhyayana 11.11–12)
He becomes one who possesses friends and kinsmen, of high birth and fair complexion; he is self-reliant, possessed of great wisdom, well-born, and endowed with fame and strength.
Having enjoyed human pleasures that are beyond reproach, he lives out his full lifespan. (Uttarādhyayana 11.3)

Having previously awakened to the pure, true Dharma and attained absolute enlightenment, and having understood that the fourfold [auspicious] opportunity is difficult to find, one should undertake self-restraint;
with karma shaken off by austerity, one becomes an eternal Siddha. (Uttarādhyayana 11.4–5)
Thus I say.
[The Immeasurable]
Do not waste your life, for it is not eternal; indeed, there is no protection for one brought low by old age.
Know this regarding people who are heedless: what harm will the uncontrolled inflict upon them?
Those men who, having taken up intoxicants, accumulate a mass of evil karma through their deeds.
Having abandoned those who walk by their side, men bound by enmity go to hell. (Utt.

117) Just as a thief caught in the act at the opening of a tunnel is punished for his own deed, so too does the evildoer suffer in this world and the next; there is no escape from deeds once they have been committed. (Utt. 118)
Having fallen into the cycle of existence for the sake of another,

whatever common karma one performs, at the time of its fruition, those relatives do not come to provide kinship. (Uttarādhyayana 11.9) One who is heedless does not find protection through wealth, neither in this world nor in the next.

Just as one who has lost his way on an island, when infinite delusion prevents him from seeing the path leading to liberation, even while he is living according to the scriptures, the wise man—alert and quick-witted—should not be complacent; for the moments are terrible and the body is frail. Like a Bhāraṇḍa bird, he should move about with vigilance. (Uttarādhyayana 12.20–21)
Moving about with circumspection, regarding whatever he perceives here as a danger,
and sustaining his life by means of whatever gain may come, he later, having fully understood, destroys all impurity.
By restraining his desires, he attains liberation, just as a horse that wears well-trained armor.
One should practice vigilantly for many years; therefore, the sage quickly attains liberation. (Utt.
12.3) He might not attain it even earlier, let alone later; this is the reproach of those who preach eternalism:
he desponds when his life is slackening and the body is overtaken by time. (Utt. 12.4)
One who is unable to quickly attain seclusion should therefore rise up, abandon sensual pleasures, and,
having understood the world with equanimity, the great sage, guarding his intake [of food], should wander heedfully.
(Uttarādhyayana 12.5) To the ascetic who wanders about, repeatedly conquering the qualities of delusion, various forms [of temptations] appear.
Unpleasant sensations touch him in various ways, yet the monk should not perceive them with his mind.
(Utt. 126) Sensations are dull and largely enticing; one should not direct the mind toward such things.
One should guard against anger, subdue pride, not resort to deceit, and abandon greed. (Utt. 127)
Those who are limited and whose doctrines are trivial are possessed by passion and hatred; they are dependent on others.
Loathing these as unrighteousness, one should seek virtues until the dissolution of the body.
Thus I say. (Uttarādhyayana 12.8)
[On Unwilling Death] In the flood of the great ocean, some alone have crossed over that which is difficult to cross.
Thereupon, one of great wisdom uttered this question:
"Two states have been declared regarding death: involuntary death and likewise voluntary death. (Uttarādhyayana 12.9–130)
For the foolish, death occurs against their will and is always involuntary; for the wise, however, it occurs with their consent and may even be voluntary at its highest degree.
Regarding this, the Great Hero has taught this first point.
Just as a fool, greedy for sensual pleasures, commits cruel deeds;
so too, one who is greedy for the enjoyments of sense-pleasures goes alone toward ruin.
"The next world has not been seen by me; this delight is visible to my own eyes. (Uttarādhyayana 13.2–3)
"These sensual pleasures have come into my hands; what of those that are past or yet to come?
Who knows whether there is another world or not? Thus the fool becomes arrogant, thinking, "I shall be together with people. (Uttarādhyayana 13.4)
Through attachment to sensual pleasures, he commits evil;
then he initiates violence against both mobile and immobile beings, whether for a purpose or without purpose, thereby harming the multitude of living beings. (Uttarādhyayana 13.5–6)
The fool who commits violence, speaks falsehood, is deceitful, slanderous, and fraudulent,
and who, while consuming liquor and meat, thinks, "This is good"— he,
intoxicated in body and speech, is greedy for wealth and women.
He accumulates defilement from both [sides], like a young snake gathering earth.
Then, afflicted by disease, he suffers as a sick man, terrified of the next world, pursued by his own karmas. (Uttarādhyayana 13.8–9)
Those places of mine in hell, and that destination of the unvirtuous,
the foolish, and those of cruel deeds, where the suffering is intense—
therein is my place of rebirth, as has been heard by me.
Going by means of improper actions, he later suffers remorse. (Utt.
141) Just as a cart-driver, having left the level high road, enters upon a rugged path and grieves when his axle breaks. (Utt. 142)
Thus, having transgressed the Dharma and embraced what is contrary to the Dharma, the fool, having fallen into the mouth of death, grieves like one whose dice have been shattered.
Then, at the end of his life, the fool trembles with fear.
One dies against one's will, like a gambler defeated by the game of dice.
This is declared to be the death of the ignorant who lack self-mastery;
now hear from me about the voluntary death of the wise. (Uttarādhyayana 14.44–45)
Even death for those of merit is as I have heard it described: serene and free from resentment, like that of the self-controlled ones who dwell in their practice.
This is not found among all monks, nor is it found among all householders.
Householders have various forms of conduct, and monks have uneven conduct. (Utt.
147) There are some monks who are superior in self-restraint to householders;
and compared to all householders, the *sādhavas* (true practitioners) are superior in self-restraint. (Utt. 148)
Neither rags nor deerskin, neither nakedness, nor matted hair, nor the patched robe, nor a shaven head—
none of these protect one who is immoral and has entered the religious life.
Like a beggar, the immoral person is not released from hell.

Whether as a mendicant or as a householder, one should perform meritorious deeds by day. (Utt. 150) A faithful layperson should practice the limbs of the householder’s code of conduct with their own body; they should observe the *poṣadha* for both fortnights and not neglect it for even a single night. (Utt. 151)
Thus, one who has undertaken the training, even while living as a householder,
is freed from the mountain of the body and goes to the world of the Yakṣas. But the monk who is restrained may belong to either of the two [orders].
Or those who have abandoned all suffering, or even gods of great power;
[they go] to the northern, delusion-free, radiant abodes, which have been successively inhabited by Yakṣas, O glorious one. (Uttarādhyayana 15.3–4)
Long-lived, possessed of supernatural power, prosperous, able to assume forms at will, appearing like those who have just been reborn, and possessing a radiance garlanded with flames—
those who have trained in self-restraint and austerity go to such stations. (Uttarādhyayana 15.5)
Whether they be mendicants or householders, those who have attained final liberation—
having heard [the teachings] from those venerable ones, the self-restrained masters of conduct, the virtuous and learned do not tremble at the end of life. (Uttarādhyayana 15.6–7)
Having weighed [the two] and grasped the distinction, the wise man, through the dharma of compassion and patience, should find peace within himself by becoming such as he is.
Then, at the appropriate time, being full of faith, he should approach the Tāliśa tree.
One should subdue the horripilation [of worldly attachment] and desire the destruction of the body.
When the time has arrived, having cast off the physical aggregate, the sage dies a death with self-control (sakāmamaraṇa), one of the three types. (Uttarādhyayana 15.9–10)
Thus I say.
[The Shorter Niyukti]
"As many men as there are who possess ignorance, they all become the source of suffering; deluded, they are repeatedly destroyed within the infinite cycle of existence.
Therefore, having observed this, the wise man should see the many paths of birth. (Uttarādhyayana 16.1)

One should personally seek the truth and cultivate compassion toward all beings. (Uttarādhyayana 16.2) Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and even one's own biological sons—these are not able to protect me when I am being tormented by my own karma. (Uttarādhyayana 16.3)
Having perceived this matter, one who possesses equanimity and right vision should abandon possessions and affection; one should not long for former acquaintances, nor for cattle,
houses, jewels, earrings, livestock, slaves, or servants.

Having abandoned all this, you will become one who can assume any form at will. (Uttarādhyayana 16.5) Neither the stationary nor the moving, nor wealth, grain, or household utensils, are able to liberate one suffering from the ripening of their own karmas. (Uttarādhyayana 16.6)
Having seen everything within oneself from every perspective, and seeing that living beings cherish their own lives, one should not kill living beings; one should desist from fear and enmity.
Seeing that grasping leads to hell, one should not take up even a blade of grass.
Having sprinkled water on his own feet, one should eat the food that has been given. (Utt.
168) In this world, some indeed believe that by knowing the teacher and not renouncing evil, one is liberated from all suffering. (Utt. 169)

Those who merely speak and do not act, though they profess [the path to] bondage and liberation, console themselves by mere verbal effort; speech does not protect the mind—whence then could there be instruction through knowledge? (Uttarādhyayana 17.0)
Sunk in their own evil deeds, these fools imagine themselves wise.

(Uttarādhyayana 17.1) Whatever beings there are in this body—whether in its color or its form—in every respect, whether by mind, speech, or body, they all originate from suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 17.2)
They have wandered for a long time through this infinite cycle of existence;
therefore, seeing in every direction, one should wander heedfully. Having cast off what is external and what is above, one should never desire anything at all.

For the sake of exhausting former karma, one should cast off this body. Having detached from the cause of karma, awaiting the [proper] time, one should wander as a mendicant; having obtained what has been prepared for the sake of alms and food, one should consume it. (Uttarādhyayana 17.4–5)
One should not form attachments; being restrained through right conduct and free from deceit, like a bird taking its wing, one should wander without looking back.
One who is conscientious regarding the search for food and possessed of a sense of shame should wander without fixed residence in a village.
Being heedful among the heedless, he should seek alms.
Thus spoke he who possesses unsurpassed knowledge, the unsurpassed seer, the bearer of unsurpassed knowledge and vision— the Arhat, the son of the Jñātṛ clan, the Blessed One, as declared at Vaiśālī.
Thus I say.
[The Chapter on the Sheep]
Just as if someone, for the sake of a certain person, were to nourish a ram,
giving it barley and fodder, and rear it within his own courtyard; then,
when that [ram] has been fed and grown, its belly becomes full.
While his body is fat and large, he longs for the command;
as long as the command does not come, he lives in misery, but once the command has arrived, he is eaten after his head has been cut off. (Uttarādhyayana 180–181)
Just as that ram, though intended for the sacrifice, thus fancies itself dear,
so the fool, longing for hellish life, acts.
The fool is a violator, a speaker of falsehood, and a deceiver on the path.
O Mother, what indeed can a thief take from one who has already given away his food?

What can a rogue take from one who is greedy for women and sensual objects, who possesses great violence and possessions, who consumes liquor and meat, and who is arrogant toward others? (Uttarādhyayana 18.3–4)
And those who eat the dregs of food from the feet, those with swollen bellies, and those with blood in their eyes, long for life in hell, just as one longs for a camel or a wild ass.
Having enjoyed seats, beds, vehicles, wealth, and sensual pleasures... [Uttarādhyayana 18.5]

Having left behind wealth that is difficult to acquire and having accumulated much dust [of karma], the living being, burdened by its actions and devoted only to the present, grieves at the end of life when the future has already arrived. (Utt. 18.6–7)
When their life-span is exhausted and they have fallen from their bodies, those foolish ones who cause violence go helplessly toward the direction of the Asuras, into darkness. (Utt.
188) Just as a man might lose a thousand [coins] for the sake of a single *kākiṇī*.
Having eaten unripe mangoes, the king lost his kingdom. (Utt.
189) In this way, human pleasures are a thousandfold less than divine pleasures; moreover, the lifespan and the pleasures in heaven are even greater. (Utt. 190)
Many are the years and ships; know that the lifespan of those of dull wit is less than a hundred years.
Just as three merchants set out, taking their capital with them... [Uttarādhyayana 19.1]
"One person gains a profit here; another has come with his original capital. (Utt.
19.2) "Another has even lost his capital and returned;
this is a comparison regarding trade for a merchant. Know that it is the same in the case of the Dharma. (Utt. 19.3)

Human birth is the root; the gain of the state of a god is through the cutting away of that root for living beings. The states of hell and of animals are certain. For the fool, there are two destinies: misfortune and slaughter as their root. (Uttarādhyayana 19.4)
Whether one attains the state of a god or the state of a human, that which is conquered by one who is free from greed and deceit—by conquering that, one becomes oneself [a victor];
for one who has gone to either of the two miserable states, the path back is difficult to find even after a very long time. (Uttarādhyayana 19.5–6)
Thus, having observed living beings and weighed the fool against the wise man, they depart from this root [of existence], those who enter the human womb.
(Uttarādhyayana 19.7) Those men who, through various trainings, observe the vows of householders...

Living beings who have truly fulfilled their karmic duties indeed enter a human womb. (Uttarādhyayana 19.8) But those whose training is extensive, who have transcended the root [of worldly existence], who are virtuous and distinguished, go to the state of the gods without despair. (Uttarādhyayana 19.9)
Having thus understood the undaunted monk and the householder,
how indeed could one who is being conquered not know that which is to be conquered? When being conquered, he does not realize it—
just as one might measure a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass by comparing it to the ocean.
Thus are human pleasures compared to the pleasures of the gods.
These pleasures are as small as the tip of a blade of grass; when life is completely cut short, for what purpose would one not strive for security from bondage? (Uttarādhyayana 20.1–2)
In this world, for one who has desisted from sensual pleasures, no harm occurs to their own welfare;
yet, having heard the path that leads to liberation, he who falls away from it again is at fault.
In this world, for one who has desisted from sensual pleasures, no harm occurs to their own welfare.
"O Goddess, I have heard that through the restraint of the body one becomes a deity. (Utt.
20.4) Where there is supreme power, splendor, fame, beauty, long life, and happiness among humans, there he is reborn. (Utt. 20.5)
Behold the foolishness of the fool who, having abandoned the Dharma and embraced unrighteousness,
finds delight in what is contrary to the Dharma and is reborn in the hells.
Behold the wisdom of the wise man who follows the true Dharma.

Having abandoned unrighteousness, one who is established in righteousness is reborn among the gods. (Uttarādhyayana 207) Having weighed the state of the fool against that of the wise, the sage abandons the state of the fool and pursues the state of the wise. (Uttarādhyayana 208)
Thus I say.
— [The Chapter on the Followers of Kapila]
In this unstable and non-eternal saṃsāra, which is filled with suffering,

what indeed should one do by way of karma so that I may not go to an evil rebirth? (Uttarādhyayana 209) Having abandoned former attachments, one should not form any affection toward anything whatsoever.
The monk is liberated from hatred and from those things that cause affection, as well as from faults and malice.

Then, endowed with knowledge and vision, for the welfare and ultimate benefit of all living beings, and for their sake of liberation, the supreme sage, free from delusion, speaks. (Uttarādhyayana 210–211)
A monk should utterly abandon all bonds and strife of such a kind;
seeing through all things born of sensual desire, he is not defiled.
[One who is] despondent due to the fault of longing for enjoyments and wealth, and whose wisdom is elevated toward what is beneficial and the ultimate good—Utt. 212.
The fool, the dull-witted, and the deluded are caught like a fly in phlegm. (Utt.
21.3) These sensual pleasures are difficult to abandon and are not easily renounced by men lacking fortitude;
yet there are well-conducted saints who cross over that which is uncrossable, like merchants [crossing the sea]. (Utt. 21.4)
"Some ascetics, speaking thus, being ignorant of the slaughter of living beings, go to hell—fools and deluded by sinful views.
(Uttarajjhāyā 21.5) "One should certainly not sanction the slaughter of living beings; [only then] might one ever be liberated from all sufferings. (Uttarajjhāyā 21.6)
Thus it has been declared by the teachers, by whom this dharma of the virtuous has been proclaimed:
"One should not kill living beings; such a person is called 'one who is established in self-restraint' (samīti).
Then his sinful karma flows away like water from dry land. (Uttarādhyayana 21.6–7)
One should not inflict punishment upon those living beings—whether mobile by name or stationary—with mind, speech, or body.
Having understood the pure ways of seeking alms, a monk should establish himself therein. (Uttarādhyayana 21.8)
One should eat the alms-food given by a wife; one should not be greedy for savory flavors. (Utt.
219) One should consume only coarse things: cold rice, old groats, or perhaps *bukkasā*, *pulāka*, or barley-flour paste (*manthu*), using these merely for the sake of sustaining life. (Utt. 220)
Those who practice the science of marks, dreams, and bodily omens are certainly not called ascetics; thus it has been declared by the teachers.
Having abandoned the life here [in this world], they have fallen away from the application of meditative concentration.
Greedily attached to the taste of sensual pleasures, they are reborn in the bodies of Asuras.
Having transmigrated even from there, they wander through the cycle of existence for a long time;
for those smeared with much karma, enlightenment is very difficult to attain. (Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 22.22–23)
"Even if one were to give this entire world, complete in its fullness, to a single person, even by that he would not be satisfied; thus, this self is difficult to satisfy.
(Uttarādhyayana 224) "As is gain, so is greed; from gain, greed increases."
A task that takes three months is not finished even in ten million years.
One should not be infatuated with rākṣasīs who have breasts like goiters and many minds;
having lured a man, they sport with him as if with slaves. (Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 225–226)
One should not seek intimacy with women; the homeless renunciant should abandon women.
Having understood the wholesome Dharma, a monk should establish himself therein.
Thus has this Dharma been proclaimed by Kapila, who possesses pure wisdom.
Those who practice [this] and those who will practice it— by them both worlds are propitiated.
Thus I say.
Having descended from the world of the gods, reborn in the human world with his deluding karma stilled, he remembers his former birth. (Uttarādhyayana 22.9)
"O Blessed One, I go forth, having established my son in the kingdom; King Namī, a self-enlightened one (Svayaṃbuddha), renounces the world for the unsurpassed Dharma.
Having entered the excellent inner apartments of that place resembling the world of the gods, he enjoys supreme pleasures."
Having enjoyed [them], King Namī, awakened, renounces enjoyments.
Having abandoned Mithilā with its towns and people, its army, elephants, and entire retinue, the Blessed One went forth and remained alone in solitude. (Uttarādhyayana 23.1–2)
When the royal sage Nami was departing for renunciation, Mithilā became filled with a great clamor;
[the people] rose up before the royal sage at that supreme place of renunciation. (Uttarādhyayana 23.3)
Sakra, in the form of a brahmin, spoke these words:
"O sir! Why is it that today in Mithilā, dreadful sounds mingled with a great clamor are heard from the palaces and the houses? (Utt. 234–235)
Having heard this matter, urged by reasons and causes, the royal sage Namī then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods:
"In Mithilā, there is a grove of *vaccha* trees, cool and delightful. (Uttarādhyayana 23.6)
"Always providing leaves, flowers, fruits, and shade, it is of great benefit to many.
When this beautiful sanctuary is being carried away by the wind, these birds, distressed and without refuge, cry out, 'O, our father! (Uttarādhyayana 23.7–8)
Having heard this matter, and being urged by reasons and causes,
the Lord of the Gods then spoke thus to the royal sage Nami:
"This fire and this wind— this palace is burning."
“O Blessed One, why do you not look back at the inner apartments?
Having heard this matter, the royal sage Nami, impelled by the reason and cause [of his renunciation], then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 240–241.
We dwell happily, we live happily, for us there is nothing whatsoever;
while Mithilā is burning, nothing of mine burns. (Uttarādhyayana 24.2) For the monk who has abandoned son and wife, who is free from worldly activity—
Nothing dear is found, nor is anything undear found. (Utt.
243) Indeed, there is much blessing for the sage, the homeless monk, who is liberated from all things and perceives solitude. (Utt. 244)
Having heard this matter, the lord of the gods, urged by reasons and causes, then spoke thus to the royal sage Nami: "Having built a wall,
as well as gate-towers and watchtowers..."
"O Kṣatriya, when the arrows are pulled from the roots, then you may go. Having heard this matter, urged by reasons and causes,
the royal sage Namī then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods.
Having made faith the city, ascetic restraint its threshold, patience its skillful rampart— triple-guarded and difficult to assail—
and having made exertion the bow and vigilance its constant string, Utt. 248.
Having made wisdom his sword, one should strike down the enemy with truth;
having pierced through the armor of karma with the arrow of austerity, the sage, free from conflict, is liberated from existence. (Uttarādhyayana 24.9–10)
Having heard this matter, and being urged by reasons and causes,
the Lord of the Gods then spoke thus to the royal sage Nami:
"After having caused palaces and increasing mansions to be built..."
"And [the distance] to the tip of a hair; then you shall go, O Kṣatriya. (Utt.
252) Having heard this matter, urged by reasons and causes, the royal sage Namī then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods. (Utt. 253)
He indeed creates doubt who builds a house on the path; wherever one intends to go, there one should build a permanent dwelling. Having heard this matter, he was urged by reasons and causes.
Then the Lord of Devas spoke thus to the royal sage Tāo:

"O Kṣatriya, having brought security to the city against those who touch [with stealth], those who steal by hair-pulling, and those who break through knots [of wealth], you may then depart. (Utt. 255–256)
Having heard this matter, and being urged by reasons and causes, the royal seer Namī then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods:
"Indeed, an unjust punishment is frequently inflicted upon men. (Uttarādhyayana 257)
"In this world, those who do not act [sinfully] are bound, while the person who acts is released. (Utt.
258) Having heard this matter, urged by reason and cause, the Lord of Devas then spoke thus to the royal sage Nami: (Utt. 259)
"O Lord of Men! Those kings who do not bow down to you—having brought them under your control, O Kṣatriya, you shall then depart. Having heard this matter, [the king] was urged by reasons and causes.
Then the royal sage Namī spoke this to the Lord of the Gods:
“One who might conquer a thousand times a thousand men in a battle difficult to win, yet conquers only himself—he has achieved the supreme victory. (Uttarādhyayana 261–262)
Fight with yourself alone; what is the use of fighting with external foes?
By conquering oneself in this way, one attains happiness.
(Uttarādhyayana 26.3) [One must conquer] the five senses, anger, pride, deceit, and likewise greed.

"The self alone is indeed difficult to conquer; when the self is conquered, everything is conquered. (Utt. 264) Having heard this matter, urged by reasons and motives, the Lord of the Devas then spoke thus to the royal sage Nami: (Utt. 265)
"O Kṣatriya, after performing extensive sacrifices, feeding śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, giving gifts, eating [the sacrificial food], and [honoring] those of noble birth— only then do you go [to heaven].
Having heard this matter, he was urged by reasons and causes.
Then the royal sage Namī spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods:
"Though one were to give a thousand times a thousand cows month after month, self-restraint is better for him than even the non-giving of anything. (Utt. 267–268)
Having heard this matter, and being urged by reasons and causes,
the Lord of the Gods then spoke thus to the royal sage Nami:
"Having abandoned your formidable hermitage, you seek another hermitage."
"Right here, O lord of men, become one who observes the fast-day (poṣadha).
Having heard this matter, urged by reasons and causes, the royal sage Namī then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods: Uttarādhyayana 270–271.

"But a fool who eats with the tip of a blade of kusa grass month after month is not worth even a sixteenth part of one who has well-proclaimed the Dharma. Having heard this matter, he was urged by reasons and causes.
Then the Lord of the Gods spoke thus to the royal sage Tāo:
"O Kṣatriya, after increasing your silver, gold, jewels, pearls, bronze, cloth, vehicles, and treasury, you may then depart. (Uttarādhyayana 273–274)
Having heard this matter, urged by reasons and causes, the royal sage Namī then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods:
"Suppose there were mountains of gold and silver... (Uttarādhyayana 27.5)

There might indeed be as many immeasurable Mount Kailāsa mountains as there are for a greedy man, yet his desire would not be satisfied by them; for desire is like space, truly infinite. (Uttarādhyayana 27.6)
"Land, rice, barley, gold, and cattle—even when all these are complete, they are not enough for one person; thus knowing this, one should practice austerity.
Having heard this matter, he was urged by reasons and causes.
The Lord of Devas spoke thus to the royal seer Tāo:
"O King, you renounce pleasures that are extraordinary and wonderful;
yet you long for desires that do not exist, and you mock yourself with such a resolve. (Utt. 278–279)
Having heard this matter, urged by reasons and causes, the royal sage Namī then spoke thus to the Lord of the Gods:
"Sensual pleasures are a dart; sensual pleasures are poison; sensual pleasures are like venomous serpents."
Those who long for sensual pleasures go unwillingly to a miserable state.
Through anger they go downward; through pride they go to a low rebirth; deceit leads to an obstacle; from greed comes fear on both sides. (Uttarādhyayana 281–282)
Having cast off his brahmin form and manifested the state of Indra, he paid homage while offering praise with these sweet words:
"O, your anger has been conquered! O, your pride has been defeated! (Utt. 283)
Oh, how deceptive is illusion! Oh, how overpowering is greed! (Utt.
284) Oh, your uprightness is excellent! Oh, your gentleness is excellent! Oh, your supreme forbearance! Oh, your supreme liberation! (Utt. 285)
"In this world you are supreme, O Blessed One! Later you will become supreme;
you shall attain the state that is the highest among the high, the perfection free from passion.
Thus he praised the royal sage with the highest faith. (Uttarādhyayana 28.6)
Performing circumambulations, Śakra paid homage again and again.
Having bowed at the feet of the best of sages, which were marked with the sign of the wheel, he ascended into the sky, adorned with swinging, swaying earrings and a diadem.

Namī humbled himself before his own self, having been exhorted by Śakra; having abandoned his home and Vaidehī, he devoted himself to the ascetic life. Thus do the fully awakened ones act—the wise and the discerning.
They turn away from enjoyments, just as Namī the royal sage did.
Thus I say.
Just as a leaf on a tree turns yellow and falls when its time has come, even so is the life of human beings; therefore, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a single moment! (Uttarādhyayana 291)

"Just as a drop of water hanging from the tip of a blade of grass remains for only a short time, even so is the life of human beings; therefore, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Uttarādhyayana 29.2). Life is transient, and existence is beset by many dangers.
Shake off the dust accumulated in the past; do not be negligent of the present moment, O Gautama! (Utt.
293) Human existence is indeed difficult to attain for all living beings, even over a long period of time; moreover, the fruition of karma is intense.
Do not be negligent of the present moment, O Gautama! (Utt. 294)
Having entered the earth-body, a living being may dwell there for an extremely long time—indeed, for a period exceeding a *saṅkhā*.
O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a single moment!
Having entered the water-body, a living being may likewise dwell there for an extremely long time.
Having calculated the time, O Goyama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt.
296) A living being who has entered the fire-body may dwell there for a maximum duration of incalculable time;
O Goyama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt. 297)
Having entered the body of the air-element, a living being may dwell there for a maximum duration of countless eons;
O Gautama, do not be negligent even for a single moment!
Having entered the body of the vegetable-element, a living being may likewise dwell there for a maximum duration... [of countless eons].
O Goyama! Do not be negligent for even a moment regarding this time that is infinite and difficult to endure.
(Uttarādhyayana 299) Even when a living being has entered the body of a two-sensed organism, it may dwell there for a maximum duration of a finite number of years.
O Goyama! Do not be negligent for even a moment. (Uttarādhyayana 300)
Having entered the body of a two-sensed being, a soul may dwell there for a maximum period of a finite number of years;
O Goyama, do not be negligent for even a single moment!
Having entered the body of a four-sensed being, a soul may likewise dwell there for a maximum period... [of a finite number of years].
O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment, even for a calculable length of time! (Utt.
302) Even if a soul were to enter the bodies of the five senses, it would dwell there for at most seven or eight births; O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt. 303)
A god or a hell-being may remain for a single birth at most; O Gautama, do not be negligent even for a moment!
Thus one wanders through the cycle of existence by means of wholesome and unwholesome karmas. (Uttarādhyayana 30.4)
A living being is full of negligence; therefore, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt. 305) Even having attained human birth, the state of being an Ārya is difficult to find again.
There are many barbarians and foreigners; therefore, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt. 306)
Even having attained the state of an Ārya, the possession of unimpaired five senses is indeed rare;

for the impairment of the senses is seen. O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Uttarādhyayana 307) Even if he should obtain the state of having unimpaired five senses, the hearing of the supreme Dharma is indeed rare.
O Gautama, do not be negligent regarding the time, while people are serving false doctrines. (Utt.
308) Even having attained the supreme faith, it is difficult to find again among people who serve falsehood; O Gautama, do not be negligent regarding the time. (Utt. 309)
Even for those who have faith in the Dharma, it is difficult to experience it with the body;
they are infatuated here by the qualities of sensual pleasure. O Gautama, do not be negligent regarding the teaching! Your body is wasting away, and your hair is turning white.
His strength in digestion wanes; O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt.
311) Your body decays, and your hair becomes white; his strength of sight wanes; O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt. 312)
Your body decays; your hair becomes white;
and your strength of smell also diminishes. O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment!
Your body decays; your hair becomes white.
If the power of your tongue fails, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt.
314) Your body decays, and your hair becomes white; if the power of your touch fails, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt. 315)
Your body decays, your hair becomes white, and all your strength wanes; O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment!
Aridity, boils, dysentery, and various ailments afflict you.
It crumbles and destroys that body; therefore, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt.
317) Sever your own attachment, as the water leaves the autumnal lotus;
when one is free from all attachment, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Utt. 318)
Having abandoned wealth and wife, you have indeed gone forth into the homeless state;
do not, O Gautama, return again to what has been vomited out! Do not be negligent regarding the teaching!
Having cast aside friends and kinsmen, as well as a vast accumulation of wealth and grain...
Do not seek a second [birth], O Gautama! Do not be negligent regarding the *samaya*.
(Utt. 320) Indeed, the Jina is no longer seen today; those who point out the path are seen in great numbers.
Now that the leaders are gone, O Gautama! Do not be negligent regarding the *samaya*. (Utt. 321)
Having cleared the path of thorns, you have descended upon a great road;
go along that path which has been purified. O Gautama, do not be negligent regarding the teaching!
Like a weak burden-carrier, do not venture onto a rugged road.
"Later there will be remorse; therefore, O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment!
You have indeed crossed the great ocean; why then do you stand having reached the shore?
Hasten to go to the further shore; O Gautama, do not be negligent for even a moment! (Uttarādhyayana 323–324)

Having cast off the multitude of bodies, O Goyama, you go to perfection, to the secure, auspicious, and unsurpassed world; O Goyama, do not be negligent regarding the teaching! When the Buddha has attained final liberation, whether wandering through villages or cities, he remains self-restrained.
One should cultivate the path of peace; O Gautama, do not be negligent regarding the right doctrine!

Having reflected upon the well-spoken words of the Buddha, which are beautifully articulated and adorned with the eightfold purification, Gautama severed passion and hatred and attained the state of perfection.
Thus I say.
— [The Veneration of the Learned]
I shall explain the conduct of the houseless monk who is liberated from all attachments; listen to me regarding this sequence. (Utt.
328) Furthermore, he who is devoid of discernment, stubborn, greedy, and unrestrained—
One who speaks excessively, being undisciplined and lacking in learning; (Utt.
329) Furthermore, there are five conditions by which one does not receive instruction: through arrogance, anger, negligence, illness, and laziness. (Utt. 330)
Indeed, by eight conditions one is called "virtuous in training": he is not arrogant, always self-controlled, and does not speak of the vital organs [of others].
He is neither devoid of virtue nor of bad character, and he should not be excessively lustful.

One who is free from anger and devoted to truth is called "one whose conduct is disciplined. (Uttarajjhāyā 332) But a restrained one who conducts himself according to fourteen points is called "undisciplined," and he does not go to Nirvāṇa. (Uttarajjhāyā 333)
One who is prone to anger constantly becomes agitated and creates persistent enmity;
even when treated with friendship, he reviles others, and having acquired sacred learning, he becomes intoxicated by it.
He is a consumer of his own sins and is prone to anger even toward his friends.
He speaks evil even to his dear friend in private. (Utt.
335) One who is boastful, difficult to please, stubborn, greedy, unrestrained, ungenerous, and incompetent is called "undisciplined. (Utt. 336)
Indeed, by fifteen points one is said to be well-disciplined:
living modestly, being steady, free from deceit, and lacking curiosity; he does not criticize others excessively, nor does he create obstacles. (Uttarādhyayana 33.7)
Being treated with affection, he fears [the loss of that favor]; having acquired learning, he does not become arrogant.
He does not squander his wealth on sinful things, nor does he become angry even with a friend who is unpleasant; in private, he speaks only what is beneficial to that friend. (Uttarādhyayana 338–339)
One who avoids quarrels and tumults,
who is wise, of noble birth, modest, and withdrawn [from worldly affairs], is called well-disciplined.
He who always dwells under the authority of his teacher, being diligent and observant of the prescribed practices, is so described.

One who acts kindly and speaks kindly shall attain the training. (Uttarādhyayana 341) Just as milk poured into a conch shell shines beautifully on both sides, so too in a learned monk do the Dharma, his fame, and his learning shine forth. (Uttarādhyayana 342)
Just as a well-bred Kamboja horse might be a noble steed preeminent in speed, so too is one who is very learned.
Just like a hero of firm prowess mounted upon a well-bred horse... (Uttarādhyayana 343).
With the roar of both [elephants], so it is with the one of great learning. (Utt.
344) Just as a sixty-year-old elephant, powerful and irresistible, surrounded by female elephants, so it is with the one of great learning. (Utt. 345)
Just as a bull with sharp horns, a well-developed hump,
and a radiant appearance shines as the leader of the herd, so does the one who is learned shine.
Just as a tiger with sharp fangs, fierce and difficult to overcome, [stands out], so too is the one who is learned.
Just as the lion is the foremost among beasts, so is the one of great learning;
just as Vāsudeva, who wields the conch, the discus, and the mace, is an invincible warrior, so is the one of great learning. (Uttarādhyayana 34.7–8)
Just as he is a universal monarch ruling over the four quarters, possessing great power and lord of the fourteen jewels, so too is the one of great learning.
Just as he is the thousand-eyed one, wielder of the thunderbolt, the destroyer of cities (Purandara).
Sakra, the lord of the gods, is thus called "the one of great learning.
Just as the sun, when it rises, destroys the darkness and blazes with its brilliance, so too is he called "the one of great learning. (Uttarādhyayana 350–351)
Just as the moon, the lord of the stars, surrounded by the constellations, is full on the night of the full moon, so is the one who possesses great learning.
Just as a storehouse of grain is well-guarded, so is the one who possesses the limbs of equanimity.
Thus is the one possessed of great learning, filled with various kinds of knowledge. (Utt.
353) Just as the Jambū tree named Sudarśanā, belonging to the god Anādṛta, is the most excellent among trees, so is the one possessed of great learning. (Utt. 354)

Just as the Sītā river, flowing from the Nīlavanta mountains, is the foremost among rivers that flow into the ocean, so is the one possessed of great learning. Just as Mount Mandara is the greatest among the mountains, so is he.
Just as the ocean Samudra-Svayambhūramaṇa is filled with various medicinal herbs and possesses inexhaustible waters, so too is one who is learned (bahussuya).
Just as that ocean Samudra-Svayambhūramaṇa is replete with various jewels, so too is one who is learned. (Uttarādhyayana 356–357)
Like the deep ocean, they are difficult to fathom, unassailable, impossible for anyone to overcome, and hard to conquer;
they are protectors filled with vast learning.
Having exhausted their karma, they have gone to the supreme state.
Therefore, one who seeks the highest goal should study the sacred scripture (suya),
by which one may bring both oneself and others to perfection (siddhi).
Thus I say.
[Harikeśin]

Born in a family of *śvapacas*, the sage named Hariesabala was a monk who had conquered his senses and possessed the highest virtues; he was perfect in the restraints of walking, eating, speaking, and excretion. (Uttarādhyayana 360)
Victory to him who is restrained in taking and laying down [his belongings], who is self-controlled and well-composed;
who guards his mind, guards his speech, guards his body, and has conquered his senses—the mendicant who has arrived at the sacrificial ground of the Brahmin for alms. (Uttarādhyayana 361–362)
Seeing him approaching,
emaciated by austerity, with but a few worn-out robes and requisites, the ignoble ones mock him—
those who are arrogant because of their birth, violent, and whose senses are unsubdued. (Uttarādhyayana 363)
The foolish ones, practitioners of unchaste conduct, spoke these words:

"From where does this one come, of such radiant appearance? He is dark, terrifying, with a protruding nose, clad in tattered rags, and like a dust-demon; he wears a rag from a rubbish heap around his neck. (Utt. 364–365)
"Who are you in this place so difficult to behold? With what hope have you come here?
You are clad in rags and have become like a demon of dust; go away! Why do you stand here?
The yakṣa dwelling there in the tinduka tree was moved by compassion for that great sage.
Having covered his own body, he uttered these words:
"I am an ascetic, restrained, a practitioner of celibacy, abstaining from wealth, grain, and possessions;
I have come here for the sake of food at the time of alms-gathering for one who has gone forth to others. (Utt. 367–368)
"It is being distributed, eaten, and enjoyed; know this, O son, that there is abundant food for you all, but I am one who lives by begging; let the ascetic receive whatever remains. (Utt.
369) "The meal for the Brahmins has been prepared, it is ready here, served for a single party."
"We will not give you such food and drink; why have you stayed here? [The mendicant replied:
"The kāśa grass sows seeds on dry land, and likewise with hope in low-lying places.
With this very faith, give to me; for this field indeed brings merit. (Uttarādhyayana 370–371)
We know the fields in this world where sown seeds grow as merit:
those brāhmaṇas who are endowed with noble birth and learning; they indeed are the most excellent fields.
But for those in whom there is anger, pride, and violence, as well as falsehood, taking what is not given, and possessiveness— [they are not such fields].
Those Brahmins are devoid of both noble birth and learning; those fields, however, are very auspicious.
O sirs! You are merely bearers of words here, yet you do not understand their meaning, even though you have studied the Vedas.
Sages wander through those very fields which are truly beautiful. (Uttarādhyayana 373–374)
Speaking in opposition to those who live the holy life, what indeed do you say in our presence?
"Let even this food and drink perish; we shall not give it to you, O Nirgrantha! (Utt.
375) [But this is said] of one who is well-composed in the *samitis*, guarded by the *guptis*, and whose senses are subdued.
"If he had not given me what was worthy of seeking, how could I have obtained the reward for my sacrifices today?
Who here are the warriors, the priests, or the teachers, along with the disciples, who would seize him by the throat and drag him away, striking him with a staff or a fruit? (Uttarādhyayana 376–377)

Having heard the words of the overseers, many youths there rushed forth with sticks, whips, and even goads, and gathered together, they beat that seer. (Uttarādhyayana 378) There, the daughter of the King of Kosala was present, named Bhadrā, whose limbs were beyond reproach.
Seeing him being tormented, Sañjaya pacified the angry prince. (Utt.

379) "He who was given by the king under the compulsion of the gods and against his will, whom that sage—who is saluted by lords of men and lords of gods—has now rejected, he is this very person. (Utt. 380)
This indeed is that one of fierce austerity, the great-souled one, the conqueror of the senses,
the self-restrained practitioner of celibacy, who at that time did not desire me even though I was being offered by my father, King Kosalika himself.
He is of great fame, of great majesty, of formidable vows, and of terrible prowess.
"Do not despise this one who is not to be despised; lest he consume you all with his fiery power. (Utt.
382) Having heard these words of hers—words that were faithful, auspicious, and well-spoken—the Yakṣas restrained the princes for the sake of serving the seer. (Utt. 383)
Those of terrible form, stationed in the sky, there strike down that people; seeing them with mangled bodies vomiting blood, Bhaddā spoke this again:
"Dig up the mountain with your nails, chew it with your teeth! (Utt. 384)
"Kill this one who is born with his feet! Strike down the monk whom you despise! (Utt.
385) "He is like a venomous serpent, a great ascetic, a master of high penance, formidable in vows and terrible in prowess.
Like a host of foot-soldiers leaping into a fire, those who strike a monk at the time of his meal [perish]. (Utt. 386)
"Come to this refuge with your heads, you all together;
if you desire life or wealth, for even when angry, he could burn up the world.
(Uttarādhyayana 387) With their backs and upper bodies bent down, their arms outstretched, they remain motionless.

With their bellies split open, vomiting blood, their tongues and eyes protruding from their mouths, and having become like pieces of wood—seeing them, that brahmin was dejected and despondent; together with his wife, he propitiated the seer, saying:
"O Venerable One, forgive our mockery and our censure! (Uttarādhyayana 388–389)
"O Bhante, forgive that for which I was mocked by fools, deluded, and ignorant!
Sages are exceedingly gracious; indeed, sages do not become subject to anger.
Neither in the past, nor now, nor in the future, have I harbored any malice in my mind."
"The yakṣas indeed performed service for them; therefore, these princes have been struck down. (Utt.
391) "Knowing both worldly affairs and the Dharma, O you of vast wisdom, do not be angry with us.
We, together with all our people, have come to take refuge at your feet. (Utt. 392)
"Welcome to you, O fortunate one! We do not refuse you anything;
please eat the boiled rice mixed with various seasonings.
I have this abundant food here; eat it as a favor to us. (Utt. 393)
"So be it," he replied, accepting food and drink; for at the conclusion of his month-long fast, the Great Soul [partook]. (Utt.
394) There, a rain of fragrant water and flowers fell, and a divine shower of wealth rained down; the gods beat their drums in the sky and proclaimed, "O, what a gift! (Utt. 395)
Indeed, the excellence of austerity is clearly seen, yet no distinction of birth is seen at all in the sage Hariesasāhu, son of a Śvapāka, who possesses such great power and majesty.
O Brahmins! Why do you, as practitioners of fire-worship, seek purification externally with water?
"That external purification which those who have entered the path practice is not declared by the wise to be well-performed. (Utt.

397) "Touching kusa grass, sacrificial wood, straw, and fire, and touching water in the evening and in the morning, the dull-witted, while harming living beings and creatures, once again commit evil. (Utt. 398)
"How should a monk conduct himself? How may we conquer? How may we cast off evil deeds?
Tell us, Sañjaya, you who are honored by the yakṣas: how do those skilled in dharma declare what is well-spoken?
"By not initiating violence against the six classes of living beings, and by not practicing falsehood or taking what is not given..."
Having fully understood possessions, women, pride, and deceit, they wander as self-controlled ones.

Well-restrained by the five restraints, not longing for life in this world, having renounced their bodies and cast them off with purity, they achieve the great victory, the sacrifice most highly praised. (Uttarādhyayana 400–401)
What is your fire, or what is your sacrificial hearth? What are your ladles, and what is your ritual vessel?
Who are these monks of yours, and with what oblation do you offer sacrifice to the fire? Austerity is the fire;
living beings are the sacrificial hearth; the yogas are the ladles; and the body is the ritual vessel. (Uttarādhyayana 32.2)
"Self-restraint, yoga, and tranquility are my sacrifice; I perform this offering praised by the seers. (Utt.
403) "Who are those lakes for you, and what are those holy bathing places? In what bath do you cast off your impurity?
O Sañjaya, honored by the yakṣas, tell us this; we wish to know from your presence. (Utt. 404)

In the Dhamma, the lake, the Brahma-faring, the sanctuary, which is undisturbed and has the appearance of self-conviction—having bathed therein, stainless and purified, having become thoroughly cooled, I abandon hatred.
This is the bath seen by the wise; it is the great bath praised by the seers.
Where the great seers, bathed, stainless, and pure, have attained the supreme state. Thus I say.
(Uttarādhyayana 406)
Defeated by birth due to the arising of passion, he indeed made a vow at Hastināpura;
Bambhadatta was reborn from a lotus clump in the womb of Culaṇī. (Uttarādhyayana 407)
Sambhūta was born in Kampilla, while Citta was born in Purimatāla into a great merchant family; having heard the Dharma, he went forth into the religious life.
Then, in the city of Kampilla, both Citta and Sambhūta met together.
They explain to one another the ripening of the fruits of happiness and suffering. (Utt.
409) The wheel-turning monarch Mahiddhi and the highly renowned Bambhadatta, out of great respect for their brother, spoke these words: (Utt. 410)
"We two brothers were once subjects to one another's will, devoted to each other, seeking each other's welfare;
we were slaves in Daśārṇa and deer in the Kāliñjara mountain. (Uttarādhyayana 4.11)
We were swans on the banks of the Mayaṅga, and we were dog-cookers in the land of Kāśī;
and we were gods in the world of the gods—highly powerful.
This is our sixth birth, which has occurred without us being separated from one another.
O King, those karmas produced by worldly attachment that you previously contemplated have resulted in this separation through the ripening of their fruit.
Karmas produced by truth and compassion were performed by me in the past.
"We enjoy these today; how indeed could even Citta have been otherwise? (Utt.
415) "All well-performed deeds bear fruit for men; there is no escape from committed karmas.
Through wealth and through the highest sensual pleasures, my self has been nourished by the fruits of merit. (Utt. 416)
"Know, Sambhūta, that he is of great majesty and great power, endowed with the fruit of merit;
know Citta to be exactly the same, O King! His splendor and glory are likewise abundant.
Possessing great wealth and beauty, and abundant in speech, his verses are sung in the midst of the assembly of men."
"Since you, O monk, endowed with the virtues of moral conduct, have been born here as a victorious ascetic;

[therefore,] enjoy this house—which possesses high towers, honey-sweetness, and the *bambha* [fragrance], which has well-constructed and delightful dwellings, and which abounds in various riches—endowed with the five qualities of Pañcāla. (Uttarādhyayana 418–419)

"O monk, enjoy these pleasures while surrounded by women, with dances, songs, and instrumental music; for I find this life of renunciation to be painful. [To him] the lord of men, who was greedy for the qualities of sensual pleasure and possessed an affection formed by former intimacy—
Devoted to the Dharma and contemplating his own welfare, Citta uttered these words:
"All singing is mere lamentation; all dancing is a mockery.
All ornaments are a burden; all sensual pleasures bring only suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 421–422)

O King, that happiness found among those who delight the foolish and bring misery—the qualities of sensual pleasure—is not equal to the happiness of those monks who have renounced desires, who possess the wealth of austerity, and who are established in the virtues of moral conduct.
O Lord of Men, the birth of those men who have gone to the two miserable states is the lowest of births for humans; such is the birth of the dog-cookers (Sovāga).
"Where we were outcasts to all people, we lived in the dwellings of dog-cookers (Sōvāgas).

Having attained this thirtieth birth, we have been born in the dwellings of dog-cookers, objects of contempt for the whole world; yet these are the results of deeds performed in the past. (Uttarādhyayana 424–425)
O King, you are now one of great majesty and vast power, endowed with the fruits of merit;
yet, having abandoned these transient enjoyments, go forth into the homeless life for the sake of the Self.
O King, in this life which is so insecure, do not fail to perform meritorious deeds with great diligence.
He grieves when brought to the mouth of death for not having practiced the Dharma in the next world.
Just as a lion here seizes a deer, Death leads away a man at the time of his end; neither mother, nor father, nor brother can share his burden at that time. (Uttarādhyayana 4.27–28)
Neither his kinsmen, nor his circle of friends, nor his sons, nor his relatives can share his suffering;
he alone must experience it himself. Karma follows only the doer.
Having abandoned bipeds and quadrupeds, as well as fields, house, wealth, and grain—all of it— (Uttarādhyayana 4.29).
Helpless, one goes to another existence—whether beautiful or wretched—driven by the seed of one's own karma. (Utt.
430) When that solitary, empty body has entered the funeral pyre and been consumed by fire, the wife, son, or kinsman do not follow it; rather, they pass on to another heir. (Utt. 431)
Life is being led away without heedfulness, O King; old age carries off a man’s beauty!
O King of Pañcāla, listen to my words: do not perform such great deeds.
I too know this, O holy man, just as you have spoken these words to me.
"These enjoyments cause attachment, O noble one, and are difficult for those like us to conquer. (Utt.
433) In Hastināpura, Citra, having seen the king of great power, made an unwholesome vow out of greed for sensual pleasures. (Utt. 434)
Since I did not turn back from that [wrong path], though I knew it, this is the kind of fruit I have obtained: that I am infatuated with sensual pleasures and the Dharma.
Like an elephant sunk in the mud and water, unable to see the dry land, he cannot reach the shore.
Thus we, greedy for the strands of sensual pleasure, do not follow the path of the monks.
Time passes away and nights fly by; yet enjoyments are not eternal for men.
Having approached, enjoyments abandon a man, just as birds leave a tree whose fruit has been exhausted. (Uttarādhyayana 436–437)
"If you are unable to renounce enjoyments, O King, then perform noble deeds;
established in Dharma and compassionate toward all beings, you will then become a god here, possessing supernormal powers.
But your mind is not inclined to renounce enjoyments; you are greedy for undertakings and possessions. (Uttarādhyayana 4.38)
"Enough of this delusion and idle talk; I am going, O King! You have been addressed. (Utt.
439) And King Brahmadatta of Pañcāla, failing to act upon the words of that sage, enjoyed unsurpassed sensual pleasures and entered an unsurpassed hell. (Utt. 440)
Citta, too, having become dispassionate toward sensual pleasures, a great sage of exalted conduct and austerity,
and having maintained unsurpassed self-restraint, went to the unsurpassed state of perfection.
Thus I say.
[The Chapter on the Usuyāra Gods] Having been gods in a previous existence, some who dwelt in a single celestial palace have now descended.

In the ancient city named Usuyāra, a prosperous mine as delightful as the world of the gods, they were born into noble families by virtue of the remnants of their past deeds. Having become disillusioned with the fear of saṃsāra, they abandoned it and took refuge in the path of the Lord of Jinas. (Uttarādhyayana 442–443)
O Prince, having attained manhood, both the family priest and his wife Yaśā,
as well as Viśākha of great fame and Susāraka, the king’s brother-in-law, and Queen Kamalāvatī,
were overcome by the fear of birth, old age, and death, and their minds became intent upon dwelling in the forest. (Uttarādhyayana 4.4–6)
Having seen those strands of sensual pleasure as the means for liberation from the wheel of saṃsāra, they became dispassionate. (Utt.

445) Both sons, dear to their father, [were born] to a brahmin who was a domestic priest and whose conduct was rooted in his own duty; having remembered their former birth there, as well as the austerity and self-restraint they had well-practiced. (Utt. 446)
Not becoming attached to sensual pleasures— whether those of humans or even those of the gods—
