those who long for liberation and have conceived faith, having approached their father, spoke thus:
"Seeing this dwelling to be impermanent and beset by many obstacles, and that life is not long..."

"Therefore, we find no delight in the household; we bid you farewell, for we shall practice the path of silence. (Utt. 448) Then the householder spoke to those sages regarding that which would cause an obstacle to their asceticism: "Those learned in the Vedas declare this [practice], so that there may be no world [of suffering] for those who have not heard [the sacred teachings]. (Utt. 449)
Having studied the Vedas and honored the Brahmins, having established your sons in the household and enjoyed pleasures with women, become forest-dwelling sages who are highly praised.
[For] by the fire of the senses, fueled by the wood of one's own virtues and fanned by the wind of delusion, there is a blazing conflagration.
Behold those princes as they observe the family priest— who is tormented by feverish distress, wailing piteously and at great length—
gradually entreating him with his sons, wealth, and indeed with the various strands of sensual pleasure, according to their respective order. (Uttarādhyayana 451–452)
The Vedas studied do not become a protection; gifts enjoyed lead from darkness to further darkness.
Sons born do not become a protection—who indeed would approve of this?
(Uttarādhyayana 453) [Worldly pleasures] provide happiness for only a moment but bring suffering for a long time; they involve constant suffering and lack lasting happiness.
Sensual enjoyments are the adversaries to liberation from *saṃsāra* and are the source of misfortunes. (Utt.
454) While wandering about, with desires uncontrolled, burning day and night, heedless of others and seeking wealth, a man encounters death and old age. (Utt. 455)
"I have this, and I lack that; this is my duty, and this is not my duty"—while one thus prattles on in this manner, the days carry one away; so how can there be negligence?
(Uttarādhyayana 456) Abundant wealth along with women, couches, and likewise sensual pleasures in abundance...

That which the world torments you for is already entirely at your disposal right here. (Utt. 457) What is the use of wealth in the undertaking of the burden of Dharma, or of kinsmen and the qualities of sensual pleasure?
We shall become ascetics, bearers of a multitude of virtues, having gone forth to dwell abroad and subsist on alms. (Utt. 458)

Just as fire is not present in the fire-drills, nor ghee in milk, nor oil in sesame seeds—even so, beings arise within the body; they coalesce and perish, they do not remain. Because of its immaterial nature, it cannot be grasped by the senses; and because of its immaterial nature, it is eternal.
Bondage is caused by one's own internal factors; they declare that bondage is the cause of saṃsāra. (Utt.
460) Just as we previously committed evil karma out of delusion, not knowing the Dharma—though being restrained and protected—we shall not practice that again. (Utt. 461)
When the world is overwhelmed and surrounded on all sides by falling delusions, one finds no delight in the home.
By what is the world overwhelmed? Or by what is it surrounded?
"What indeed is called 'non-delusion,' O Jāyā? I shall become one who has conquered thought. (Utt.
463) "The world is assailed by death and surrounded by old age; non-delusion is called the night. Know it thus, my dear! (Utt. 464)
Each night that passes does not return;
for one who commits unrighteousness, the nights go by fruitlessly.
Each night that passes does not return.
And for one who practices the Dhamma, the nights pass fruitfully. (Utt.
466) Having lived together at one time, both endowed with right conviction, we shall later go forth as wanderers, seeking alms from family to family. (Utt. 467)
He who has a confrontation with death, or he who has an escape from it—
he who thinks "I shall not die"— he alone might have doubts regarding his sons.
This very day let us adopt the Dharma, having entered which we shall not be born again.

When there is nothing whatsoever in the future, and one has not discarded passion through faith and patience—O Vāsiṣṭhī, for one who has abandoned his son, there is no dwelling; it is time for the life of alms.
A tree attains stability when its branches are [intact], but when the branches are severed, it becomes a mere stump. (Uttarādhyayana 469–470)
Just as a bird here deprived of its wings, or a king in battle deprived of his servants, or a merchant on a ship whose essence is lost, even so am I, bereft of my son. (Utt.
471) These qualities of sensual pleasure are well-prepared for you, gathered together, possessing the finest flavors and abundance.

"Let us enjoy the qualities of sensual pleasure to our heart's content; afterwards we shall go upon the path of the supreme. "O householder! Once tastes have been enjoyed, one eventually abandons them. I do not abandon pleasures for the sake of life itself;
rather, reflecting upon gain and loss, as well as happiness and suffering, I shall practice silence (mona)."
Do not remember your kinsmen; like an old swan moving against the current, enjoy pleasures together with me—for the life of a wandering mendicant is indeed painful.
Just as a snake casts off its thin skin and departs, having abandoned it, so should you go.

"These people abandon pleasures; how then shall I alone not follow them? (Uttarādhyayana 475) Like fish that have broken through a weak net, having abandoned the strands of sensual pleasure, those of firm character, noble in their austerity, and steadfast, truly wander for alms. (Uttarādhyayana 476)
"Indeed, having passed beyond the huts, the swans fly forth, shattering the nets;
my sons and my husband are in their midst—how shall I, all alone, not follow them? (Utt.
477) Having heard that the priest, along with his daughter and his wife, had renounced the world and abandoned worldly pleasures, [she likewise did so].
"O King, the queen repeatedly approached the king with vast and supreme wealth, the very essence of her household.
'O King, a man who lives on what has been vomited is not praised by a Brahmin;
you desire wealth that has already been cast away. (Uttarādhyayana 478–479)
Even if you possessed the entire world or all wealth, it would all be insufficient for you; it could not serve as your protection.
O King, whether today or tomorrow, you shall die, having abandoned these delightful strands of sensual pleasure.

"O King, the Dharma alone is the refuge; nothing else exists here as a protection. (Uttarādhyayana 481) "I do not delight in being like a bird in a cage. Having severed my ties, I shall practice the vow of silence—possessing nothing, straightforward, free from worldly desires, and having turned away from the faults of possession and violence. (Uttarādhyayana 482)
Just as when a forest fire is burning the creatures in the woods, other beings, fallen under the sway of passion and hatred, rejoice;
even so we, deluded and infatuated with sensual pleasures, [rejoice]. (Uttarādhyayana 4.3)
We do not perceive the world being consumed by the fire of passion and hatred.
Having enjoyed and then vomited up worldly pleasures, those who live with lightness of being go about laughing, like those who act according to their whims during the day.
"And these bound ones are struggling, having come into the very palm of my hand; we too, as beings amidst sensual pleasures, shall become like these. (Utt.
486) Having seen a vulture with flesh being caught while it was without flesh, one should reflect.
Having abandoned all material things, we shall dwell free from worldly attachments. Having understood that sensual desires are like a snare for the greedy, which increase the cycle of transmigration,
one should move about with a restrained body, as a serpent wary of a golden trap.
Like a serpent that has severed its bonds, one should go to one's own abode;
this is the desired goal, O Great King! I have heard it said that one who is full of longing is called "ussuyāri. Having abandoned a vast kingdom and sensual pleasures so difficult to renounce...
Free from the realm of worldly objects, free from sensual desires, free from craving, and free from possessions;

having rightly understood the Dharma and abandoned the strands of sensual pleasure, those of formidable prowess should practice formidable austerity, embracing the vow of total renunciation (ahakkhāya).
Thus, in due order, all those Buddhas were devoted to the Dharma;
terrified by the fear of birth and death, they sought the end of suffering. In the teaching of those who have overcome delusion, they were previously purified by spiritual cultivation.
In no long time, having reached the end of suffering—
the king together with the queen, the brahmin priest, the brahmin woman,
and the children— all of them attained final liberation.
Thus I say.
[The Chapter on the Monk]
"I shall practice silence, having realized the Dharma; together with companions who are upright and have severed the root of worldly existence, one should abandon intimacy, desiring nothing at will.

Seeking what is unknown, he wanders as an ascetic—he is a bhikkhu. (Uttarādhyayana 4.15) "Restraining himself from passion, he should wander among the Lāḍhas, being free from violence and protected by the Veda. (Uttarādhyayana 4.16)
Having overcome all attachments and seeing everything, he who is not infatuated with anything—he is a bhikkhu.

(Uttarajjhayaṇa 4.96) Knowing that it brings insults, the wise sage should wander in Lāḍha, always guarding his conduct, with an undistracted mind and free from elation, enduring everything—such a one is a bhikkhu. (Uttarajjhayaṇa 4.97)

Having accepted coarse bedding and seats, and having endured various cold and heat, as well as gadflies and mosquitoes, with an undistracted mind and free from elation— he who endures all this completely is a monk. (Uttarādhyayana 498) He does not desire honor, nor worship, nor even salutation, nor praise from anywhere.
He who is restrained, well-awakened, an ascetic, patient, and seeking his own welfare—he is a monk. (Utt.
499) The ascetic who renounces life itself, or who completely subdues delusion, and who always abandons men and women, never succumbing to curiosity—he is a monk. (Utt. 500)

He who does not live by means of the following sciences—the interpretation of sounds, omens on the ground, or in the sky; dreams; bodily marks; the science of staffs; the science of building sites; the analysis of limbs; the victory of sounds; spells; various root-herbs; medical treatments; emetics; purgatives; medicinal smoking; and eye-salves—that one is a bhikkhu.
(Uttarādhyayana 5.1)
Having fully understood that physicians and medical treatment are but a refuge for the sick, one who wanders as an ascetic is a true monk. (Utt.

502) Whether they be groups of Kṣatriyas, sons of high-ranking kings, Brāhmaṇas, householders, or various artisans—one does not seek praise or honor from them; having fully understood this, one who wanders as an ascetic is a true monk. (Utt. 503)

Those householders whom he has seen as a renunciant, or with whom he has become intimate while not yet a renunciant— if he does not cultivate intimacy with them for the sake of worldly fruits, he is a monk. (Uttarādhyayana 504) Having obtained from others various kinds of bedding, seating, drinks, food, snacks, and delicacies...
The Nirgrantha who has rejected all [worldly things], and who does not desire anything therein—he is a bhikṣu. (Utt.

505) Whatever various kinds of food and drink, or solid and soft foods, he obtains from others, he does not show compassion for them in three ways; being well-restrained in mind, speech, and body—he is a bhikṣu. (Utt. 506)
He who does not despise boiled rice with meat, nor cold sour gruel, nor even tasteless boiled rice, and who wanders among humble families—he is a bhikkhu. (Utt.
5.7) Various sounds exist in the world: celestial, human, and those of animals. (Utt. 5.8)
He who, having heard terrifying, fearsome, and formidable things, is not disturbed—he is a bhikkhu. (Utt.

508) Having understood the various doctrines in the world, being patient, following the path of discernment, wise, having overcome all [false] views, and being tranquil, he does not revile others—he is a bhikkhu. (Utt. 509)

One who does not live by a craft, who is homeless and without enemies, who has conquered the senses, who is liberated from all bonds, who is free from latent passions, who eats light food, and who wanders alone having abandoned the household—that one is a bhikkhu.
Thus I say. (Uttarādhyayana 5.10)

[The Foundations of the Ascetic Life] Thus have I heard, O Venerable One: it was said by the Blessed One. Here, indeed, ten foundations of the ascetic life (*brahmacarya-samādhi-sthāna*) have been proclaimed by the venerable elders; having heard and fully understood them, a monk should dwell ever heedful—abounding in self-restraint, abounding in restraint, abounding in concentration, guarded, with senses guarded, and guarding his ascetic conduct.

Which indeed are those ten foundations for the concentration of celibacy (*brahmacarya-samādhi-sthāna*) proclaimed by the Blessed Elders, which a monk—having heard and having reflected upon them—should dwell, being abundant in self-restraint (*saṃyama*), abundant in restraint (*saṃvara*), abundant in concentration (*samādhi*), guarded, with senses guarded, a celibate practitioner with guarded conduct, always heedful? These indeed are those ten foundations for the concentration of celibacy proclaimed by the Blessed Elders, which a monk—having heard and having reflected upon them—should dwell, being abundant in self-restraint, abundant in restraint, abundant in concentration, guarded, with senses guarded, a celibate practitioner with guarded conduct, always heedful.

That is as follows: he who resorts to secluded lodgings and seats is a Nirgrantha; he does not resort to lodgings and seats occupied by women, animals, or eunuchs—he is a Nirgrantha. If it is asked, "How so? the Teacher says: For a Nirgrantha who observes the vow of celibacy while resorting to lodgings and seats occupied by women, animals, or eunuchs, there may arise doubt, hesitation, or uncertainty regarding his celibacy; he may suffer a breach of it, fall into madness, or incur a chronic illness, and he may fall away from the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin. Therefore, he who resorts to lodgings and seats occupied by women, animals, or eunuchs is not a Nirgrantha.

A Nirgrantha does not engage in conversation with women. If one asks, "Why is that? the Teacher says: For a Nirgrantha who is a practitioner of celibacy (*brahmacārin*) and who engages in conversation with women, there may arise doubt regarding his celibacy, and he may even fall away from the Dharma. Therefore, he should not engage in conversation with women.

A Nirgrantha does not dwell sitting on the same seat as women. Why is that? The Teacher says: For a Nirgrantha who practices celibacy while sitting on the same seat with women, there may arise suspicion regarding his celibacy, or he may even fall away from the Dharma. Therefore, a Nirgrantha should not dwell sitting on the same seat as women.

A Nirgrantha does not look at or gaze upon the captivating and enchanting organs of women. Why is that? The Teacher says: For a Nirgrantha who looks at or gazes upon the captivating and enchanting organs of women, there may arise a doubt regarding his practice of celibacy, or he may even fall away from the Dharma. Therefore, a Nirgrantha should certainly not look at or gaze upon the captivating and enchanting organs of women.

A *nirgrantha* should not, having heard the sound of women crying, weeping, singing, laughing, moaning, wailing, or lamenting from behind a wall, a curtain, or a partition, continue to be a *nirgrantha*. If it is asked, "How so? the Teacher says: For a *nirgrantha* who is a practitioner of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) listening to the sounds of women from behind a wall, a curtain, or a partition, up to the sound of lamentation, there may arise doubt regarding his celibacy, and he may even fall away from the Dharma. Therefore, a *nirgrantha* should not dwell while listening to the sounds of women from behind a wall, up to the sound of wailing or lamentation.

A Niggantha does not pursue former sexual indulgence or former play; he is indeed a Niggantha [who refrains from this]. If it is asked, "How so? the Teacher says: For a Niggantha who pursues former sexual indulgence or former play with women, while practicing celibacy (*brahmacarya*), there may arise doubt, or perplexity, or hesitation regarding his celibate conduct; or he may suffer a breach [of his vows], or fall into madness, or incur a chronic illness, or fall away from the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin. Therefore, a Niggantha indeed should not pursue former sexual indulgence or former play.

A Nirgrantha does not consume refined food; he who does so is not a Nirgrantha. If it is asked, "How is that so? the Teacher replies: For a Nirgrantha who consumes refined food while practicing celibacy, there may arise suspicion regarding his celibate conduct, or even his fall from the Dharma. Therefore, a Nirgrantha indeed should not consume refined food.

A Nirgrantha does not consume food and drink with excessive deceit. If it is asked why that is so, the Teacher says: For a Nirgrantha who consumes food and drink with excessive deceit, even while practicing celibacy, there arises suspicion regarding his celibate conduct, which may lead him to fall away from the Dharma. Therefore, a Nirgrantha indeed should not consume food and drink with excessive deceit.

A Nirgrantha does not become one who pursues adornment. If it is asked why that is so, the Teacher says: by engaging in adornment and adorning his body, he becomes desirable to women; then, for that practitioner of celibacy (*brahmacārin*) who is being desired by women, there may arise suspicion regarding his celibacy, or even its destruction. Therefore, a Nirgrantha indeed should not be one who pursues adornment.

He who does not pursue sounds, forms, tastes, smells, or tactile sensations is a Nirgrantha. If it is asked, "How so? the Teacher says: For a Nirgrantha who pursues sounds, forms, tastes, smells, or tactile sensations, while practicing celibacy (*brahmacarya*), there may arise suspicion, doubt, or hesitation; he may suffer a breach, fall into madness, or incur a chronic illness, and he may fall away from the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins. Therefore, he who is a Nirgrantha should not pursue sounds, forms, tastes, smells, or tactile sensations. This is the tenth station of concentration regarding celibacy. There are verses on this subject as follows: [The verses follow.]
One should frequent a dwelling that is secluded, uninhabited, and devoid of women, for the sake of protecting one's celibacy.
[Such a place] produces mental delight and increases sensual passion. (Uttarādhyayana 5.22)
A monk devoted to celibacy should avoid conversation with women;
a monk devoted to celibacy should always and constantly avoid intimacy with women and frequent conversation with them. (Uttarādhyayana 5.23–24)
One devoted to celibacy should avoid the beautiful configuration of the limbs and members, as well as the charming speech and glances of women, which are objects of the eye.
One should also avoid wailing, weeping, singing, laughing, moaning, and crying. (Utt. 5.25)
One devoted to celibacy should avoid women, who are objects of longing;
one devoted to celibacy should never contemplate laughter, play, passion, pride, or sudden and terrifying things regarding women. (Uttarādhyayana 5.26–27)

A monk devoted to celibacy should always avoid delicious food and drink, which quickly increase intoxication. One who possesses right intention should accept what is obtained in accordance with the Dharma, in moderation, and at the proper time, for the sake of sustenance.
One who is ever devoted to the holy life (*brahmacarya*) should not eat to excess;
one who is devoted to the holy life should avoid adornment and the embellishment of the body;
a monk devoted to the holy life should not wear [ornaments] for the sake of vanity. (Utt. 529–530)
One should always avoid the fivefold qualities of sensual pleasure: sounds, forms, smells, tastes, and likewise touches.
(Uttarādhyayana 5.31) A place crowded with women is a source of distraction, as is delightful conversation with women.
Familiarity with women, and the beholding of their limbs;
wailing, weeping, and singing; laughter, eating, and sitting together; and exquisite food and drink, as well as intoxicating beverages and meals. (Uttarādhyayana 5.32–33)
Ornaments for the body and sensual pleasures are difficult for a man seeking his own welfare to conquer, like a palm-fruit smeared with poison.
Sensual pleasures are hard to overcome; one should always avoid them.
One who is composed should avoid all dangerous places.

A monk should wander delighting in the Dharma—steadfast, having the Dharma as his refuge, finding joy in the delight of the Dharma, self-controlled, and established in the concentration of celibacy. (Uttarādhyayana 5.35–36)
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and kiṃnaras pay homage to the one who practices self-restraint, who performs what is difficult to do.
This Dharma is stable, eternal, and everlasting, as taught by the Jina.
By this [path], those who have attained perfection have attained it, and others likewise shall attain it.
Thus I speak.

[On the Life of a Wandering Ascetic] Whosoever has gone forth as a *niyantha*, having heard the Dharma and become endowed with discipline, and having obtained the very rare attainment of enlightenment (*bodhilābha*), may thereafter wander according to his pleasure. (Uttarādhyayana 5.39)
"The bed is firm, there is clothing, food arises just as it is for drink;
I know, O Venerable One, that all this is provided! What indeed shall I do with learning?
(Uttarādhyayana 540) "Whosoever among those who have gone forth is of a sleepy disposition and gluttonous..."
Having eaten and then sleeping comfortably, he is called a "wicked ascetic" (pāvasamaṇi). (Utt.
541) When he is taught the scripture and discipline by the teachers and preceptors, that fool reviles them; he is called a "wicked ascetic. (Utt. 542)
One who does not properly serve or honor the teachers and preceptors, being arrogant and lacking in reverence, is called a "wicked ascetic" (pāvasamaṇi).
[Such a one] tramples upon living beings, seeds, and green plants.
One who perceives attachment where there is no attachment is called a "wicked ascetic" (pāvasamaṇi).
One who ascends onto a straw mat, a wooden plank, a bench, a seat,
or a foot-cloth without having wiped them clean is called a "wicked ascetic."
He wanders about restlessly, being constantly negligent, leaping over obstacles, and fierce; such a one is called a "wicked ascetic.
Being negligent, he fails to inspect his bedding and lets his foot-cloth fall into disrepair.
One who performs the inspection of his utensils without being attentive is called a "wicked monk" (pāvasamaṇi). (Utt.
547) One who performs the inspection while being negligent, or who listens to something [worldly] while doing so, constantly treats the Guru with contempt; he is called a "wicked monk. (Utt. 548)

One who is full of deceit, talkative, stubborn, greedy, unrestrained, lacking in sharing, and disrespectful is called a "wicked ascetic" (pāvasamaṇi). Such a person incites disputes and, being ignorant of the self, persists in unrighteousness.
One who is quarrelsome and addicted to strife is called a wicked ascetic (pāvasamaṇi). (Utt.
550) One who is unstable in posture, fidgety, and sits here and there on a seat without restraint is called a wicked ascetic. (Utt. 551)
He sleeps with his feet unprotected and does not inspect his bedding;
being unprepared regarding his mat, he is called a "wicked monk.
(Uttarādhyayana 5.52) He frequently consumes milk, curd, and fermented products as food.

One who performs ascetic practices for the sake of gain is called a "wicked ascetic" (pāvasamaṇi). (Uttarādhyayana 5.53) Furthermore, one who eats food while the sun is setting, and who, being repeatedly urged, accepts [food] that has been brought back, is called a "wicked ascetic. (Uttarādhyayana 5.54)
One who abandons the teacher, serves heretical sects, and is a corrupter of the community is called a "wicked ascetic" (pāvasamaṇi).
Having abandoned his own home, he busies himself in the homes of others. (Uttarādhyayana 5.5–6)
One who deals with signs (of status) is called a wicked ascetic. (Utt.

556) One who eats alms-food obtained through formal invitations, who does not desire the alms-gathering of the community, and who frequents the beds of householders, is called a wicked ascetic. (Utt. 557)
One who is thus restrained by the fivefold virtues of conduct, though possessing a beautiful form, is among the lowest of the best of sages;
in this world, such a person is as censurable as one in a state of peril, for they find no success neither in this world nor in the world beyond.
But he who always avoids these faults becomes a sage worthy of praise among the wise.
In this world, he who is honored like nectar shall attain success in both worlds.
Thus I say.
(Uttarādhyayana 5.59)
In the city of Kampilla, there was a king named Sañjaya, who possessed an arrayed army and vehicles; he went out for the purpose of hunting. (Uttarādhyayana 5.60)
Surrounded on all sides by a great force consisting of cavalry, elephant corps, chariot corps, and likewise infantry,
the king, mounted on his horse, having released his prey, [entered] the Keśara garden of Kampilla.
There, while the lion was terrified, calm, and composed, he carried away the elephant who was intoxicated by the [elephant's] ichor. (Utt.
562) Then, in the Keśara garden, the homeless ascetic, rich in austerity, engaged in study and meditation, remained absorbed in the meditation on the Dharma. (Utt. 563)
In a pavilion on the bank of the Appho river, he whose taints were extinguished was meditating;
when the deer came within his sight, the king of men set his arrow upon him. Then the king, descending from his horse, quickly arrived there.
Having looked around, he saw there a homeless ascetic (anagāra).
Then the king, greatly agitated there, said: "By me, of little merit, greedy for flavors, this homeless ascetic was seized. (Uttarādhyayana 5.65–66)
Having released his horse, that king reverently bowed at the feet of the homeless ascetic, saying: "O Blessed One, forgive me for this!
But the Blessed One, the homeless ascetic, remained in silence, absorbed in meditation.
He did not address the king; then the king became terrified.
"I am a restrained ascetic," [the monk said]. "O Blessed One, call me by my name when you are angry;
an *anagāra* could burn even tens of millions of hells with his fiery power. (Uttarādhyayana 5.68–69)
"Fear not, O King! Be a giver of fearlessness, for this world of living beings is impermanent; why do you persist in violence?
Since you must inevitably depart, abandoning everything. (Uttarādhyayana 5.70)

In this impermanent world of living beings, why do you set your heart so strongly on sovereignty? O King, life and beauty are as flickering as a flash of lightning; yet you are deluded by them and do not perceive what lies beyond. (Uttarādhyayana 5.71–72)
Wives, sons, friends, and likewise kinsmen support one while he is alive, but they do not follow him when he is dead.
When he is dead, his sons carry him out, being themselves deeply afflicted by grief.
"O King, one should practice self-restraint toward one's father, likewise toward one's son, and toward one's kinsmen.
Then, when wealth has been acquired by him and his wife is well protected, other men, adorned and joyful, sport [with their own], O King. (Uttarādhyayana 5.74–75)
Whatever karma— whether pleasant or painful— has been performed by him,
he goes to the next existence joined with that very karma. Having heard that Dharma from the presence of that homeless ascetic...
Overcome by great spiritual urgency and world-weariness, the lord of men,
having renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness under the teaching of the Jina, in the presence of the Blessed One Gaddabhāli, who was a wandering mendicant. (Uttarādhyayana 5.77–78)
Having abandoned the kingdom and gone forth as a wanderer, the Kṣatriya addressed him:
"As your form appears, so too does your mind seem serene.
What is your name? What is your clan? And for what purpose have you become a Māhana? (Uttarādhyayana 5.7–9)

"How do you serve the Buddhas? How are you called 'the disciplined'? (Uttarādhyayana 5.80) "By name I am Sañjaya, and by clan I am Gautama; my teachers are Gaddabhāli, who have reached the further shore of knowledge and conduct. (Uttarādhyayana 5.81)
O Great Sage, what does one who knows the truth proclaim through these four positions: action, non-action, discipline, and ignorance?
The Buddha, the Knower, the one who has attained final liberation, has explained this clearly.
Those endowed with knowledge and conduct, devoted to truth and striving for truth; those men who perform evil deeds fall into terrible hells,
while those who have practiced the noble Dharma go to a divine state.
"This is merely a fabrication; it is false and meaningless speech.
Even though I am practicing restraint, I live and I move about. [Thinking thus,] "All these are known to me as those of wrong view and ignoble conduct. (Uttarādhyayana 5.8–9)
Since the other world exists, I know myself correctly:
"I was once Mahāpāṇa, possessing splendor for a duration of a year;
she who was Pālī, the great Pālī, possessed divine splendor for a duration of a year. (Uttarādhyayana 5.86–5.87)
When one has passed away from the realm of the Bambhas and come to a human birth,
one should know the lifespan of oneself and of others exactly as it is.
A restrained monk should avoid various inclinations and personal whims.
"Neither non-purpose nor all purposes"—thus one should practice the science [of knowledge].
"I confess my questions," or again, "by the words of others";
"O, having risen, for day and night"—thus one should practice the science of austerity. (Uttarādhyayana 5.89–5.90)
And whatever you ask me at the proper time with a pure consciousness, the Buddha shall explain that clearly; such is the knowledge in the teaching of the Jina.
The wise man approves of action, yet he avoids [unwholesome] action.
With right view, endowed with vision, practice the Dharma that is so difficult to practice.
Having heard this path of merit, which is augmented by the wealth of the Dharma, even Bharata abandoned desires for the land of Bhārata and went forth into the homeless life. (Uttarādhyayana 592–593)
Sagara, the lord of men, having renounced his sovereign power over the entire Bharata region as far as the ocean's edge, attained final liberation through compassion.
Having abandoned the land of Bharata, that wheel-turning monarch of great majesty—
Having undertaken the life of renunciation, the one named Maghavan, possessed of great glory, [became a Jina].
Sanatkumāra, the lord of men and a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) of great power, having established his son in the kingdom, that king also practiced asceticism. (Uttarādhyayana 595–596)
Having abandoned the land of Bhārata, the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) of great power, Śānti—
who brings peace to the world— attained the unsurpassed state.
Kunthu by name, a bull among kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty and a lord of men, [did likewise].
The Blessed One, whose fame is far-reaching, has attained supreme liberation.
Having abandoned Bharata up to the edge of the ocean, the most excellent lord of men has indeed reached the stainless state;
he has attained the unsurpassed goal.
Having renounced the land of Bhārata, the wheel-turning monarch of great power,
having renounced supreme enjoyments, Mahāpadma practiced self-restraint. Having brought the earth under a single umbrella, that hero who subdues the proud—
Hariṣeṇa, the lord of men, attained the unsurpassed state;
having renounced [his wealth] along with thousands of kings, he practiced self-restraint.
Jayanāma, who was proclaimed by the Jina, attained the unsurpassed state. (Uttarādhyayana 601–602)
Having abandoned the kingdom of Daśārṇa with joy, the sage Daśārṇabhadra wandered forth, having been directly exhorted by Śakra. Namī, directly exhorted by Śakra, humbles himself before his own self.
Having abandoned his home, Vaidēhī entered the ascetic life.
Karakaṇḍu among the Kaliṅgas, Dummuha among the Pañcālas, King Namī among the Videhas, and Naggai among the Gandhāras [likewise entered the ascetic life]. (Uttarādhyayana 6.4–5)
These preeminent bulls among kings, having departed under the teaching of the Jina and having established their sons in the kingdom, devoted themselves to the life of a recluse.
The preeminent king of Sauvīra, having renounced the world, wandered as a sage.

Uddāyana went forth as a monk and attained the unsurpassed state. (Uttarādhyayana 6.7) In the same way, the King of Kāśī, Śreṇika, possessed of true prowess, renounced sensual pleasures and destroyed the great forest of karma. (Uttarādhyayana 6.8)
In the same way, King Vijaya, possessing great fame, abandoned his kingdom—which was abundant in virtues—for the sake of practicing the homeless life;
likewise, having performed severe austerity with an undistracted mind... [Uttarādhyayana 6.9]

How could the steadfast royal sage Mahābala, having taken glory upon his head, wander the earth like a madman due to causeless [fears]? Having taken up these [virtues], the brave ones of firm exertion [proceed]. (Uttarādhyayana 6.10–11)

"Enduring until the ultimate end of existence, speaking only words of truth, they have crossed over; some are crossing now, and those yet to come shall cross. How, O steadfast one, can you distress yourself with groundless arguments?
Completely liberated from all attachments, he becomes a perfected one (siddha), free from passion.
Thus I say.
In the delightful city of Suggīva, adorned with groves and gardens, there was a king named Balabhadra; Mṛgā was his chief queen. (Uttarādhyayana 6.14)
Their son was Balaśrī, known as Miyāputta, beloved by his mother and father; he was the crown prince and a subduer of the senses.
That son played with women in the palace.

The god Dōgunda, his mind constantly delighted, stood upon the balcony of his palace on a floor paved with jewels and gems, and gazed upon the city’s crossroads, triple-junctions, and squares. (Utt. 616–617)
Then he saw the ascetic Sañjaya staying there,
bearing penance, restraint, and self-control, enriched by virtue, a treasury of good qualities.
Miyāputta gazed upon him with an unblinking eye.

"Where have I ever seen such a form before? (Utt. 619) Upon seeing that ascetic, as his mental disposition became pure, he—who was tranquil and had fallen into a state of delusion—attained the recollection of his former births. (Utt. 620)
Having fallen from the world of the gods and come to human existence, when conscious knowledge has arisen, he remembers his former birth.
(Uttarādhyayana 6.21) When the memory of former births had arisen,
Miya-putta possessed great power.
He remembered his former births and the ascetic life he had previously led.
Not finding delight in sense objects, yet finding delight in self-restraint, he approached his mother and father and spoke these words: (Uttarādhyayana 6.22–23)
I have undertaken the five great vows;
I am weary of the suffering in the hells and among the animal births,
and I am disgusted with the great ocean of sensual desires.
"Grant me permission, mother; I shall go forth into the religious life.
"Mother and father! I have experienced sensual pleasures like poisonous fruits, which result in bitterness later and bring about continuous suffering."
This body is impermanent, impure, born of impurity,
a dwelling place for what is non-eternal, and a vessel for the seeds of suffering.
In this transient body, I find no delight.
In this human existence, which is as insubstantial as a bubble on foam, one must eventually cast it off—whether later or earlier;
since it is a mere abode for afflictions and diseases, and a vessel for old age and death, I do not find delight in it even for a moment. (Uttarādhyayana 6.27–28)
Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, and diseases and deaths—
alas, cyclic existence is indeed suffering, wherein living beings suffer. Fields, houses, gold, children, wives, and kinsmen [are likewise sources of suffering].
Having abandoned this body, I must go against my will. (Utt.
630) Just as the ripening of the kimpāka fruit is not pleasant, so too the ripening of enjoyed pleasures is not pleasant. (Utt. 631)
He who, unable to abandon it, embarks upon a long journey,
becomes miserable as he goes along, oppressed by hunger and thirst.
In the same way, he who departs for the next existence without having practiced the Dharma [suffers likewise].
One who travels while carrying a heavy load becomes miserable, oppressed by diseases and afflictions.
But he who sets out on a long journey having provided for his needs becomes happy as he goes, free from hunger and thirst. (Uttarādhyayana 6.33–34)
Thus, having practiced the Dharma, he who goes to the next world becomes happy as he departs— possessing little karma and free from suffering.
Just as when a house is on fire, he who is the master of that house [is safe].

He takes away the essential goods and abandons the worthless. (Uttarādhyayana 6.36) In this same way, while the world is ablaze with old age and death, I shall deliver myself; may you grant me your permission. (Uttarādhyayana 6.37)
His parents said to him: "Son, the ascetic life is difficult to practice;
indeed, thousands of virtues must be maintained by a monk.
He must maintain equanimity toward all beings in the world, whether they be enemies or friends. (Uttarādhyayana 6.38)

Abstaining from taking life for as long as one lives is difficult. (Uttarādhyayana 6.39) Speaking what is beneficial and true, while always remaining vigilant and avoiding false speech, is difficult. (Uttarādhyayana 6.40)
For one who knows the taste of sensual pleasures,
it is difficult— even for a man of self-restraint— to avoid taking what is not given, such as a tooth-stick, or anything that is not free from impurities.
(Uttarādhyayana 6.41) Abstaining from unchaste conduct is likewise difficult for one who is acquainted with the flavors of sensual enjoyment.
The austere Great Vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) must be maintained; it is extremely difficult to perform.

(Utt. 642) In the case of wealth, grain, and servants, the avoidance of possessions and the renunciation of all undertakings—being free from the sense of "mine" (nirmama)—is extremely difficult to achieve. (Utt. 643)
The fourfold food, the avoidance of eating at night, and the renunciation of storing up provisions— these must be avoided, for they are very difficult to practice.
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and the pain caused by gadflies and mosquitoes [must likewise be endured].
Abuse, uncomfortable bedding, the touch of grass, and indeed dirt; beatings and threats, as well as the hardships of flogging and imprisonment;
the suffering of the mendicant’s alms-round, begging, and the failure to obtain alms. (Uttarādhyayana 6.45–6.46)
"This livelihood is like a bitter gourd, and the shaving of the hair is harsh;
it is difficult for a great soul to maintain the terrible vow of celibacy.
You are accustomed to comfort, my son, delicate and well-groomed. (Uttarādhyayana 6.47)
"O son, you are not capable of maintaining the state of a renunciant!
For as long as life lasts, this great burden of virtues is heavy, like a load of iron, O son, and it is difficult to bear. (Uttarādhyayana 6.48–49)
Like the current of the Ganges in the sky, like a counter-current, or like the ocean itself, difficult to cross with one's arms; yet the ocean of virtues must be crossed.
Like a mouthful of sand, self-restraint is indeed tasteless.
Traversing the edge of a sword and practicing austerities are indeed difficult;
O son, moving with eyes fixed on a snake is difficult, and to draw iron arrows from a bow is very difficult indeed. (Uttarādhyayana 6.51–6.52)
Just as a blazing flame of fire is very difficult to grasp, so too is it difficult for one to practice the state of a śramaṇa while in youth.
Just as it is difficult for one to fill a winnowing basket with wind. (Uttarādhyayana 6.53)
Just as it is difficult for one who has committed evil deeds to attain the state of a śramaṇa by means of their body;
and just as Mount Mandara is difficult to lift even with a scale, so too is the state of a śramaṇa difficult to maintain in silence and without fear. (Uttarādhyayana 6.54–55)
Just as it is difficult to cross the ocean of jewels by means of one's arms,
so too is the ocean of self-restraint difficult for one who does not practice tranquility.
Enjoy, therefore, the human pleasures characterized by the five senses.
"O parents, once you have enjoyed your worldly pleasures, you shall later practice the Dharma.
He said to his mother and father: "This is indeed so, as it is clear;
for one who is free from thirst in this world, nothing at all is difficult to do. (Utt. 657–658)
Infinite physical and mental agonies, terrifying and endless, as well as countless sufferings and fears,
have been endured by me in the wilderness of old age and death, which is four-cornered and a pit of terror. (Uttarādhyayana 6.59)
I have endured terrifying births and deaths. Just as fire is hot here, the heat in those hells is infinitely greater; there, I experienced agonizing heat. (Uttarādhyayana 6.60–61)
Just as this cold here is experienced, so too in those hells the cold sensation is infinitely greater;
such unpleasant suffering was experienced by me while crying out in the *kanduka* and *kumbhī* vats, with feet upward and head downward. (Uttarādhyayana 662)
In the blazing fire of the funeral pyre, he has been roasted countless times;
in the great forest fire, resembling a desert of burning sand and *kalamba* sand, he has been burnt countless times. (Uttarādhyayana 6.63–64)

Crying out as they are boiled in cauldrons and jars, bound above yet friendless, they are cut to pieces again and again with saws and axes; they have been thus severed countless times on the high *śimbalī* tree bristling with exceedingly sharp thorns. (Uttarādhyayana 6.65)
It was drunk by one bound with ropes, through repeated dragging, a difficult ordeal. (Utt.
666) Like sugarcane among great beasts, crying out most piteously, I was crushed by my own deeds; being of evil karma, [I suffered] infinitely. (Utt. 667)

Barking like jackals, he was struck down, split apart, and cut by dark-skinned and powerful men; writhing in many ways, he was pierced by swords the color of iron, by spears, and by javelins. (Uttarādhyayana 6.68)
Cut, broken, and shattered, he has entered into evil karma.
Helpless, he is yoked to a blazing iron chariot joined with wooden poles, driven by goads, like a wild ox that has fallen [into the fire]. (Uttarādhyayana 6.69–670)
In a blazing fire, like a buffalo roasted on a funeral pyre, helpless and cooked, he is brought there by his evil deeds;
forcibly seized by birds with tongs-like beaks and iron beaks. (Uttarādhyayana 6.71)
Wasted away and tormented, I was devoured countless times by vultures and jackals.
Exhausted by craving, I ran until I reached the Veyarī river;
thinking, "I shall drink the water," I was cut to pieces by its razor-sharp blades.
Afflicted by heat, he arrives at the great forest of sword-leaves;
there, by falling sword-leaves, he has been cut many times before.
[He is struck] with clubs, with musaṇḍhīs, with spears, and with pestles.
Having his limbs shattered, he experienced endless suffering. (Utt.
675) With sharp-edged hooves, knives, and razors, he was shorn, split, cut, and flayed in many ways. (Utt. 676)
Like a deer powerless, driven by snares and deceptive nets,
or bound and confined, he has been greatly tormented;
or like a fish powerless, caught in gill-nets and whale-nets, so am I.
He was torn apart, split open, seized, and killed countless times.
Like a bird caught by nets, snares, or glue, he was trapped, bound, and killed countless times. (Uttarādhyayana 6.78–79)
Like a tree, he was repeatedly hewn, split, cut, and carved with axes, hatchets, and the like;
and by princes, he was struck with kicks and fists as if he were an iron statue. (Uttarādhyayana 6.8–10)
He was beaten, crushed, split, and ground to powder in infinite ways.
He was made to drink molten copper, bronze, and lead, all boiling and seething, while he cried out with a most terrible roar. (Uttarādhyayana 6.81–82)
"You ate meat that you liked, as well as sweets and roasted meats; many times you ate meat that was glowing like fire.
You liked wine, liquor, rum, and honey. (Uttarādhyayana 6.8–9)
I drank boiling fat and blood;
constantly terrified, trembling, suffering, and wounded, I experienced sensations connected with supreme misery. (Uttarādhyayana 6.84–6.85)
I have experienced in the hells torments that are sharp, fierce, intense, terrible, most difficult to endure,
greatly fearsome, and horrific— such as these,
O Father, are seen among the world of men.
In the hells, the experience of painful sensation is infinite times greater than this.

In all states of existence, unpleasant sensations have been experienced by me; there was not even for the duration of a single blink of an eye any pleasant sensation whatsoever. (Uttarādhyayana 6.8–9)
His parents said to him: "By your own will, my son, you may go forth;
however, in the ascetic life, there is suffering due to the lack of remedies.
He replied to his parents: "It is even so, as is well known."

Who performs the retaliation against the deer and birds in the forest? (Uttarādhyayana 690) Just as a deer wanders alone in the forest, so shall I practice the Dharma through self-restraint and austerity. (Uttarādhyayana 691)
Just as when a deer suffers from an ailment while staying at the foot of an isolated tree in the great forest, who then would treat it?
Who would give it medicine, or who would ask after its well-being? (Uttarādhyayana 6.9–12)
Who would bring him food or drink and offer it with reverence?
When he becomes happy, then he goes into the range for the sake of food and drink, to the thickets and the lakes. (Uttarādhyayana 693–694)
Having drunk water from streams and rivers, and having wandered the forest like a deer, he goes forth as one who lives like a deer.
Thus has the monk arisen; even so is he manifold.
Having practiced the way of the deer, he departs toward the uninhabited quarter.
Just as a deer wanders alone, dwelling in many places, moving constantly from one feeding ground to another,
even so does the sage enter upon his alms-round.
"One should neither despise nor revile [others].
'I shall practice the deer-like wandering,' thus, O son, being permitted by your mother and father, you may go as you please; then he abandons his possessions. (Uttarādhyayana 697–698)

"I shall practice the deer-like wandering, which brings liberation from all suffering; O Mother! I have been permitted by you. Go, my son, as you please! (Uttarādhyayana 6.9–10) Having thus obtained the permission of his mother and father in many ways, he...
Then he cuts off his sense of "mine," just as a great elephant sheds its skin.
Wealth, property, friends, children, wife, and kinsmen—having shaken them off like dust clinging to a garment, he has gone forth. (Uttarādhyayana 700–701)
Endowed with the five great vows, restrained in the five ways, guarded by the three guptis,
upright in the practice of austerity regarding both internal and external matters,
free from possessiveness, free from egoism, unattached, and having abandoned pride.
He is equal toward all beings, both those that move and those that are stationary;
he is equal in gain and loss, in pleasure and pain, as well as in life and death; likewise, he is equal in blame and praise, and in honor and dishonor. (Uttarādhyayana 7.03–7.04)
Withdrawn from the forms of respect and the passions, and from the infliction of blows and thorns;
free from laughter and sorrow, without worldly motives and without attachments;
independent in this world and independent in the world beyond. (Uttarādhyayana 7.05)
One who regards an axe and sandalwood alike, whether there is food or no food;
with all influxes closed by means of the doors praised by the noble ones, through the application of internal meditation, one is praised for the teaching of self-control. (Uttarādhyayana 7.6–7)
Thus, having properly cultivated the self through knowledge, conduct, vision, austerity, and pure meditative states, and having observed the state of a śramaṇa for many years— Utt. 708.

By means of a monthly fast, he attained unsurpassed perfection. (Uttarādhyayana 7.9) Thus do the perfectly awakened ones, the wise and discerning, turn away from enjoyments, just as did Mṛgāputra. (Uttarādhyayana 7.10)
Having heard the speech of the son of Mṛgā, who possesses great majesty and great glory—
his supreme conduct characterized by the excellence of austerity, and his excellent destiny renowned throughout the three worlds—
and having understood that wealth increases suffering, that it binds one to possessiveness, and that it brings about great fear; (Uttarādhyayana 7.11).
One should bear the unsurpassed yoke of the Dharma, which brings happiness and bestows the great qualities of Nirvāṇa. Thus I say.
Having paid homage with devotion to the perfected ones (siddhas) and to those who are self-restrained (sañjaya),
listen to me regarding the instruction on the true nature of the goal and the Dharma. (Uttarādhyayana 7.13)
King Śreṇika, the lord of Magadha, possessed of abundant jewels,
went out on a pleasure excursion to the Maṇḍikuñcha shrine, which was filled with various trees and creepers and frequented by various birds. (Uttarādhyayana 7.14)
A garden covered with various flowers, like the Nandana grove; there he saw the ascetic Sañjaya, well-composed, seated at the foot of a tree, delicate and accustomed to comfort. (Utt. 715–716)
Having beheld his form, the king felt an exceeding devotion toward that ascetic;
his wonder at his beauty was intense: "Oh, what a complexion! Oh, what a form! Oh, what sanctity this venerable one possesses! (Uttarādhyayana 7.17)
"O wonder! Patience! O wonder! Liberation! O wonder! Non-attachment to enjoyments!
(Uttarādhyayana 718) Having bowed at his feet and performed a circumambulation, standing neither too far nor too near, he questioned him with palms joined in reverence. (Uttarādhyayana 719)

"You are young, noble sir! You have gone forth as a renunciant; you have entered the ascetic life at the very time one ought to enjoy pleasures. I hear this matter, O Great King: 'I am without a protector; no protector exists for me.'"

"I do not perceive anyone who is compassionate or even well-disposed toward me. Then King Śreṇika, the lord of Magadha, laughed and said: "How is it that for you, who possess such great power, no protector is to be found? (Uttarādhyayana 7.21–22)

"O Śreṇika, Lord of Magadha! You are yourself without a protector; enjoy the pleasures, O restrained one, surrounded by friends and kinsmen, for human birth is indeed very difficult to obtain. (Uttarādhyayana 7.23)
"Being yourself without a name and being peaceful, whose name will you be? (Utt.
724) Thus addressed by the monk, who spoke words never heard before, that king was greatly agitated and filled with wonder, his amazement reaching its peak.
Horses, elephants, and people are mine; my city and my inner apartments are mine.
I enjoy human pleasures, and command and sovereignty are mine. Amidst such abundance, with every desire fulfilled—Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.26.
"How does one become homeless? Do not speak falsely, O Blessed One!
"You do not understand the meaning and the purpose of being homeless, O King; how one becomes homeless or how one becomes 'with-home,' O lord of men! (Uttarādhyayana 7.27–28)
Listen to me, O Great King! With an undistracted mind, hear how one becomes masterless and how this matter has come to pass. There is a city named Kauśāmbī, the destroyer of ancient cities.

There, O Great King, my beloved was my wife and I possessed abundant wealth. In the first watch of the night, O Lord of the Earth, there arose in me a severe pain in the eye and a great burning sensation throughout all my limbs.
"Just as an enraged enemy might thrust a most sharp weapon into the opening of the body, so too is the pain in my eye;
it torments my inner cavity and my head. (Uttarādhyayana 7.32)
The pains, like thunderbolts from Indra, are terrible and most cruel.
My teachers have approached me—those who are skilled in spells, mantras, and medical treatment; they are fearless, experts in the surgical arts, and well-versed in the roots of mantras.
They provide me with medical treatment, yet they do not liberate me from suffering, even though it is beneficial and fourfold; this is my misfortune.
Even if my beloved were to give me his entire wealth for my sake, [it would still not avail].
She who would liberate me from suffering—she is my protector, O Great King.
Even Māyā, though distressed by grief for her son, does not liberate me from suffering; she is my protector, O Great King. (Uttarādhyayana 7.36–37)
"O Great King! My brothers, both elder and younger, do not release me from my suffering; this is my helplessness.
O Great King! My sisters, both elder and younger..."
They do not release me from suffering; this is my unavoidable [fate]. O Great King, my wife is devoted and faithful; with eyes full of tears, she drenches my chest. (Uttarādhyayana 7.39–7.40)
"Food, drink, bathing, perfumes, garlands, and ointments—whether known to me or unknown—that foolish girl does not enjoy.
O Great King! Not even for a moment has she departed from my sight."

"Nor does it liberate one from suffering; this is my conviction. Then they said this to me: "Those who must repeatedly experience painful sensations in this infinite saṃsāra, they call 'suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 7.42–43)
If I myself were to renounce this world, I would endure vast suffering;
therefore, O King of Men, being patient, self-controlled, and free from worldly undertakings, I shall go forth into the homeless life.
Having reflected thus, I lay down to sleep, O Lord of Men!
As the night was passing away, my pain came to an end. Then, at dawn on the following day, having taken leave of my kinsmen,
I— patient, self-controlled, and free from worldly undertakings— went forth into the homeless life.
Then I became the Knower (Nātha) of myself, of others, and indeed of all beings—both the mobile and the immobile.
(Uttarādhyayana 7.47) The self is the Vaitaraṇī river; the self is the Kūṭaśālmalī tree.
The self is a cow that milks all desires; the self is my own Nandana grove.
The self is both the doer and the undoer of suffering and happiness; the self is both the friend and the enemy, depending on whether it is established in evil or established in goodness.
"O Nivāpas, listen with one-pointed mind and tranquility to this other teaching of the Nirgrantha, having obtained which some men, being very cowardly, grow weary.
He who, having gone forth, does not properly observe the great vows due to negligence..."

Those who are unrestrained and greedy for flavors do not cut the bond at its root. (Uttarādhyayana 751) He who possesses no application whatsoever regarding his conduct, speech, and search for food, nor regarding the carefulness in taking up and putting down [his belongings], does not follow the path that has been generated by the heroic ones. (Uttarādhyayana 752)
Even if one has long delighted in the tonsured state, yet remains unsteady and falls away from penance and restraint;
even after tormenting oneself for a long time, one truly does not attain the further shore in the cycle of rebirth.
Like a fistful of chaff that is essence-less, or like a deceptive, hollow balance-beam, such a person is without substance.
A ruby of Rāḍhā, brilliant like a beryl, becomes indeed priceless among those who know it. (Utt.

754) But he who wears here the outward mark of one of bad conduct, who sustains his life by the banner of a sage, and who calls himself "restrained" while being unrestrained—he meets with ruin even after a long time. (Utt. 755)
Just as the poison Kālakūṭa kills when drunk, or as a weapon kills when wrongly grasped,
so too this Dharma, if fallen into error, kills like a malevolent spirit that has not been properly subdued.
Those who practice the interpretation of bodily marks and dreams, and who are deeply engrossed in omens and curiosity, [are lost].

One who lives by the magic arts of *kuheḍa* and the granting of boons finds no refuge at that time. Indeed, that person of immoral conduct is perpetually miserable; having violated the vow of silence (*mauna*), he wanders through the realms of hell and animal birth, experiencing the reversal of fortune. (Uttarādhyayana 7.5–8)

One who does not renounce food prepared for him, bought for him, or offered as a sacrifice, and who eats anything that is unfit to be sought after— like a fire that devours everything— having committed such evil, he goes [to a lower state] when he passes away from here.
(Uttarādhyayana 7.59) The enemy who cuts one's throat does not do what that person of evil mind does to himself.
When he has fallen into the jaws of death, devoid of compassion, he suffers with remorse; his attachment to the city-dweller’s way of life is useless.
He who fails in the supreme goal finds no purpose even in this world, nor in the world beyond; thus he perishes in both worlds. (Uttarādhyayana 7.60–7.61)

In this very way, those who are like the *chanda* bird—corrupt in conduct and having abandoned the path of the supreme Jinas—become greedy for the taste of sensual pleasures; like female ospreys, they suffer the torment of useless lamentation.
Having heard this well-spoken instruction, which is endowed with the quality of knowledge, the wise man [should follow it].
Having abandoned the entire path of the unvirtuous, one should follow the excellent way of the great *niyaṇṭhas*.

Then, being devoted to the qualities of conduct and observance, and having maintained supreme self-restraint, with no further influx and having exhausted all karma, one attains a vast, unsurpassed, and eternal state. (Uttarādhyayana 7.63–64)
Even though the great ascetic was thus deeply resolute, the great sage of great vows, great fame,
and a great self-restrainer recited this great scripture with great detail.
Then King Śreṇika, being satisfied, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
"The untaught [truth] has been well demonstrated by you according to reality.

(Utt. 766) "Truly, a human birth has been well gained by you; well obtained are the gains, O great sage! You, along with your kinsmen and relatives, are well protected, since you are established on the path of the supreme Jinas. (Utt. 767)

"You are the protector of those who are protectorless; O self-controlled one, I ask forgiveness from you for all living beings, O fortunate one! I wish to be instructed by you regarding the question I asked you and whatever disturbance to your meditation I may have caused."
"Whatever [faults] I have committed against you regarding enjoyments, please forgive all of that for me.

Having thus praised the lion among ascetics with supreme devotion, that lion among kings, together with his harem, his retinue, and his kinsmen, remained devoted to the Dharma with a stainless mind. (Uttarādhyayana 7.69–70)

With the hairs on his body standing on end, having performed a circumambulation and saluted with his head, the lord of men departed. Likewise, another who is enriched by virtues, guarded by the three restraints, and free from the three staves [of sin], [departs].
Like a bird that has escaped [from a cage], he wanders over the earth, free from delusion.
Thus I say.
(Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.72)
In Campā, at the port named Pāṭalī, there was a merchant named Sāvae;
he was a great-souled disciple of the Blessed One Mahāvīra. (Uttarādhyayana 7.3)
In the Nigaṇṭha doctrine, that merchant,
being skilled in trade, while conducting business, arrived at the city of Pihuṇḍa.
While he was trading in Pihuṇḍa, a merchant gave him his daughter.
Having abandoned that wife, he set out for his own country. (Uttarādhyayana 775) Then the wife of Samudrapāli gave birth upon the ocean;
when a son was born there, he was named Samudrapāli. (Uttarādhyayana 776)
Having arrived at Campā by means of his craft, he prospered in the house of a lay follower (śrāvaka) merchant;
his son was well-disposed toward him. Trained in statecraft, he learned the seventy-two arts.
Endowed with youth, handsome, and pleasing to behold,
his father brings him a beautiful wife of lovely form; he sports in delightful palaces like the god Dogundaga.
Then, on another occasion, standing in the palace window,
Samudrapāla saw a man condemned to death, adorned with the ornaments of one about to be executed. Having seen him, he was deeply moved and spoke as follows:
"Alas! This is the terrible outcome of impure deeds.
Having attained supreme spiritual agitation at that moment, the Blessed One, the Fully Awakened One, took leave of his mother and father and went forth into the homeless life.
Having cast off the great affliction of worldly ties, the vast delusion, and all that is entirely terrifying,
one should take delight in the dharma of the religious life (paryāya), as well as in the vows, moral conducts, and hardships.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, then celibacy, and non-possessiveness [are the five vows].
Having undertaken the five great vows, the wise one should practice the Dharma taught by the Jina.

Compassionate toward all living beings, patient and enduring, restrained and practicing celibacy, and avoiding all blameworthy activity, the monk should wander with his senses well-composed. (Uttarādhyayana 7.8–9)
From time to time he should wander through the kingdom, knowing his own strength and weakness;
like a lion, he should not be terrified by sounds, nor should he be agitated upon hearing the application of words.
Observing [the world], he should wander about, enduring all that is pleasant and unpleasant.
One should not find pleasure in everything everywhere, nor should one be attached to honor or blame. (Utt.

787) In this world, there are men of many different inclinations; the monk who practices according to his true disposition will encounter terrifying fears there—whether they be divine, human, or animal. (Utt. 788)
The many hardships are difficult to endure, wherein many cowardly men shiver;
having encountered them there, a monk should not be shaken, like a king of elephants at the head of the battle.
Cold and heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, and various afflictions touch the body.
There, one should endure without agitation; one should wear away the karmic dust previously accumulated.

Having abandoned passion as well as hatred and delusion, O monk, always discerning, like Mount Meru unshaken by the wind, you should endure the hardships with your senses guarded. (Uttarādhyayana 790–791)
The great sage, neither elated nor dejected, and being self-restrained, neither seeks honor nor censures it;
having adopted uprightness, that self-restrained one, practicing renunciation, follows the path to Nirvana.
Enduring both aversion and delight, having abandoned worldly attachments, he is a renunciant devoted to his own welfare and intent on what is supreme.

He dwells with the highest goals in view—his passions severed, free from "mine-ness," and possessing nothing. (Utt. 793) He should frequent secluded dwellings that are free from attachments and not crowded; they were practiced by sages of great renown. He should physically endure all hardships. (Utt. 794)
The great sage, having attained the knowledge of perfect wisdom and having practiced the unsurpassed accumulation of Dharma,
shines like the sun in the sky— possessing unsurpassed knowledge, endowed with glory,
and free from passion, liberated in every respect after exhausting both merit and demerit.
Having crossed over the great flood of existence as if crossing the ocean, O Samuddapāla, you have gone to the state from which there is no return. Thus I say.
In the city of Soriyapura, there was a king of great power named Vasudeva, endowed with the marks of royalty. (Uttarādhyayana 7.9–10)
He had two wives, Rohiṇī and Devakī; from those two, two beloved sons were born, Rāma and Kēśava.
In the city of Sōriyapura, there was a king of great power.

There was one named Samudravijaya, endowed with the marks of royalty. His wife was named Śivā, and their son was the illustrious Blessed One Ariṣṭanemi, the leader of the world and the subduer of the senses.
He was named Ariṣṭanemi, endowed with auspicious marks and a beautiful voice, possessing the eight thousand minor marks; he was Gautama, with a complexion like black antimony.
He had a diamond-like adamantine constitution (*vajrarṣabhasaṃhanana*) and a symmetrical, square-shaped body, with eyes like those of a fish.
From him was born a son, Kesava, the son of Rājamatī.
Then that excellent royal maiden—virtuous, beautiful of form, endowed with all auspicious marks, and possessing the brilliance of lightning, the moon, and jewels—[was born]. (Uttarādhyayana 802–803)
Janaka said to her: "Let the highly powerful Prince Vāsudeva come here; to him I shall give my daughter.
She was bathed with all medicinal herbs, and the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony was performed.
Clad in a divine pair of garments and adorned with ornaments,
he shines even more brilliantly when mounted upon the intoxicated scent-elephant that is the elder brother of Vāsudeva, like a crest-jewel upon the head. (Uttarādhyayana 805–806)
Then, surrounded on all sides by the circle of the Daśārhas, he was adorned with an uplifted parasol and chowries;
he was accompanied by a fourfold army arrayed in due order.
With the resonance of musical instruments and with divine [splendor], he touched the sky.
With such supernatural power (ṛddhi) and supreme majesty,
that bull among merchants departed from his own palace.
Then, as he was being led there, he saw animals terrified by fear, confined within pens and cages, suffering greatly;
though they had attained life, they were to be devoured for the sake of their meat. (Uttarādhyayana 8.10)
Having seen this, that one of great wisdom spoke thus to the charioteer:
"For whose sake are these living beings—all of whom desire happiness—remaining here, confined within cages and enclosures? (Uttarādhyayana 8.11–12)
Then Sārahi said: "These auspicious living beings are for your marriage ceremony, in order to feed many people.
Having heard his words, which involve the slaughter of many living beings, [the prince]...
The one of great wisdom reflects with compassion for living beings:
"If these very many living beings are being harmed on my account, this will certainly not lead to anything beneficial for me in the next world. (Uttarādhyayana 814–815)
The highly illustrious one offered the pair of earrings, the necklace,
and all his ornaments to the charioteer; then,
having made a mental resolve, the gods descended as was appropriate.
Having performed his renunciation with all his splendor and his retinue, he—surrounded by gods and men—then ascended a jeweled palanquin;
having departed from Vārāṇasī, the Blessed One halted at Mount Revata. (Uttarādhyayana 817–818)
Having arrived at the garden, he descended from his excellent palanquin surrounded by a thousand attendants; then he went forth under the constellation Citrā.
Then, with fragrant scents and swift, well-curled [fans]...
He himself plucked out his hair in five handfuls with a concentrated mind.
And Vāsudeva said to him, whose hair was shorn and whose senses were conquered: "O Lord of the Tamed, quickly fulfill your desired wish! (Uttarādhyayana 8.20–21)
"May you increase in knowledge and vision, as well as in conduct, forbearance, and liberation.
Thus spoke Rāma and Keśava, along with many people from the Daśārha clan.
Having paid homage to Ariṣṭanemi, they arrived at the city of Bārāṇasī. Hearing of the renunciation of the Jina, the king’s daughter was devoid of smiles and joy, and she fainted from grief.
Rājimati reflected: "Fie upon my life, since I have been abandoned by him; it is better for me to go forth as a nun.
Then she [climbed] onto those [palanquins] resembling bees, adorned with side-panels like the hoods of serpents.
The wise and resolute ones pluck out their own hair themselves. And Vāsudeva says to him whose hair has been plucked and who has conquered his senses:
"O you who have plucked your hair, cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra very quickly, very quickly! (Utt. 826–827)
Having become a female ascetic, she caused many kinsmen and attendants there to likewise renounce the world— those who were virtuous and learned.
While traveling toward Mount Revatī, she was caught in the rain midway.
In the springtime darkness, inside his cave, as she was spreading out her robes, Rathanemi saw her just as she was born;
then he too was seen by her, his heart broken. (Uttarādhyayana 829–830)
And seeing Sañjaya there, she, out of fear, covered her private parts with her arms and sat down trembling. Then that prince, the son of Samudravijaya—
Seeing her trembling with fear, he spoke these words:
"O auspicious one, O beautiful one, O sweet-spoken one! I am Rathanemi;
come to me, O fair-limbed lady, and you shall suffer no pain. (Utt. 8.32–33)
"Come now, let us enjoy pleasures; for human birth is indeed very difficult to obtain.
Having enjoyed these pleasures, we shall afterwards follow the path of the Jina. [Seeing that Rathanemi had been defeated by his broken pride...]
Ratimati, undisturbed, restrained herself there.

I shall properly restrain that [craving] at the throat by means of the training in the Dharma.

"Excellent, Gautama! Your wisdom is such that this doubt of mine has been severed. Yet there is another doubt of mine; tell me that, O Gautama!
A boat is tossing about in the vast ocean with its great waves."

"The body is called the boat, and the living being (jīva) is called the sailor. (Uttarādhyayana 9.18)
"Saṃsāra has been called an ocean, which the great seers cross over.

In blinding, terrible darkness, many living beings remain;

"I have a doubt regarding this; tell me that, O Gautama!

"And what is this 'place' that has been mentioned? Keśin asked Gautama.

"Nirvāṇa," "freedom from affliction," "perfection," and "the very summit of the world"—that which is secure, auspicious, and free from harm, which the great seers cross over. (Uttarādhyayana 9.28–29)
That eternal abode, the summit of the world so difficult to ascend, which the sages who have reached it do not grieve over, for they have brought an end to existence.
Well said, Gautama! Your wisdom is profound; this doubt of mine has been severed.

9.31) When his doubt had thus been severed, Keśin, of formidable prowess, bowed his head in reverence to the highly illustrious Gautama. (Utt. 9.32)
