[The Fivefold Methods of the Doctrine]
There are eight principles of the doctrine (pavayaṇamāyā), as well as the fivefold carefulness (samiī) and the three restraints (guttī). These are:
carefulness in walking, speaking, eating, taking up objects, and disposing of waste. (Uttarādhyayana 9.36)
Guarding of speech, guarding of mind, and guarding of body as the eighth;
these eight *samitis* have been explained in brief.
Wherein the twelvefold teaching proclaimed by the Jina is found, therein lies the doctrine (*pravacana*).
"A self-restrained monk should practice walking with care, purified by four causes: by means of an object, by time, by the path, and by carefulness.
(Uttarādhyayana 24.39) In this context, the "object" consists of knowledge, vision, and conduct.

When the proper time and day have been stated, and the path is free from obstacles, [the following applies]. (Uttarādhyayana 9.40) Regarding substance, location, time, and likewise state—discipline is said to be fourfold. Listen as I proclaim it to you. (Uttarādhyayana 9.41)

Substantially, he should look with his eyes [only] the distance of a yoke; spatially, as far as he might walk; and temporally, while remaining attentive, he should be so in terms of mental state. Having avoided the objects of the senses, one should practice the fivefold recitation of the scriptures.
Devoted to that liberation and honoring it, one should practice right conduct with focused application.
One should avoid being absorbed in anger, pride, deceit, and greed;
likewise, one should avoid laughter, fear, frivolity, and idle talk.
Having avoided these eight points, the restrained and wise one should speak speech that is blameless, measured, and timely.
[This applies] to the search for food, its acquisition, and the inspection of it for consumption.
One should purify these three: food, clothing, and bedding.

(Uttarādhyayana 9.46) Regarding the first [food], one should purify the origin and procurement; regarding the second [clothing], one should purify the acquisition; and regarding the third [bedding], one should purify the acceptance.
Furthermore, in the matter of consumption, the ascetic who strives for self-restraint should purify the fourfold [set of faults]. (Uttarādhyayana 9.47)
When taking up or putting down two kinds of implements that have been grasped by day or by night, the sage should follow this procedure:
having inspected them with his eyes, the ascetic should wipe them with care.
One should deposit [these things] upon returning, always remaining composed in both respects. (Utt.
9.49) Excrement, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, sweat, food, clothing, the body, or anything else of a similar nature. (Utt. 9.50)
Without entry and without contact, yet there is indeed entry and contact; with entry and without contact, yet there is indeed entry and contact.
(Uttarādhyayana 9.51) Without entry and without contact, it does not cause harm to another.
On level ground that is dry, or even recently cleared, where [the earth] has been turned over for some time,
where it is free from living beings, deeply buried far away, not too close, devoid of holes,
and free from mobile creatures and seeds— one should void excrement and other waste. (Uttarādhyayana 9.52–9.53)
These five types of carefulness (samiti) have been explained in brief; next, I shall describe the three restraints (gupti) in their proper sequence. [Regarding speech:
that which is true, likewise that which is false, and likewise that which is both true and false.
The fourth is truthfulness and non-falsehood; and the guarding of the mind is fourfold.
(Uttarādhyayana 9.55) When the mind is engaged in intent, preparation, or actual undertaking [of harmful action], the striving ascetic should restrain it. (Uttarādhyayana 9.56)
Speech is fourfold: truthful, false, both truthful and false, and neither truthful nor false; such is the restraint of speech.
Likewise, there is instigation (*saṃrambha*), preparation (*samārambha*), and actual undertaking (*ārambha*). (Uttarādhyayana 9.57)
A monk should restrain his body while it is in motion;
whether in standing, sitting, or likewise in lying down, in jumping, leaping, or in the engagement of the sense faculties. (Uttarādhyayana 9.58–59)
A striving ascetic should restrain the body as it is engaged in agitation, preparation, and likewise in actual undertaking.
These are the five types of carefulness (samiti) for the practice of conduct.

Guarding is said to consist in total withdrawal from all unwholesome objects. (Uttarādhyayana 9.61) The sage who properly practices these principles that are the mothers of the teaching is quickly liberated from the entire cycle of existence; he is a wise man. (Uttarādhyayana 9.62)
Thus I say.
— [The Chapter on Sacrifices]
Born into a brahmin family, he was a highly renowned priest named Jayaghoṣa, who performed the sacrifice for Yama;
he was a great sage who restrained the collection of his senses and followed the path.
Wandering from village to village, he reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Outside Vārāṇasī, in a delightful and peaceful garden, he took up residence upon a prepared bed.
Now at that very time, in that city,
there was a Brahmin named Vijayaghosha who performed sacrifices and was learned in the Vedas.
Then, while he was there, an ascetic (anagāra) arrived on the day of breaking his month-long fast.
At the sacrifice of Vijayaghosa, when [the monk] had approached for the sake of alms—while he was standing there in that place—the host refused him, saying:
"I will not give you alms, O monk; beg elsewhere! (Utt. 9.67–68)
Those Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, those twice-born ones devoted to sacrifices, those who are experts in astrology, and those who have reached the further shore of the dharmas—
those who are capable of uplifting both others and themselves.
"O monk! This food, which fulfills all desires, should be given to them. Thus forbidden there by his kinsman, the great sage was neither angry nor pleased, as he was seeking the supreme goal.
Neither for the sake of food, nor for the sake of life, nor even for the sake of livelihood, nor for the sake of their liberation, did he utter these words:
"You do not know the mouth of the Veda, nor do you know that which is the mouth of the sacrifices. (Uttarādhyayana 9.72)

That which is the mouth of the constellations, and that which is the mouth of all phenomena—those who are capable of uplifting both others and themselves, you do not know them; if you know them, then speak. (Uttarādhyayana 9.73–74)
Not missing even a single syllable of that [teaching], he stood there with his retinue, palms joined in reverence; then the Great Sage asked him:
"Tell me, what is the mouth of the Vedas? Tell me, what is the mouth of the sacrifices? (Uttarādhyayana 9.75)
Tell me the mouth of the constellations, or tell me the mouth of all phenomena.
O Sage, you who are capable of uplifting both yourself and others—answer this entire doubt of mine when I have questioned you. (Uttarādhyayana 9.76–77)
The Vedas have the fire-sacrifice as their mouth; the sacrifice has the Vedas as its mouth;
the moon is the mouth of the constellations; and among all things, the Kāśyapa is the mouth.
Just as the planets and other celestial bodies remain with palms joined in reverence toward the moon, so do they stand before him.
Worshipping and paying homage to the most excellent and captivating [Teacher],
those ignorant ones who proclaim sacrifices— possessing the status of Vedic Brahmins—
are deluded by their recitation and austerity, like fires concealed by ashes. (Uttarādhyayana 9.79–80)
In this world, he is called a brahmin, who is honored like fire;
he whom the wise have always perceived as such, him we call a muni.
He who does not cling to what comes to him, and who does not grieve when departing.
He who delights in the words of the noble ones—him we call a brāhmaṇa.
Just as gold that has been refined, from which dross and impurities have been rubbed away, and which is free from passion, hatred, fear, and so forth—him we call a brāhmaṇa. (Uttarādhyayana 9.82–983)
One who is ascetic, emaciated, self-controlled, with flesh and blood wasted away, well-restrained, and having attained nirvāṇa—him we call a brāhmaṇa.
Having understood mobile beings and, by inclusion, stationary beings as well. (Uttarajjhāyā 9.36)

He who does not harm by means of the three [modes of action], him we call a Brāhmaṇa. (Uttarajjhayaṇa 9.35) Whether out of anger, or through laughter, or out of greed, or even out of fear—he who does not speak a falsehood, him we call a Brāhmaṇa. (Uttarajjhayaṇa 9.36)
Whether it be animate or inanimate, small or large, he who does not take what is not given—that person we call a brāhmaṇa.
(Uttarādhyayana 9.36) He who does not indulge in sexual intercourse—whether divine, human, or animal—is a brāhmaṇa. (Uttarādhyayana 9.37)
One who is not defiled by mind, body, or speech— we call him a brahmin.
Just as a lotus born in the water is not smeared by the water,
so too one who is unsmeared by sensual pleasures— we call him a brahmin.

One who is free from greed, living as a sage, a homeless wanderer without possessions, unattached to householders—him we call a *māhaṇa*. [Having abandoned former associations, as well as excessive attachment to kinsmen; he who does not cling to enjoyments—him we call a *māhaṇa*.
All animal sacrifices, all Vedic rituals, and asceticism performed through evil action...
Karmas are indeed powerful; they do not protect one who is immoral. (Utt.
991) One is not a śramaṇa by being shaven-headed, nor a brāhmaṇa by the syllable *oṃ*;
one is not a muni by dwelling in the forest, nor an ascetic by wearing a garment of kusa grass. (Utt. 992)
One becomes a śramaṇa through equanimity, a brāhmaṇa through celibacy,
a muni through knowledge, and an ascetic through austerity. Indeed,
one is a brāhmaṇa by action, and by action one becomes a kṣatriya.
One becomes a Vaiśya by one's actions; one becomes a Śūdra by one's actions. (Utt.
9.36) These [criteria] have been clearly proclaimed by the Buddha, by which one becomes a Snātaka—one liberated from all karma, him we call a Brāhmaṇa. (Utt. 9.37)
"Those who are thus endowed with such qualities and are supreme among men are capable of rescuing both others and themselves.

"O supreme monks, show us favor by [accepting] alms.

Do not wander in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with fear."
One who enjoys sense-pleasures becomes smeared; one who does not enjoy them is not smeared.

Two lumps of clay, one wet and one dry, were thrown [into the mud]. (Uttarādhyayana 10.2)
"Both have struck against a wall; there, the one that is wet sticks. (Utt.
10.3) "In this same way, those of dull intellect who are greedy for sensual pleasures stick [to the world], but those who are dispassionate do not stick, just like that dry ball. (Utt. 10.4)
Thus Vijayaghoṣa, having gone forth as a homeless ascetic in the presence of Jayaghoṣa and having heard the unsurpassed Dharma,
destroyed his former karmas through self-restraint and austerity.
With cries of "Victory! and cries of "Triumph!", they attained unsurpassed success. Thus I say.
[I shall explain] the proper conduct (*sāmāyārī*), which brings liberation from all suffering;
by practicing it, the *nirgranthas* have crossed the ocean of *saṃsāra*. (Uttarādhyayana 10.07)
The first is called *āvaśyakī*, the second is *naiṣedhikī*, and the third is *āpracchanā*; the fourth is *prati-pracchanā*.
The fifth is called *chandanā*, and the sixth is *icchākāra*.
The seventh is *micchākāra* (wrong-doing), and the eighth is *tahakkāra* (so-be-it).
Rising up is the ninth, and the tenth is *uvasampadā* (acceptance); this ten-fold proper conduct (*sāmācārī*) of the monks has been proclaimed. (Uttarādhyayana 10.9–10)

One should perform the *āvaśyikī* (request for permission) when going; one should perform the *naiṣedhikī* (announcement of arrival) when standing; there should be a formal request (*āpṛcchanā*) when performing an act oneself, and a counter-request (*pratipṛcchanā*) when having another perform it.
There is the act of *chandana* (offering) regarding the types of material requisites, and the expression of *icchākāra* (acting according to one's wish) in matters of remembrance.
The expression "micchākāra" is used for blame; "tahakkāra" is used for what has been heard.
Rising to greet, honoring the guru, and attending upon him—thus, when combined in groups of two and five, the *sāmācārī* (code of conduct) is proclaimed. (Uttarādhyayana 10.12–13)
In the first quarter of the day, when the sun has risen,
having inspected one's belongings and having paid homage to the teacher,
one should ask with palms joined: "What must be done by me here?"
"O Venerable One, I desire to be appointed to service or to the study of the scriptures. (Utt.
10.15) "One who is appointed to service should perform it without weariness;
likewise, one appointed to the study of the scriptures should do so for the sake of liberation from all suffering. (Utt. 10.16)
A discerning monk should divide the day into four parts;
then, throughout all four divisions of the day, he should practice the higher virtues.
During the first watch, he should engage in recitation; during the second, he should meditate in dhyāna.
During the third [watch] one should go for alms, and during the fourth, one should engage in study.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, there are two *pauruṣīs*; in the month of Pauṣa, there are four;
and in the months of Caitra and Aśvayuja, there are three *pauruṣīs*.

"In seven nights it increases or decreases by one finger-breadth, in a fortnight by two finger-breadths, and in a month by four finger-breadths; [this occurs] in the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and in Bhādrapada, Kārttika, and Pauṣa. (Uttarādhyayana 10.20)
In the months of Phālguna and Vaiśākha, the days to be subtracted (ōmaratta) are to be known [as two].
In Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha, the inspection (paḍilēhā) is with six fingers;
in the second [month] it is with eight, and in the third with ten and eight in the fourth.
A discerning monk should divide his time into four parts for pleasure;
then he should apply himself to the higher virtues during all four watches of the night:
during the first watch, he should engage in study; during the second, he should practice meditation.
In the third [watch] one should indeed take rest from sleep, and in the fourth, once again, study (svādhyāya). When the constellation that brings the night has reached the fourth quarter of the sky,
one should cease study at the time of dawn.
On that very constellation, when the sky has three-quarters remaining [and it is] even during the night-watch, the sage, having inspected [his requisites], should act;
in the first quarter, having inspected his belongings.

Having paid homage to the teacher, one should perform the recitation (svādhyāya) which brings liberation from suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 10.27) When a fourth part of the *pauruṣī* remains, having then paid homage to the teacher and without yet performing the ritual of confession (*pratikramaṇa*) for the time, one should inspect the alms-bowl. (Uttarādhyayana 10.28)
Having inspected the mouth-cloth (muhapotti), one should inspect the dust-heap (gocchaga);
with fingers placed within the dust-heap, one should inspect the robes.
First, one should inspect the robe itself—upwards, steadily, and without haste.
One should shake off dust once, and a second time one should wipe it away;
[this constitutes] not dancing, not leaping, not being continuous [in movement], and indeed not being a "mosalī" (one who strikes with the hand).
These are the six "purimas" and nine "khōḍas," along with the cleansing of hands with hands. (Uttarādhyayana 10.30–31)
Ārabhaḍā, sammaddā, and thirdly mōsalī which must be avoided;
fourth is papphōḍaṇā, and sixth is vikkhittā vēiyā. [These are] loose, hanging, and swaying; single-sided, and shaking in many ways.

One should not commit negligence regarding the measure; one should perform the counting with apprehension. (Utt. 1033) The inspection should be neither deficient nor excessive, and likewise free from transposition.
Of these, the first case is praised, while the remaining ones are unpraised. (Utt. 1034)
While performing the inspection (*paḍilehaṇa*), he engages in conversation with others, discusses worldly affairs, gives a formal renunciation (*paccakkhāṇa*), recites [scriptures], or receives them.
[He thus harms] the earth, water, fire, air, plants, and mobile beings. (Uttarādhyayana 10.35)
One who performs the inspection of his alms-bowl with negligence becomes a violator of all six [classes of living beings].
(Uttarādhyayana 10.36) During the third watch of the day, one should seek food and drink when any of the six permissible causes has arisen. (Uttarādhyayana 10.37)

For the sake of alleviating pain, for the sake of service, for the sake of proper movement, for the sake of self-restraint, for the sake of sustaining life, and sixthly, for the sake of reflecting upon the Dharma;
a wise Nirgrantha, as well as a Nirgranthī, should not [consume food] except for these six reasons. (Uttarādhyayana 10.38)
By these circumstances, moreover, he remains without transgression:

[in cases of] illness or affliction, through endurance, for the protection of the vows of celibacy, for the sake of compassion toward living beings, for the purpose of austerity, and for the sake of the destruction of the body. (Uttarādhyayana 10.39–40)
The sage should greedily seek out any remaining goods, inspecting them with his eyes from a distance of less than half a *yojana*, and then wander through the monastery.
Having set down his bowl during the fourth watch of the day...
Then he should perform recitation (*sajjhāya*), which reveals all states of existence.
During the fourth quarter of the *pauruṣī*, having paid homage to the teacher and having performed the ritual of confession (*pratikramaṇa*) for the time, he should inspect his bedding.
A mendicant should carefully inspect the ground for defecation and urination;
then he should perform the *kāyotsarga* (meditative posture), which brings liberation from all suffering.
He should reflect upon his transgressions of the day in their proper sequence.
In knowledge, in vision, and likewise in conduct;
having completed the kāyotsarga and having saluted the guru, one should confess the transgressions of the day according to the rule. (Uttarādhyayana 10.45–46)
Having performed the pratikramaṇa and become free from thorns (nirśalya), and having then paid homage to the Guru,
one should perform the kāyotsarga for liberation from all suffering.
Having established a connection with the Siddhas and then paid homage to the Guru...
Having performed the auspicious rites at dawn, one should observe the proper time.
One should engage in recitation during the first watch, practice meditation during the second,
take rest during the third, and resume recitation during the fourth.

During the fourth *pauruṣī*, when the time has been inspected, one should then perform the study (*svādhyāya*), provided that the unrenounced ones (*asaṃyata*) have not yet awakened. During the fourth quarter of the *pauruṣī*, having then paid homage to the teacher...
Having performed the confession at the proper time, one should inspect [the area].

When the time for the release from bodily activity has arrived—that which brings liberation from all suffering—one should then perform the *kāyotsarga*, the liberation from all suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 10.51–52)

Having completed the kāyotsarga and having saluted the guru, one should then reflect in due order upon the transgressions of the night regarding knowledge, vision, conduct, and austerity. (Uttarādhyayana 10.53)
One should confess one's nightly transgressions according to their actual occurrence.
Having performed the pratikramaṇa and become free from the "thorns" (of inner affliction), one should then pay homage to the guru and perform the kāyotsarga for liberation from all suffering.
"What shall I undertake?"— having thus reflected there,
and having completed the *kāyotsarga*, one should perform the praise of the Jina. Having completed the *kāyotsarga* and then having paid homage to the Guru...
Having fully adopted this, one should cultivate intimacy with the perfected ones (siddhas).
This code of conduct (sāmācārī) has been explained in brief;
by practicing it, many beings have crossed the ocean of saṃsāra. (Uttarādhyayana 10.57–58)
Thus I say.
[The Chapter on the Wild Colt]
The elder Garga was a leader of the group (gaṇadhara), a sage, and an expert; having entered into the state of a leader, he maintained his composure.
For one who carries a load across a wilderness, the desert is traversed.
For one who exerts himself in yoga, saṃsāra passes away. (Utt. 1060) But he who yokes a wild horse suffers while struggling; he experiences lack of composure, and his goad breaks. (Utt. 1061)
One bites its tail; one repeatedly pierces [others];
one breaks a yoke-pin; one has set out upon a wrong path. One falls on its side; it lies down and rests.
He leaps up and bounds about; like a rogue young cow, he falls down.
When deluded, he falls headlong; when angry, he goes in the opposite direction.
With a murderous look, he stands still; and with great speed, he runs away. (Uttarādhyayana 10.63–64)
Just as a stallion cuts through a leather strap and breaks both its yokes, even after being thoroughly weakened and exhausted, it flees;
so too are bad disciples like unruly horses. (Uttarādhyayana 10.65)
Those who are yoked to the chariot of Dharma, yet are weak in fortitude, are being burned [by their passions]. Some here are proud of their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*);
some are proud of their taste for flavors; some are proud of their comfort; and some are long-simmering with anger. (Uttarādhyayana 10.66–67)
Some are lazy regarding alms-gathering; some are afraid of being humiliated; and some, being stubborn, do not accept instruction through various reasons and arguments.
Such a person speaks intermediately [between truth and falsehood] and commits only evil.
She constantly opposes the words of the teachers.
She does not recognize me, nor will she give [to me]; she has gone out, I think—let some other monk go there. (Uttarādhyayana 10.69–70)
They deceive by means of [false] weights; they wander about on all sides, imagining themselves to be royal ministers, and they knit their brows in their faces.
Though they have been honored, gathered around, and nourished with food and drink, (they act thus).
Like swans belonging to their own flock, they fly off in every direction. (Utt.
1072) Then the charioteer thought:
"What use have I for these wicked-natured, unruly horses? I am being brought to ruin by them. (Utt. 1073)
As are my disciples, so are the Galigaddahas;
having abandoned the Galigaddaha state, he firmly undertakes asceticism—endowed with gentleness and mildness, profound, and well-composed. (Uttarādhyayana 10.7–8)
The Great-Souled One dwells upon the earth with himself made of virtue. Thus I say.
Listen to the true path to liberation as spoken by the Jina,
which is endowed with four causes and characterized by knowledge and vision. (Uttarādhyayana 10.76)
Knowledge and vision, as well as conduct and austerity—
this is declared to be the path by the Jinas, the seers of the supreme.
Knowledge and vision, as well as conduct and austerity.
Having entered this path, living beings go to a happy destination.

Therein, knowledge is fivefold: scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), perceptual knowledge (*ābhinibodhika*), the third being clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*), as well as mental knowledge (*manah-paryaya*) and omniscience (*kevala*).
This fivefold knowledge of all substances, qualities, and modifications has been taught by the possessors of knowledge (the Jinas).
Substance is the locus of qualities, and qualities reside in a single substance.
The characteristics and the modes, however, are both inherent in them. (Utt.
1081) Dharma, adharma, space, time, and soul-beings—this is declared to be the world by the Jinas, the supreme seers. (Utt. 1082)
Dharma, adharma, and space—each of these is a single substance; substances are infinite, as are time, matter, and souls.
(Uttarādhyayana 10.18) Furthermore, Dharma has the characteristic of motion, while Adharma has the characteristic of stationariness.
Space is the container of all substances; its characteristic is to provide accommodation.
Time is characterized by the occurrence of change; the soul is characterized by the capacity for effort (upayoga), as well as by knowledge, vision, pleasure, and pain. (Uttarādhyayana 10.84–85)
Knowledge and vision, conduct and likewise austerity, energy and apprehension— this is the characteristic of the soul.
Or rather, sound, darkness, light, radiance, shadow, and heat [are its characteristics].
Color, taste, smell, and touch are the characteristics of persons (pudgalas). Unity and plurality, number, configuration,
conjunction, and disjunction are the characteristics of modes (paryāyas).
Living beings, non-living beings, bondage, merit, demerit, influx, as well as stoppage, shedding, and liberation— these nine are established by the Truthful One (Uttarādhyayana 10.89).
Indeed, the instruction regarding these real entities concerns their true existence.
For one who has faith through inner disposition, that is declared to be right conviction (*samyaktva*). [Uttarādhyayana 28.10] It consists of:

natural faith, faith through instruction, faith through the command, faith through scripture, faith through the seed, faith through comprehension, faith through expansion, faith through action, faith through summary, and faith through the Dharma. [Uttarādhyayana 28.11]
Living beings and non-living beings, merit and demerit, as well as influx and restraint, are understood through their essential meaning; one who approves of renunciation indeed destroys them.
He who himself has faith in the fourfold states perceived by the Jina, [attains liberation].
"He who says, 'It is exactly thus,' is to be known as one whose faith is innate (nisargaruci). (Utt.

1093) "Furthermore, he who has faith in these very doctrines as they have been taught by another—whether by a Kevalin or by a Chadmastha—is to be known as one whose faith is derived from instruction (upadeśaruci).
He from whom passion, hatred, delusion, and ignorance have departed,
and who delights in the Command, is indeed one who delights in the Command (āṇāruī).
He who, while studying the Sūtras, penetrates right conviction through the Sūtra [is one who delights in the Sūtra].

Whether by means of a single limb or all of them, he who is devoted to the scriptures is to be known as one who delights in the scriptures (*sūtra-ruci*). (Uttarādhyayana 10.96) He who, from a single word, causes many words to flow forth—just as a drop of oil spreads upon water—is to be known as one who delights in the meaning (*bīja-ruci*). (Uttarādhyayana 10.97)

He indeed possesses the light of comprehension (*abhigamaruī*), for whom the meaning of the eleven *aṅgas*, the *Païnnagas*, and the *Diṭṭhivāya* has been seen through scriptural knowledge (*suyanāṇa*).
He is one by whom all the states of substances have been apprehended through all the means of valid cognition (*pamāṇa*).
One who delights in all the methods of reasoning (nayavidhi) is to be known as one who delights in elaboration (vitthārarui). (Utt.

1099) He who delights in right view, knowledge, and conduct, as well as in austerity, discipline, truthfulness, the equanimities, and the restraints—that one is indeed called a "delighter in action" (kiriyāruī). (Utt. 1100)

One who does not hold dogmatic views and whose faith is based on the *saṅkheva* (the essential summary) should be known as one who is not averse to the teaching (*pavayaṇa*) and who is non-dogmatic regarding the remaining [doctrines].
He who [upholds] the doctrine of the substantial entities (*atthikāya*), the doctrine of the scriptures (*suyadhamma*), and indeed the doctrine of conduct (*carittadhamma*)...
He who has faith in what is taught by the Jina should be known as one who delights in the Dharma. (Utt.

1102) Faith in right conviction consists of: intimacy with the ultimate truth, devotion to those who have clearly perceived the ultimate truth, and the avoidance of those with perverted views. (Utt. 1103)

There is no conduct devoid of right view; however, regarding vision (darśana), it should be understood that right view and conduct may arise either simultaneously or with right view coming first. There is no knowledge for one who lacks vision, and without knowledge, the qualities of conduct do not exist.

For one devoid of virtues there is no liberation; for one who has not attained liberation there is no nirvāṇa. (Uttarādhyayana 11.05) Freedom from doubt, freedom from hesitation, freedom from indecision, and unclouded vision; then encouragement, stabilization, affection, and glorification—these are the eight [ways to support the Saṃgha]. (Uttarādhyayana 11.06)
The first is for the purpose of equanimity (sāmāyika); the second is that of restoration after a breach (chedopasthāpana);
then there is that of purification through renunciation (parihāraviśuddhi), as well as the subtle (sūkṣma) and that which pertains to the passions (saṃparāya);

[finally] there is that which is free from passions (akaṣāya), known as the "as it is spoken" (yathākhyāta), belonging either to one still possessed of the fourfold veil (chadmastha) or to a Victor (jina).
This conduct, which brings about the accumulation [of merit], is declared to be the highest conduct. (Utt. 1108) Austerity is said to be twofold: external and likewise internal.
External austerity is said to be sixfold; likewise, internal austerity is sixfold. (Utt. 1109)
Through knowledge one knows the states of existence; through vision one has faith;
through conduct one restrains them; and through austerity one becomes purified.
Having exhausted former karmas by means of self-restraint and austerity, [one attains liberation].
The great seers, having abandoned all suffering, depart. Thus I say.

[On Right Effort] I have heard this, O Venerable One: thus it was declared by that Blessed One. Indeed, here is the chapter named "Right Effort" (Sammattaparakkama), which has been proclaimed by the Śramaṇa, the Blessed Mahāvīra, the Kāśyapa. Having correctly believed, trusted, found pleasure in, touched, protected, fulfilled, praised, honored, and followed it according to the command, many living beings attain perfection, awaken, are liberated, reach final nirvāṇa, and make an end to all suffering.

For him, this meaning is thus proclaimed, namely: spiritual agitation (*saṃvega*), detachment (*nirveda*), faith in the Dharma (*dharmaśraddhā*), service to the guru and fellow-monks (*guru-sādharmika-śuśrūṣaṇatā*), confession (*ālocanā*), self-reproach (*nindanā*), and censure by others (*garhaṇā*); the *sāmāyika* (equanimity), the *caturviṃśatistava* (praise of the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras), the *vandana* (salutation), the *pratikramaṇa* (repentance), the *kāyotsarga* (renunciation of the body), the *pratyākhyāna* (renunciation of activities), the *stava-stuti-maṅgala* (auspicious hymns and praises), the inspection of time (*kāla-pratilekhanā*), the performance of penance (*prāyaścitta-karaṇa*), asking for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*), sacred study (*svādhyāya*), teaching (*vācanā*), questioning (*paripṛcchanā*), recitation (*parivartanā*), reflection (*anuprekṣā*), religious discourse (*dharmakathā*), the cultivation of the scriptures (*śruta-ārādhanā*), the concentration of the one-pointed mind (*ekāgra-manas-saṃniveśanā*), self-restraint (*saṃyama*), austerity (*tapas*), purification (*vyavadāna*), the experience of happiness (*sukha-āsvāda*), lack of attachment (*apratibaddhatā*), the use of secluded lodgings and seats (*vivikta-śayanāsana-sevanā*), withdrawal from worldly affairs (*vinivartanā*), renunciation of communal enjoyment (*sambhoga-pratyākhyāna*), renunciation of requisites (*upadhi-pratyākhyāna*), renunciation of food (*āhāra-pratyākhyāna*)... renunciation of the passions (*kaṣāya-pratyākhyāna*), renunciation of activities (*yoga-pratyākhyāna*), renunciation of the body (*śarīra-pratyākhyāna*), renunciation of companions (*sahāya-pratyākhyāna*), renunciation of meals (*bhakta-pratyākhyāna*), renunciation of internal states (*sadbhāva-pratyākhyāna*); propriety (*pratirūpatā*), service (*vaiyāvṛtya*), the possession of all virtues (*sarvaguṇa-sampannatā*), freedom from passion (*vītarāgatā*); forbearance (*kṣānti*), equanimity (*mukti*), gentleness (*mārdava*), uprightness (*ārjava*), truthfulness of intention (*bhāva-satya*), truthfulness of action (*karaṇa-satya*), truthfulness of activity (*yoga-satya*); restraint of mind (*manoguptatā*), restraint of speech (*vāgguptatā*), restraint of body (*kāyaguptatā*); concentration of mind (*manaḥ-samādhāraṇā*), concentration of speech (*vāk-samādhāraṇā*), concentration of body (*kāya-samādhāraṇā*); perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-sampannatā*), perfection of vision (*darśana-sampannatā*), perfection of conduct (*cāritra-sampannatā*); control of the sense of hearing (*śrotrendriya-nigraha*), control of the sense of sight (*cakṣurindriya-nigraha*), control of the sense of smell (*ghrāṇendriya-nigraha*), control of the sense of taste (*jihvendriya-nigraha*), control of the sense of touch (*sparśendriya-nigraha*); conquest of anger (*krodha-vijaya*), conquest of pride (*māna-vijaya*), conquest of deceit (*māyā-vijaya*), conquest of greed (*lobha-vijaya*), conquest of attachment, aversion, and false vision (*prema-dveṣa-mithyādarśana-vijaya*); the state of being like a mountain (*śaileśī*), and the state of being free from karma (*akarmatā*).

"Venerable sir, what does agitation (*saṃvega*) produce in a living being? Agitation produces unsurpassed faith in the Dharma. Through unsurpassed faith in the Dharma, one quickly attains agitation. One destroys the infinite-binding (*anantānubandhi*) anger, pride, deceit, and greed. One does not bind new karma. And by performing the purification of wrong belief (*mithyātva-viśodhi*) based upon that, one becomes an *ārādhaka* of right vision (*darśana*). And when the purification of vision is thoroughly cleansed, some attain perfection, awaken, are liberated, become cooled, and make an end to all suffering in that very same birth. And when the purification is thoroughly cleansed, one does not exceed a third birth."

"Venerable sir, what does equanimity (nirveda) produce for the soul? Through equanimity, one quickly attains detachment from divine, human, and animal sensual pleasures. One becomes dispassionate toward all objects of the senses. Becoming dispassionate toward all objects of the senses, one abandons worldly undertakings (ārambha). By abandoning worldly undertakings, one cuts off the path of saṃsāra and becomes one who has entered the path to liberation (siddhi)."

"Venerable Sir, what does faith in the Dharma produce for a living being? Through faith in the Dharma, one who is attached to worldly pleasures becomes dispassionate. He abandons the householder's life and, as a homeless ascetic, brings about the cessation of physical and mental sufferings—such as cutting, piercing, and binding—and he accomplishes the bliss of freedom from affliction."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through service to the guru and fellow-monks? Through service to the guru and fellow-monks, one produces the practice of humility (*vinayapratipatti*). And the living being who has practiced humility becomes characterized by a nature free from disrespect; he blocks the miserable destinies of hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods. Through praise, kindling of devotion, and great respect, he secures the human and divine destinies, and purifies the path to liberation and a happy state. Furthermore, he accomplishes all commendable tasks rooted in humility. Moreover, he becomes one who disciplines many other living beings."

“Venerable sir, what does confession (*ālōyaṇā*) produce for the soul? Through confession, one effects the uprooting of the thorns of deceit, worldly attachment, and false view—which are obstacles on the path to liberation and causes of bondage in infinite saṃsāra. It also produces rectitude (*ujjubhāva*). And the soul that has attained rectitude does not bind the female or neuter passions; rather, it wears away those previously bound.”

"Venerable sir, what does self-reproach produce for a living being? Self-reproach produces remorse. Through remorse, becoming dispassionate, one enters the ladder of the stages of refinement (*karaṇaguṇaseḍhi*). And having entered the ladder of the stages of refinement, the monk eradicates the deluding karma (*mohanijja-kamma*)."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through reproach (*garahaṇayā*)? Through reproach, it produces a lack of self-regard (*apurakkāra*). When a living being is devoid of self-regard, it desists from unwholesome activities (*aprasasta-yoga*) and adopts wholesome ones (*prasasta-yoga*). Having adopted wholesome activities, the mendicant (*anagāra*) destroys infinite destructive states (*ananta-ghāti-paryāya*). Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through equanimity (*sāmāiya*)? Through equanimity, it produces the renunciation of blameworthy activities (*sāvadya-yoga-virati*). Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through the praise of the twenty-four [Tīrthaṅkaras] (*cauvvīsatthaya*)? Through the praise of the twenty-four, it produces the purification of right vision (*darśana-viśodhi*)."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through salutation (*vandana*)? Through salutation, one exhausts the karma of low status (*nīcāgotra*) and binds the karma of high status (*uccāgotra*). Furthermore, it produces unimpeded good fortune (*saubhāgya*) as the fruit of its command, and it generates a disposition of respectfulness (*dākṣiṇya*). Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through repentance (*pratikramaṇa*)? Through repentance, one closes the fissures of one's vows. When the fissures of one's vows are closed, the living being dwells with the influxes (*āsrava*) restrained, with conduct free from blemish, engaged in the eight fundamentals of the teaching (*pravacanamātṛkā*), without duplicity, and well-composed."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through *kāyotsarga* (posture of renunciation)? Through *kāyotsarga*, one purifies past and present transgressions. And when his transgressions are purified, the living being, with his welfare at peace, like a burden-carrier who has laid down his load, attains auspicious meditation and dwells in happiness upon happiness.

Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through *pratyākhyāna* (renunciation)? Through *pratyākhyāna*, one blocks the doors of influx (*āsrava*). Through *pratyākhyāna*, one produces the restraint of desire. And when the living being has attained the restraint of desire, he dwells with craving for all things subdued and become cool."

"Venerable sir, what does the auspiciousness of praise and hymns produce for the soul? The auspiciousness of praise and hymns produces the attainment of right knowledge, right vision, right conduct, and spiritual awakening (*bodhi*). And the soul, endowed with the attainment of right knowledge, right vision, right conduct, and spiritual awakening, achieves the perfection of practice leading to liberation and rebirth in celestial palaces (*kappa-vimāna*).
Venerable sir, what does the inspection of the time produce for the soul? The inspection of the time destroys the karma that obscures right knowledge."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce by performing expiation (*pāyacchitta*)? By performing expiation, it produces purification from evil karma (*pāpakamma*). It also becomes free from transgression (*niraticāra*). Furthermore, one who correctly receives and undertakes expiation purifies both the path and the fruit of the path, and he accomplishes both right conduct (*ācāra*) and the fruit of right conduct."

"Venerable sir, what does the act of asking for forgiveness produce in a living being? The act of asking for forgiveness produces a state of gladness. Having attained a state of gladness, one generates a sense of friendship toward all breathers, beings, living things, and souls. And having generated a sense of friendship, the living being, having performed purification of the internal state, becomes fearless.
Venerable sir, what does self-study produce in a living being? Through self-study, one exhausts the karma that obscures knowledge."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through recitation (*vāyaṇā*)? Through recitation, one produces *nirjarā* (the shedding of karma). One remains engaged in the non-neglect and non-disparagement of the sacred scripture. Remaining engaged in the non-neglect and non-disparagement of the sacred scripture, one upholds the religion of the *Tīrthaṅkara*. Upholding the religion of the *Tīrthaṅkara*, one becomes characterized by great *nirjarā* and a great final liberation.

Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through questioning (*paḍipucchaṇā*)? Through questioning, one purifies the scripture, its meaning, and both together. One eradicates the karma that causes delusion through doubt (*kaṅkhāmōhaṇijja-kamma*)."
"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through recitation? Through recitation, it produces phonemes and brings about the attainment of phonemes."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through subtle reflection (*aṇuppēhā*)? Through subtle reflection, the soul transforms the seven types of karma—excluding that which determines lifespan—from being bound with tight bonds into being bound with loose bonds. It transforms those with long duration into those with short duration; it transforms those with intense fruition into those with mild fruition; and it transforms those with many particles into those with few particles. Furthermore, regarding the karma of lifespan, it may bind it, or it may not bind it. Moreover, it no longer repeatedly accumulates karma that results in unpleasant sensation. And it quickly traverses the wilderness of the fourfold cycle of existence, which is beginningless, endless, and of long duration."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through religious discourse (*dhammakahā*)? Through religious discourse, the soul produces the wearing away of karma (*kamma-nijjarā*). Through religious discourse, it glorifies the teaching (*pavayaṇa*). By glorifying the teaching, the soul binds karma that leads to auspiciousness in the future. "Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through the practice of study (*suyassa ārāhaṇā*)? Through the practice of study, the soul destroys ignorance and does not become defiled. "Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through the settling of the mind in one-pointedness (*ēgaggamanasaṁnivēsaṇā*)? Through the settling of the mind in one-pointedness, the soul effects the restraint of the mind (*cittanirōha*)."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through self-restraint? Through self-restraint, it produces the state of non-influx. Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through austerity? Through austerity, it produces purification. Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through purification? Through purification, it produces non-action. Having attained non-action, thereupon it becomes perfected, enlightened, liberated, and cooled, making an end to all suffering."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through the pursuit of happiness? Through the pursuit of happiness, it produces freedom from envy. Through freedom from envy, the living being, out of compassion, becomes gentle and free from sorrow, and exhausts the karma that deludes conduct (*cāritramohanīya-karma*). Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through non-attachment (*apratibaddhatā*)? Through non-attachment, it produces lack of worldly ties (*niḥsaṅgatva*). Through lack of worldly ties, the living being remains alone with a one-pointed mind, neither clinging nor attached, wandering day and night."

"Venerable sir, what does the practice of using secluded lodgings and seats produce for a living being? The practice of using secluded lodgings and seats produces the protection of conduct (*carittagutti*). And when a living being has protected conduct, eats secluded food, possesses firm conduct, is devoted to solitude, and has entered the state of liberation, he wears away the eightfold knot of karma."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through withdrawal (*viniyaṭṭaṇayā*)? Through withdrawal, one applies oneself to the non-committal of evil karmas. Furthermore, through the wearing away (*nijjaraṇayā*) of previously bound [karma], evil is turned back. Thereafter, one traverses the wilderness of the fourfold cycle of existence (*cāurantasaṃsārakantāra*)."

"Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of social enjoyment produce for the soul? Through the renunciation of social enjoyment, one destroys the supports [for attachment]. For one who is without support, the yogas become established in the self. One is satisfied with one's own gains; one does not covet the gains of others, nor does one long for them, nor desire them, nor crave them, nor yearn for them. Not coveting, not longing for, not desiring, not craving, and not yearning for the gains of others, one dwells having attained a second kind of easy sleep."

"Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of possessions (*uvahipaccakkhāṇa*) produce for the soul? Through the renunciation of possessions, it produces freedom from entanglement (*apalimantha*). Being without possessions, the soul is free from doubt and is not defiled by the absence of possessions.

Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of food (*āhārapaccakkhāṇa*) produce for the soul? Through the renunciation of food, it cuts off the attachment to life (*jīviyā-saṁsappaōga*). Having cut off the attachment to life, the soul is not defiled by the absence of food."

"Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of passions (*kasāya-paccakkhāṇa*) produce in the soul? The renunciation of passions produces the state of being free from passion (*vīyarāga-bhāva*). And when the soul has attained the state of being free from passion, it becomes equal toward pleasure and pain.

Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of activity (*joga-paccakkhāṇa*) produce in the soul? The renunciation of activity produces the state of non-activity (*ajōgatta*). Being in a state of non-activity, the soul does not bind new karma and wears away (*nijjarēi*) that which was previously bound."

"Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of the body produce for the soul? Through the renunciation of the body, it brings about the manifestation of the hundredfold qualities of the perfected ones (siddhas). And the soul, endowed with those hundredfold qualities of the perfected ones, having reached the summit of the universe, becomes supremely happy."

"Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of companions produce for the soul? The renunciation of companions produces singleness (*egībhāva*). And the soul, having attained singleness and contemplating unity, becomes one who has little noise, little clamor, little quarreling, little passion, and little mutual resentment; it becomes abundant in self-restraint (*saṃyama*), abundant in restraint (*saṃvara*), and also becomes concentrated (*samāhita*).
Venerable sir, what does the renunciation of food (*bhattapaccakkhāṇa*) produce for the soul? Through the renunciation of food, it obstructs many hundreds of existences."

"Venerable sir, what does a soul produce by means of sincere renunciation? By sincere renunciation, it produces non-returning (*aniyaṭṭi*). Having attained non-returning, the homeless ascetic destroys the four remaining portions of karma, namely: feeling (*vedanīya*), lifespan (*āyu*), name (*nāman*), and status (*gotra*). Thereafter, he attains perfection, awakens, is liberated, and puts an end to all suffering."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through propriety (*paḍirūvayā*)? Through propriety, one produces lightness (*lāghaviya*). Being light, the living being becomes heedful, possessing manifest signs, possessing praiseworthy signs, possessing pure right conviction (*sammatta*), perfected in the seven codes of conduct (*sattasamiī*), trustworthy toward all breathers, beings, souls, and living creatures, free from blemish, with senses subdued, and endowed with extensive austerity and conduct.
Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through service (*veyāvacca*)? Through service, one binds the karma of a Tīrthaṅkara (*titthayaranāmakamma*)."

"Venerable sir, what does a soul produce by being endowed with all virtues? By being endowed with all virtues, it produces non-return [to rebirth]. Having attained non-return, the soul no longer becomes a partaker of physical or mental sufferings. Venerable sir, what does a soul produce by being free from passion (*vītarāgatā*)? It severs the bonds of affection and the bonds of craving; it becomes dispassionate toward pleasant and unpleasant sounds, touches, forms, tastes, and smells, whether they be animate, inanimate, or mixed."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through forbearance (*khanti*)? Through forbearance, one conquers the afflictions (*parīsaha*). Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through detachment (*mutti*)? Through detachment, one produces non-possession (*akiñcaṇa*). And a living being who is without possessions becomes undesirable to men who are greedy for wealth. Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through honesty (*ajjava*)? Through honesty, one produces rectitude of action (*kāujjuyaya*), rectitude of intention (*bhāvujjuyaya*), rectitude of speech (*bhāsujjuyaya*), and non-deceptiveness (*avisaṃvāyaṇa*). Through the attainment of non-deceptiveness, a living being becomes a fulfiller of the Dharma."

"Venerable sir, what does gentleness produce in a living being? Gentleness produces freedom from arrogance. Through freedom from arrogance, a living being endowed with mildness and gentleness brings to an end the eight grounds of pride. Venerable sir, what does truthfulness of disposition produce in a living being? Truthfulness of disposition produces purity of disposition. Abiding in purity of disposition, a living being applies himself to the practice of the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats. Having applied himself to the practice of the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats, he becomes one who practices the Dharma pertaining to the next world."

"Venerable sir, what does a soul produce through truthfulness of action (*karaṇasacca*)? Through truthfulness of action, it produces the power of action. When abiding in truthfulness of action, the soul becomes one who acts according to its speech. Venerable sir, what does a soul produce through truthfulness of conduct (*jōgasacca*)? Through truthfulness of conduct, it purifies its conduct. Venerable sir, what does a soul produce through the guarding of the mind (*managuttayā*)? Through the guarding of the mind, the soul produces one-pointedness of mind. With a one-pointed mind, the soul that guards its mind becomes an achiever of self-restraint (*sañjama*)."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through the restraint of speech (*vayaguttayā*)? Through the restraint of speech, one produces freedom from agitation (*nivviyāra*). A living being who is free from agitation and restrained in speech dwells endowed with the accomplishment of internal mental application (*ajjhappajōga*). Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through the restraint of body (*kāyaguttayā*)? Through the restraint of body, one produces restraint (*saṃvara*). Being restrained in body by means of that restraint, one effects the cessation of the influx of evil (*pāvāsava*)."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through mental assimilation (*manasamāhāraṇā*)? Through mental assimilation, it produces one-pointedness (*egagga*). Having produced one-pointedness, it produces the modes of knowledge (*nāṇapajjava*). Having produced the modes of knowledge, it purifies right conviction (*sammatta*) and wears away wrong belief (*micchatta*).

Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through vocal assimilation (*vaïsamāhāraṇā*)? Through vocal assimilation, it purifies the modes of vision (*daṃsaṇapajjava*). Having purified the modes of vision, it brings about the state of having easily attained enlightenment (*sulahabōhiyatta*) and wears away the state of having difficulty attaining enlightenment (*dullahabōhiyatta*)."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through the concentration of the body (*kāyasamāhāraṇā*)? Through the concentration of the body, it purifies the states of conduct (*carittapajjava*). Having purified the states of conduct, it purifies the conduct of the 'as-it-is-spoken' (*ahakkhāyacaritta*). Having purified the conduct of the 'as-it-is-spoken', it destroys the four types of *kevalī-karma*. Thereafter, it becomes perfected (*sijjhaï*), awakened (*bujjhaï*), liberated (*muccaï*), and completely extinguished (*parinivvāyaï*), making an end to all suffering."

"Venerable sir, what does a soul produce through the possession of knowledge? Through the possession of knowledge, a soul produces the comprehension of all states of existence. A soul possessed of knowledge does not perish in the fourfold wilderness of *saṃsāra*. It attains the application of knowledge, discipline, austerity, conduct, and yoga; it becomes an expert in its own doctrine and the doctrines of others, and one who cannot be led astray. Just as a needle with its thread remains intact even if it falls, so too a soul that possesses the 'thread' (knowledge) does not perish in *saṃsāra*. (Uttarādhyayana 11.73)

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce through the possession of right vision (*darśana*)? Through the possession of right vision, one effects the cutting off of the delusion of worldly existence (*bhava-mithyātva*) and does not become further deluded. Not becoming further deluded, and disciplining oneself with supreme knowledge and vision, one dwells properly cultivating [the self]."

“Venerable Sir, what does a soul produce through the perfection of conduct (*carittasampannayā*)? Through the perfection of conduct, it produces the state of being like a mountain (*selēsībhāva*). And the mendicant who has attained the state of being like a mountain destroys the four remaining portions of *karma*. Thereafter, he is perfected, awakened, liberated, and becomes completely cooled; he makes an end to all suffering.

Venerable Sir, what does a soul produce through the restraint of the sense of hearing (*sōindiyaniggaha*)? Through the restraint of the sense of hearing, it produces the restraint of passion and aversion toward pleasant and unpleasant sounds. It does not bind *karma* caused by that [restraint], and it wears away previously bound [karma].”

"Venerable sir, what does the soul achieve by the restraint of the sense of sight? By the restraint of the sense of sight, it achieves the restraint of passion and aversion toward pleasant and unpleasant forms. It does not bind karma caused thereby, and it wears away previously bound karma.

Venerable sir, what does the soul achieve by the restraint of the sense of smell? By the restraint of the sense of smell, it achieves the restraint of passion and aversion toward pleasant and unpleasant odors. It does not bind karma caused thereby, and it wears away previously bound karma."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce by the restraint of the tongue-faculty? By the restraint of the tongue-faculty, it produces the restraint of passion and aversion toward pleasant and unpleasant tastes; it does not bind karma caused by that, and it wears away previously bound karma.

Venerable sir, what does the soul produce by the restraint of the touch-faculty? By the restraint of the touch-faculty, it produces the restraint of passion and aversion toward pleasant and unpleasant tactile objects; it does not bind karma caused by that, and it wears away previously bound karma."

"Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through the conquest of anger? Through the conquest of anger, it produces forbearance; it does not bind karma to be experienced as anger, and it wears away karma previously bound.

Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through the conquest of pride? Through the conquest of pride, it produces humility; it does not bind karma to be experienced as pride, and it wears away karma previously bound.

Venerable sir, what does the soul produce through the conquest of deceit? Through the conquest of deceit, it produces uprightness; it does not bind karma to be experienced as deceit, and it wears away karma previously bound."

"Venerable sir, what does a living being produce by the destruction of greed? By the destruction of greed, it produces contentment; it does not bind karma to be experienced as greed, and it wears away karma previously bound."

"Venerable Sir, what does a soul produce by the conquest of attachment, aversion, and wrong belief? By the conquest of attachment, aversion, and wrong belief, it exerts itself toward the attainment of right knowledge, right vision, and right conduct. Through the loosening of the knots of karma and by means of the stages [of purification], it destroys in due order the twenty-eight types of deluding karma (*mohanīya-karma*). It also simultaneously exhausts these three categories of karma: the fivefold obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya*), the ninefold obscuration of vision (*darśanāvaraṇīya*), and the fivefold obstructive karma (*antarāyika*). Thereafter, it brings forth supreme, complete, perfect, unobscured, stainless, and pure omniscient vision and knowledge (*kevalavarajñānadarśana*) which illuminates the entire world and the non-world. As long as it remains with vibratory activity (*sayogī*), it binds *airyāpathika* karma—which is pleasant to the touch and lasts for two time-units (*dusamaya-sthitika*). That karma is bound in the first moment, experienced in the second moment, and exhausted in the third moment. Thus, that karma becomes bound, touched, activated, experienced, and exhausted; and thereafter, it becomes free from karma."

Then, having preserved his life-force until only an internal moment (*antōmuhutta*) remains, while practicing the suppression of activity (*jōganirōha*), he meditates upon the subtle-activity, non-retrogressive pure meditation (*suhumakiriya-appaḍivāi-su-kkajjhāṇa*). At that very first moment, he suppresses the mental activity (*maṇajōga*), suppresses the vocal activity (*vaïjōga*), and suppresses the bodily activity (*kāyajōga*). He effects the cessation of inhalation and exhalation (*ānapāna-nirōha*). And for the duration of the utterance of five very subtle syllables, the monk, meditating upon the uninterrupted, non-returning pure meditation (*samucchaïnnakiriya-aniyaṭṭi-sukkajjhāṇa*), simultaneously exhausts these four types of karma: feeling (*vēyaṇijja*), life-force (*āuya*), name (*nāma*), and status (*gotta*).

Then, having abandoned all physical karmic matter through every means of abandonment, having attained a straight course with a non-touching motion, he goes upward in a single moment without an intermediate body; having gone there, he becomes perfected, awakened, and so on, until he makes an end of suffering.
This indeed is the meaning of this chapter on "Exertion in Right Faith" as proclaimed, explained, demonstrated, shown, and illustrated by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra.
Thus I say.
[The Path of the Tathāgata] Just as evil karma, accumulated through passion and hatred, [is destroyed by the path].
The monk, with one-pointed mind, should listen to how he exhausts [karma] through austerity.

By abstaining from killing living beings, false speech, taking what is not given, sexual intercourse, and possessiveness, and by abstaining from eating at night, the soul becomes free from the influx of karma (*anāsava*).

One who is restrained by the five [vows], guarded in three ways, free from passions, master of the senses, without attachment, and free from thorns [of defilement], becomes a soul without influxes (anāsava).
But by the opposite of these qualities, one accumulates passion and hatred.
Listen with one-pointed mind to how the monk causes [the karmic matter] to be exhausted:
Just as the water of a great lake, when the inflow of water is completely blocked, becomes dry through bailing out and evaporation, gradually reaching total desiccation. (Utt. 11.92–93)
In this way, even for Sañjaya, whose evil karma was exhausted, the karma accumulated over ten million existences was worn away through austerity.
That austerity is said to be twofold: external and internal.
External austerity is said to be sixfold; internal austerity is likewise.
Fasting, reduced diet, alms-gathering, renunciation of flavors, bodily mortification, and withdrawal constitute external austerity. (Uttarādhyayana 11.95–96)
The time of death may be limited, and fasting (anaśanā) is of two kinds:
the first is with expectation, and the second is without expectation.
That which is limited austerity is, in brief, of six types.
The ladder-like austerity (seḍhitava), the layer-like austerity (payaratava), the solid austerity (ghanatava), and likewise the group austerity (vaggatava);
then the group-of-groups austerity (vaggavaggatava) as the fifth, and the sixth is the chosen austerity (païṇṇatava),
which fulfills one's heart's desire and is known to be of limited duration.
That fasting unto death is explained as being of two kinds:
with movement and without movement; it may involve physical activity, or else it is described as being with or without ritual preparation.
One who is not a carrier of cold [food] should avoid taking food from both [types of donors]. (Uttarādhyayana 1201) Moderation in eating is explained briefly as being fivefold:
by way of substance, place, time, state, and modifications. (Uttarādhyayana 1202)
Whatever food one has, if one makes it less than that— even by as little as a single grain of rice— then by way of substance (*dravya*), there would be [reduction].
Whether in a village, a town, a capital city, a market town, a mine, or a mountain fort;
In villages, market towns, port cities, fortified towns, and border settlements;
in hermitages, monasteries, camps, and royal encampments; on caravans, and at the junctions of roads and fortresses. (Uttarādhyayana 12.04–12.05)

In villages or in countries, or in houses—such a limited area is permissible; thus it may be by way of the field. A "box" (peḍā), a "half-box" (addhapeḍā), a "cow's path" (gomutti), and likewise the "ant-path" (payaṅgavihiyā).
The sixth [period] is for going out and returning from the *sambukka-vaṭṭa* (the conch-shell circuit).
Of the four *pauruṣīs* of the day, however many periods there may be, one who wanders in this manner should indeed know the measure of time. (Uttarādhyayana 1207–1208)
Or else, in the third watch of the night, seeking food when [the time] is deficient, or when it is less by a fourth part— thus it may be by way of time.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whether adorned or even unadorned.
Whether by means of a particular object, or by means of a particular garment,
or by some other distinction such as color— those who thus infer the internal state [of others] while practicing in this way should indeed be known as those who measure the internal state.

Those states that are declared with respect to substance, space, time, and disposition—one who moves within these [limits] is a monk who moves within the bounds; he becomes one who moves within the limits of the modifications [of objects]. (Utt. 12.12) Furthermore, there is the eightfold field of activity, as well as the seven modes of seeking food (eṣaṇā).
And whatever other observances (abhigrahas) there are that are taught for the practice of alms-gathering:
the avoidance of milk, curds, ghee, and so forth, as well as fine food and drink;
this is called the "renunciation of flavors" (rasavivajjana), which is the avoidance of savory tastes. (Uttarādhyayana 12.13–14)

Standing postures, the hero’s pose (*vīrāsana*), and other such strenuous positions that bring comfort to the living being— when these are maintained, that is declared to be bodily mortification (*kāyakilesa*).
[One should practice] in a solitary place free from disturbances, avoided by women and animals.

By resorting to secluded lodgings—this secluded lodging is external austerity; it has been explained in brief. Hereafter, I shall describe internal austerity in its proper sequence. (Uttarādhyayana 12.16–17)
Expiation, humility, service, as well as study,
meditation, and relinquishment— this is internal austerity. Expiation consists of ten types, beginning with that which is worthy of confession.

Whatever a monk undergoes properly, that is declared to be his penance (pāyacchitta). Rising [to greet], joining the palms in reverence, likewise offering a seat, devotion to the guru, and a desire to hear—this is explained as discipline (vinaya). (Uttarādhyayana 12.19–20)
Service rendered according to one's ability toward the tenfold duties beginning with the teacher—that is declared to be service (vaiyāvṛttya).
Recitation, questioning, and likewise review; Utt. 12.21.
Contemplation and religious discourse, as well as self-study, constitute the fivefold [duty].
Having avoided the *ārta* and *raudra* meditations, one who is well-composed should meditate upon the *dharma* and *śukla* meditations;
that indeed is the meditation which the wise praise. (Utt. 12.22–23)
Whether on a bed, a seat, or while standing, that monk who does not neglect the relinquishing of the body is praised as the sixth [type].
Thus, the sage who practices this twofold austerity correctly— Utt. 12.24.
That wise one is quickly liberated from the entire cycle of existence. Thus I say.
I shall proclaim the rule of conduct, which brings happiness to the living being;
by practicing it, many beings have crossed the ocean of saṃsāra. (Uttarādhyayana 12.26)

One should practice restraint in one respect and engagement in another: desisting from non-restraint and engaging in restraint. Both passion and hatred are evils that cause the setting in motion of sinful karma.
The monk who constantly restrains himself does not remain within the circle. (Utt.
12.28) The monk who constantly abandons each of the three types of rods, the three types of pride, and the three types of thorns, does not remain within the circle. (Utt. 12.29)
The monk who always endures divine afflictions, as well as those arising from animals and humans,
does not remain within the circle [of worldly existence]. Discursive thought, the passions, and false perceptions, as well as the two types of meditation— Uttarādhyayana 12.30.
The monk who always exerts himself regarding faults does not remain within the circle. (Utt.
12.31) The monk who always exerts himself regarding the objects of the senses, the codes of conduct, and the activities, does not remain within the circle. (Utt. 12.32)
The monk who constantly conquers the six passions (*lesā*), the six bodies (*kāya*), and the six causes of taking food (*āhārakāraṇa*) does not remain within the circle [of worldly existence].
[He likewise masters] the postures for accepting alms (*piṇḍoggahapaḍimā*) and the seven bases of fear (*bhayaṭṭhāṇa*).

The monk who always exerts himself in the restraints, in the protections of celibacy, and in the tenfold duty of a monk—he does not remain within the circle. (Uttarādhyayana 12.34) The monk who always exerts himself in the restraints, in the protections of celibacy, and in the tenfold duty of a monk—he does not remain within the circle. (Uttarādhyayana 12.35)
The monk who always exerts himself in the vows of the lay followers (*uvāsaga*) and in the vows of the monks (*bhikkhu*), he does not remain within the circle [of worldly existence].
[He is also diligent] in the various activities, in the villages, and among those who perform supreme religious duties.

The monk who always conquers [the senses] does not remain within the circle. (Utt. 1237) Likewise, the monk who always conquers through the sixteen verses on the householders and through non-restraint does not remain within the circle. (Utt. 1238)
The monk who always exerts himself, remaining concentrated upon the Bambhacerāim, the Nāyādhammakahāo, and the Thāṇaṃga, does not remain within the circle [of rebirth].
[He overcomes] the twenty-one forces and the twenty-two hardships.

The monk who constantly conquers [the senses] does not remain within the circle. (Uttarādhyayana 12.40) In the twenty-three Sūtrakṛtāṅga [sections], and among the gods who possess beautiful forms—he who as a monk constantly conquers them does not remain within the circle. (Uttarādhyayana 12.41)

The monk who constantly exerts himself in the twenty-five meditations (bhāvanās), in the chapters (uddesas) of the Daśāśrutaskandha and other scriptures, and in the qualities of the homeless state as well as in the prescribed discipline (pragappa), does not remain within the circle of worldly existence. (Uttarādhyayana 12.42)

The monk who always exerts himself does not remain within the circle. (Utt. 12.43) The monk who always exerts himself against attachments to evil teachings and against the very grounds of delusion does not remain within the circle. (Utt. 12.44)

The monk who always exerts himself regarding the qualities of the perfections (*siddhaguṇa-yoga*) and the thirty-three sources of non-prosperity (*āsādanā*) does not remain within the circle [of worldly existence].
Thus, the monk who always exerts himself in these states [does not remain in saṃsāra].
The wise person is swiftly liberated from the entire cycle of existence. Thus I say.
[The cause of negligence:
Listen with a focused mind to me as I speak of that which is for your ultimate benefit—the complete liberation from all suffering, including its very roots, throughout all time. (Utt. 12.47)
Through the illumination of all knowledge, through the avoidance of ignorance and delusion,
and through the destruction of passion and hatred, one attains liberation, which is absolute bliss.
(Uttarādhyayana 12.48) The path to that [liberation] is service to those who have been instructed by their gurus, and the total avoidance of foolish people from afar.

Recitation of the scriptures, dwelling in solitude, reflecting upon the meaning of the Sūtras, and steadfastness; (Uttarādhyayana 12.49) A mendicant ascetic desiring meditative concentration should seek food that is measured and pure; he should seek companions whose intellect is skilled in the true meaning; he should seek a dwelling suitable for seclusion. (Uttarādhyayana 12.50)
Or if he does not find a skillful companion—one superior in virtues or equal in virtues—he may wander alone, avoiding sinful deeds and remaining unattached to sensual pleasures.
Just as a crane is born from an egg, and an egg is produced from a crane; ||| Utt. 12.51 ||| Just as it is.
In this very way, they say that craving is indeed the abode of delusion, and delusion is the abode of craving.
Passion and hatred are the seed of karma; they say that karma originates from delusion.
Karma is the root of birth and death, and they say that birth and death are suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 12.52–53)

Suffering is destroyed for one who has no delusion; delusion is destroyed for one who has no craving; craving is destroyed for one who has no greed; greed is destroyed for one who possesses nothing at all.
(Uttarādhyayana 12.54) By one desiring to uproot passion, hatred, and likewise delusion, along with their roots and networks...
I shall proclaim those various means that are to be adopted, in their proper sequence:
Sensual flavors should not be indulged in excessively; for the most part, such flavors cause excitement in men.
And once excited, desires assail them, just as birds attack a tree laden with sweet fruit. (Utt. 12.55–56)

Just as a forest fire in a thicket of abundant fuel does not subside once it has broken out, so too the fire of the senses of one who indulges in sensual pleasures does not lead to the welfare of any practitioner of celibacy (*brahmacārī*).
[But for those] who move about with beds and seats spread out, who sit on low seats, and who have tamed their senses— Utt. 12.57.
The enemy that is passion does not seize the mind, just as external foes cannot overcome one by means of medicines (Utt.
1258). Just as mice find no favorable dwelling at the foot of a cat’s lair, even so, a residence in the midst of a woman’s abode is not suitable for one who practices celibacy (Utt. 1259).
A monk practicing austerities should not, having fixed his mind upon the beauty, grace, charm, laughter, speech, gestures, or glances of women, look at them with longing. Indeed,
he should avoid seeing them, avoiding desiring them, avoiding thinking of them, and avoiding praising them.

It is suitable for noble meditation for women who are always devoted to the practice of celibacy. (Uttarādhyayana 12.61) Granted, even by goddesses adorned with ornaments, one who is protected by the three guptis cannot be shaken;
nevertheless, knowing it to be exclusively beneficial, dwelling in solitude is praised for sages. (Uttarādhyayana 12.62)
For a young man who longs for liberation, who fears cyclic existence, and who is established in the Dhamma,
there is nothing in this world so difficult to cross as these women, who are so enchanting to the mind of a fool.
Having transcended these attachments, all other remaining bonds become truly easy to cross.

Just as one who has crossed the great ocean would not fear even a river equal to the Gaṅgā, so too does the one free from passion reach the end of whatever suffering there is for the entire world, including the gods—whether it be physical or mental—which arises indeed from attachment to sensual desires. (Utt. 1264–1265)

Just as the *kimpāka* fruit is delightful in its taste and color while being eaten, yet causes one to suffer when it ripens in a short life— such is the outcome of the qualities of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). One should never direct one's inclination toward those objects of the senses that are pleasing.
A śramaṇa, an ascetic desiring meditative concentration, should not direct his mind even toward pleasant things.

(Utt. 12.67) They say that the apprehension of form by the eye is the cause of passion; they call that which is pleasant the cause of passion, and they call that which is unpleasant the cause of aversion. He who is equanimous toward these is one free from passion. (Utt. 12.68)
They say that the eye is the grasper of form, and they say that form is the object grasped by the eye;
they call that which is agreeable the cause of passion, and that which is disagreeable the cause of hatred.
He who develops an intense greed for forms meets with destruction at an untimely hour.
Just as a moth, greedy for color and lusting after light, meets its death;

so too, the person who gives way to intense hatred meets with suffering at that very moment through his own unrestrained malice. No external form whatsoever is at fault in this. (Uttarādhyayana 12.70–71)
If a fool harbors malice toward a beautiful form that is pleasing to him alone, he undergoes the torment of suffering; yet the dispassionate sage is not stained by it.
Furthermore, a living being who follows the pursuit of forms harms both mobile and immobile beings of all kinds.
The fool torments himself with his own thoughts; defiled and heavy with self-interest, he oppresses himself. (Utt.
1273) What happiness can there be for one through forms and sounds, or through possessions—in their acquisition, protection, attachment, loss, and separation?
And even at the time of enjoyment, there is no attainment of satisfaction. (Utt. 1274)
One who is unsatisfied with forms and attached to possessions finds no contentment;
through the fault of discontent, being distressed by the greed of another, he takes what is not given.
For one who is overcome by craving, who takes what is not given, and who remains unsatisfied with forms and possessions— Utt. 12.75.
Through the fault of greed, one increases deceitful falsehood; even there, one is not liberated from suffering. (Utt.
1276) Both before and after falsehood, and at the time of its application, one is miserable; thus it has a wretched end.
Likewise, by taking what is not given, one who is unsatiated with forms remains miserable and without refuge. (Utt. 1277)
For a person thus attached to form, how could there ever be any happiness whatsoever?

Even in the enjoyment of that very thing, there is the suffering of defilement, for which suffering itself is produced as the cause. In this very way, one who has fallen into aversion toward form encounters a succession of miseries.

One with a corrupted mind accumulates karma, which results in suffering for him in its maturation. (Uttarādhyayana 12.79) A man who is detached from forms and free from sorrow is not stained by this succession of miseries, even while remaining in the midst of existence, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (Uttarādhyayana 12.80)

They say that sound is the object of hearing; they say that which is pleasant is the cause of passion, and that which is unpleasant is the cause of aversion. He who is equanimous toward these is one free from passion. They say that hearing is the object of sound; they say that sound is the object of hearing.
They say that what is agreeable is the cause of passion, and what is disagreeable is the cause of hatred.
He who develops intense greed for sounds meets with destruction before his time; like a foolish deer overcome by passion, he meets death while still unsatiated with sounds. (Uttarādhyayana 12.8–9)

If a person gives way to intense hatred, at that very moment he experiences suffering through his own unrestrained fault; no external sound is at fault for him. (Uttarādhyayana 12.84) One who is exclusively attached to a pleasant sound harbors malice toward one who does not praise it.
The fool undergoes the torment of suffering; the dispassionate sage is not defiled by it. (Utt.

12.85) But the living being who follows the pursuit of sounds harms various kinds of mobile and immobile creatures; that fool, heavy with his own self-interest and defiled, causes them distress and pain. (Utt. 12.86)

Through attachment to sounds, through acquisition, and through their production, protection, employment, loss, and separation—how can there be happiness for him? And even at the time of enjoyment, when satisfaction is not attained; being attached to sound and attached to possession, one who is obsessed does not find contentment. (Uttarādhyayana 12.8–9)
Suffering due to the fault of discontent, one who is turbid with greed takes what is not given from another.

For one overcome by craving who seizes what is not given, and who remains unsatisfied with sounds and possessions, deceit and falsehood increase through the fault of greed; even there, he is not liberated from suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 12.8–9)

One who acquires things not given is miserable both before and after [the acquisition], and miserable at the time of the undertaking; thus, at the end, he is likewise miserable. One who is not self-controlled and remains unsated with sounds becomes even more miserable. (Uttarādhyayana 12.9) For a man thus addicted to sounds, how could there ever be any happiness whatsoever?
