Even when there is only a small amount of enjoyment, suffering born of defilements arises for one on whose account that suffering was produced. (Utt.
12.91) In exactly the same way, one who has directed malice toward sound encounters a succession of increasing sufferings;
and with a corrupted mind, he accumulates karma, which results in further misery for him in its maturation. (Utt. 12.92)

A person detached from sounds is free from sorrow; by this, even while remaining in the midst of existence, he is not defiled by the succession of miseries, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
They say that the nose perceives odor; they call that which is agreeable a cause for passion.

They say that which is unpleasant is the cause of aversion; he who is equanimous toward them is one free from passion. (Uttarādhyayana 12.94) They say that the nose is the perceiver of odor, and they say that odor is the object of the nose.
They say that what is pleasant is the cause of attachment, and they say that what is unpleasant is the cause of aversion. (Uttarādhyayana 12.95)
He who develops intense greed for fragrances meets with untimely destruction;
like a snake emerging from its hole, he perishes when overcome by passion and greedy for the scent of medicinal herbs.
And he who likewise develops intense hatred encounters suffering at that very moment.
By his own unrestrained fault, no scent whatsoever offends him. Even toward a beautiful scent that is utterly indifferent to him, the fool harbors malice;
he undergoes the crushing pressure of suffering. But the sage who is free from passion is not defiled by it. (Uttarādhyayana 12.97–98)

And the fool, following after scents and following after those who follow after scents, harms various kinds of living beings, both mobile and immobile; with his thoughts, he torments them, being afflicted by his own self-interest and defiled.
(Uttarādhyayana 12.9–10) Through the pursuit of scents and through possessiveness, there is the acquisition, protection, and attachment [to objects].
How can there be happiness for him in separation from wealth, or in the enjoyment of it when no satisfaction is attained?

Being attached and deeply immersed in possessions regarding perfumes and the like, he finds no contentment; through the fault of discontent, he becomes miserable and, driven by greed, takes what belongs to another without it being given. (Uttarādhyayana 13.00–13.01)

For one who is overcome by craving, who takes what is not given, and who is insatiable regarding fragrances and possessions, deceit and falsehood increase through greed and hatred; even there, he is not liberated from suffering.
He is miserable in the past, in the future, and at the time of action, for his end is wretched.
Thus, acquiring things that have not been given, one who is insatiable regarding scents becomes miserable and lacks independence. (Utt.

1303) For a man thus addicted to scents, how could there ever be any happiness therein? Even in the enjoyment of them, there is the suffering of defilement; he for whose sake that suffering was produced [reaps it]. (Utt. 1304)
In this very way, one who harbors malice toward a smell encounters a succession of misfortunes;

with a corrupted mind, he accumulates karma which results in suffering for him in its maturation. But the person who is detached from smell is free from sorrow, and thus [is spared] from this succession of misfortunes.
One who dwells even in the midst of existence is not defiled, just as the lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (Utt.

13.06) They say that the apprehension of taste through the tongue is the cause of passion when it is pleasant, and they say it is the cause of aversion when it is unpleasant; but one who is equanimous toward these is free from passion. (Utt. 13.07)
They say the tongue is the perceiver of taste; they say the perception of taste by the tongue is the cause of passion when it is agreeable, and the cause of aversion when it is disagreeable.
He who develops intense greed for tastes meets with destruction at an untimely hour.

Just as a fish, greedy for the enjoyment of its bait, has its body pierced by a hook when it is overcome by passion; so too, the living being who gives way to intense hatred experiences suffering at that very moment through his own unrestrained malice. No external flavor whatsoever is at fault in this matter. (Uttarādhyayana 13.9–10)

If a fool harbors malice toward a single taste that is pleasing to him, he incurs suffering and oppression; yet the dispassionate sage is not stained by it. Furthermore, a living being who follows the pursuit of tastes harms many kinds of beings, both mobile and immobile.
The fool torments himself with his own thoughts; defiled and burdened by his own self-interest, he oppresses himself. (Utt.

1312) How can there be happiness for him in the pursuit of flavors, in possession, in acquisition, in guarding, in using, or in loss? And even at the time of enjoyment, there is no attainment of satisfaction. (Utt. 1313)
One who is not satiated with flavors and is attached to possessions does not find contentment;
through the fault of discontent, he becomes miserable and, corrupted by greed, takes what is not given from another.
For one who is overcome by thirst, who steals what is not given, and who is unsatiated with flavors and possessions— Utt. 13.14.
Through the fault of greed, one increases deceitful falsehood; even therein, one is not liberated from suffering. (Utt.
13.15) Both before and after falsehood, and at the time of its commission, one is miserable; thus it has a wretched end.
Likewise, one who acquires what is not given is miserable and lacks refuge, being unsatisfied with flavors. (Utt. 13.16)
For a man thus addicted to tastes, how could there ever be any happiness?

Even in the slight enjoyment thereof, there arises suffering through the toil by which it is produced. In this very way, one who has developed an aversion toward taste encounters a succession of miseries.
One with a defiled mind accumulates karma, which later becomes suffering for him in its fruition. (Utt.

1318) A man who is detached from flavors is free from sorrow; by means of this, even while remaining in the midst of existence, he is not smeared by the succession of miseries, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (Utt. 1319)

They say that the body’s grasping of touch is the cause of passion when it is pleasant, and they say it is the cause of hatred when it is unpleasant; one who is equanimous toward these is free from passion. They say that touch is the grasping of the body, and they say that the body is the grasping of touch.
They say that which is agreeable is the cause of passion, and that which is disagreeable is the cause of hatred.

He who develops an intense greed for pleasant sensations meets with destruction at an untimely hour; like a buffalo overcome by passion, sinking in cold water and seized by crocodiles, he perishes. (Uttarādhyayana 13.21–22)

If a person gives way to intense hatred, at that very moment he experiences suffering through his own unrestrained fault; no external object of touch is at fault toward him. (Uttarādhyayana 13.23) One who is single-mindedly attached to a pleasant touch develops malice toward one who does not stroke him.
The fool undergoes the oppression of suffering; the dispassionate sage is not defiled by it. (Utt.

1324) Furthermore, a living being who follows the pursuit of pleasant sensations harms many kinds of mobile and immobile creatures; that fool, heavy with self-interest and defiled, causes them torment and afflicts them. (Utt. 1325)

Through the acquisition of pleasant objects and through possessiveness—whether in their procurement, protection, attachment, loss, or separation—how can there be happiness for him? And even at the time of enjoyment, when satisfaction is not attained? One who is insatiable regarding pleasant objects and possessiveness, being obsessed and deeply attached, finds no contentment. (Uttarādhyayana 13.26)
Suffering due to the fault of discontent, he takes what is not given from another, his mind clouded by greed. (Utt.

13.27) For one who is overcome by craving, who takes what is not given, and who remains unsatisfied with sensory objects and possessions, deceitful falsehood increases through the fault of greed; even there, he is not liberated from suffering. (Utt. 13.28)
For one who acquires things not given, there is suffering both before and after, as well as at the time of acquisition;
thus, with a miserable end, he remains unsatisfied regarding tactile objects, suffering and without refuge.
(Uttarādhyayana 13.29) For a man thus addicted to tactile objects, how could there ever be any happiness whatsoever?

Even in the mere enjoyment of that [object], suffering born of defilements arises for one by whose action suffering was produced. (Utt. 13.30) In the very same way, one who has gone to aversion toward a tactile sensation encounters a succession of misfortunes; and with a corrupted mind, he accumulates karma which results in suffering for him again in its maturation. (Utt. 13.31)

A person who is detached from pleasant things and free from sorrow is not stained by this succession of floods of suffering, even while remaining in the midst of existence, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
They say that the state of the mind is "grasping"; they call that which is the cause of passion "agreeable."
They say that which is unattractive is the cause of aversion; he who is equanimous toward these is one free from passion (vītarāga).
They say that the mind is the grasper of mental objects, and they say that mental objects are the grasper of the mind;
they say that what is attractive is the cause of attachment, and what is unattractive is the cause of aversion.

He who develops intense greed for sensual objects meets with untimely destruction; like an elephant infatuated with passion and greedy for the qualities of sensory pleasure, he is caught in the path of the female elephant.
And he who develops intense hatred toward something meets with suffering at that very moment.
By his own unrestrained fault, no external object offends that person. (Utt.
13.36) When a fool is intensely attached to a pleasing object, he harbors malice toward what is not so;
thus the fool undergoes the pressure of suffering. But the dispassionate sage is not defiled by it. (Utt. 13.37)
The soul that follows after states of being follows after acquisitions; it harms various kinds of beings, both mobile and immobile, and with its thoughts, the fool torments them.
Heavy with self-interest and defiled, he oppresses them through the acquisition of possessions, their procurement, their protection, and their attachment. (Uttarādhyayana 13.38)
How can there be happiness for him in separation from wealth, nor satisfaction during the time of enjoyment? (Utt.
13.39) Since he is unsatisfied with his possessions, being obsessed and deeply attached to them, he finds no contentment.
Due to the fault of discontent, he becomes miserable; and through greed-tainted by passion, he takes what is not given from another. (Utt. 13.40)

For one who is overcome by craving, who takes what is not given, and who is unsatisfied with possessions, deceit and falsehood increase through the fault of greed; even there, he is not released from suffering.
He is miserable in the future, in the past, at the time of action, and in the end.
Thus, acquiring things not given, one remains unsatisfied with worldly states, miserable, and dependent. (Utt.

1342) For a man thus enamored of worldly states, how could there ever be any happiness? Even in the enjoyment of those very things, there is the suffering of affliction for him because of whom that suffering was produced. (Utt. 1343)
In this very way, one who has gone toward aversion for existence encounters a succession of miseries;
and with a corrupted mind, he accumulates karma which later becomes suffering for him in its fruition.
One who is detached from existence and free from sorrow does not [encounter] this succession of miseries.
A sage, even while in the midst of existence, is not defiled, just as the stalk of a lotus is not wetted by water.
(Uttarādhyayana 13.45) The objects of the senses and the objects of the mind are the causes of suffering for a passionate human being;
yet those very same things never cause even the slightest suffering to one who is free from passion. (Uttarādhyayana 13.46)

Sensual enjoyments do not bring about tranquility, nor do enjoyments lead to the cessation of passion; he who is devoted to them and possessed by possessiveness undergoes delusion and the loss of tranquility because of them.
(Uttarādhyayana 13.47) Anger and pride, as well as deceit, greed, disgust, aversion, and attachment—
He reflects upon laughter, fear, the perception of men and women, the perception of neuter beings, and various other states.

Thus, in many forms, he who is attached to such sensual qualities considers others as well who are produced from these same sources—those who are compassionate, miserable, or modest. (Uttarādhyayana 13.48–49)

One who desires a companion would not seek [one] for an eon; yet, through subsequent regret, one reflects upon that very lack of influence in this world of manifold immensity, and thus falls prey to the thieves of the senses.
Then, various purposes arise for him, causing him to sink into the great ocean of delusion.
Those seeking happiness strive for the removal of suffering, yet one who is still possessed of passion exerts himself toward its causes.
However, for one who is becoming dispassionate, all such objects of the senses—sounds and the rest, however they may appear—produce neither attraction nor aversion in him. (Uttarādhyayana 13.51–52)

Thus, for one who has attained equanimity by ceasing the conceptualization and discrimination of thoughts, his craving for the objects of sensual pleasure is abandoned. Free from passion and having accomplished all that was to be done, he destroys the veil of knowledge in an instant.

Likewise, whatever karma he obscures as deluding (darśanāvaraṇīya) and whatever karma he performs as obstructive (antarāya), he knows all that and sees it; he becomes undeluded, free from obstructions, without influx (anāsrava), and endowed with meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi). Upon the exhaustion of his lifespan, the pure one attains liberation. (Uttarādhyayana 13.54–55)

That is the release from all that suffering which constantly oppresses this living being; one who is liberated from this long-lasting malady is praised, and thus becomes one who has attained ultimate happiness and fulfilled his purpose.
This is the path of liberation from all suffering that has arisen since time immemorial. (Uttarādhyayana 13.56)
It has been declared that by following [this path], sentient beings, having attained it, gradually become possessed of ultimate happiness.
Thus I say.
I shall explain the eight types of karma in their proper sequence, by which this soul is bound and wanders through the cycle of existence. (Uttarādhyayana 13.58)
The karma that obscures knowledge, likewise that which obscures vision,
the karma of sensation, and likewise delusion; the karma of lifespan,
as well as name-karma, status-karma, and likewise obstructive karma.
Thus, these eight types of karma in brief:
knowledge-obscuring karma is fivefold—scriptural knowledge, sensory-cognition knowledge, clairvoyant knowledge as the third, mind-reading knowledge, and perfect knowledge. (Uttarādhyayana 13.60–61)
Drowsiness (niddā), as well as sleep (payalā), drowsiness-drowsiness (niddāniddā), and sleep-sleep (payalapayalā);
and then the fifth, known as *thīṇagiddhī*, should be understood.
[These are] the veils of vision through the eyes, vision without the eyes, vision through the mind, and perfect vision (*kevala*). Utt. 13.6–7.
Thus, the obscuration of vision (*darśanāvaraṇa*) should be known to have nine varieties.
Furthermore, the feeling-producing karma (*vedanīya*) is said to be of two kinds: pleasant and unpleasant;
there are many subdivisions of the pleasant, and likewise for the unpleasant.
Deluding karma (mohanīya) is also twofold: pertaining to vision (darśana) and likewise to conduct (cāritra).
Regarding vision, it is said to be threefold; regarding conduct, it is twofold:
right faith (samyaktva), wrong faith (mithyātva), and mixed faith (samyagmithyātva).

These three types [of karma] belong to deluding karma regarding vision (darśana). (Uttarādhyayana 13.66) Deluding karma of conduct (cāritra-mohanīya-karma) is explained as being of two kinds: that which consists of the passions (kaṣāya-mohanīya) and likewise that which consists of the quasi-passions (no-kaṣāya). (Uttarādhyayana 13.67)
Karma born of the passions (kaṣāya) is of sixteen types, seven types, or nine types; and there is also karma not born of the passions.
[These include] the life-span of hell-beings, animals, and likewise that of humans.
The lifespan-karma is fourfold, and the age-karma is likewise fourfold.
Name-karma, however, is said to be twofold: auspicious and inauspicious.
There are many subdivisions of the auspicious, and the same is true for the inauspicious.

This karma is said to be of two kinds: high and low, as it has been taught; the high is of eight types, and the low is likewise taught to be so. [It is classified] with respect to giving, gain, enjoyment, use, and likewise vigor.
The fivefold obstruction has been explained in brief. (Utt. 1372) These are the root categories and the derivative categories that have been declared.
Regarding the spatial points, the field, the time, and the derivative state—now hear [the explanation]. (Utt. 1373)

The spatial extension of all karmas, including those bound within the *granthi*, is infinite; however, for the perfected ones (*siddhas*), it is said to be within [the space of] the liberated souls. For all living beings, karma is comprised within the six directions.
In all regions, everything is bound by everything. (Utt.
1375) For those whose names are like the oceans, the maximum duration is thirty *koṭī-koṭīs* [of years], while the minimum is an *antarmuhūrta*. (Utt. 1376)
Regarding both types of obstructive karma (*āvaraṇīya*), as well as the karma to be experienced (*vedanīya*) and the obstructive (*antarāya*) karma, this duration has been explained:
for those [karmas] whose names are like the ocean, it is seventy *koṭi-koṭīs*.

The maximum duration of deluding karma (*mohanīya*) is thirty-three *sāgaropamas*, while the minimum is stated to be one *antarmuhūrta*. The maximum duration of life-determining karma (*āyu-karma*) is explained as thirty-three *sāgaropamas*, while the minimum is one *antarmuhūrta*.
The maximum number of instances of name and family karma (nāma-gotta) is twenty quadrillion (20 koṭikoṭīs), equal to the number of oceans; the minimum is within a single muhūrta.
Furthermore, the instances of fruition-intensity (anubhāga) of the perfected ones (siddhas) constitute an infinite fraction.
In all [beings], the foremost portion is desired by all living beings.
Therefore, having understood the intensity (anubhāga) of these karmas, a wise person should strive for their restraint and their destruction. (Uttarādhyayana 13.81–82)
Thus I say.
[The Lesson on Leśyā]
I shall proclaim the chapter on the *leśyās*, in their proper sequence and according to order;
hear from me the power (*anubhāva*) of all six *karmaleśyās*.
[I shall also explain] their names, and their characteristics regarding color, taste, smell, touch, transformation, and state (*sthāna*).
Now hear from me regarding their duration, their destinies, and their lifespans, as well as the leśyās:
black, blue, and grey, fiery, lotus-colored, and the white leśyā as the sixth; these are their names in their proper order. (Uttarādhyayana 13.84–85)
Resembling a dark cloud, similar to a buffalo's horn or emerald, and like the eye of a wagtail; such is the black *leśyā* in color.
It resembles the blue *asōka* flower and has a luster like the wing of a blue jay.

The blue radiance (*nīla-leśyā*), by way of color, resembles a *vairūrya* gem, or like the *ayasī* flower, or similar to the eye of a cuckoo, or like the throat of a pigeon. (Utt. 13.87–88) The black radiance (*kāū-leśyā*), by way of color, resembles a *kāka-puṣpa* flower, or like the eye of a cuckoo, or similar to the throat of a pigeon. (Utt. 13.88)
Resembling the mineral cinnabar, resembling the rising sun,
and resembling the flame of a parrot's beak— such is the fiery leśyā (tēūlēsā) by color.
Resembling a variety of turmeric and possessing a luster like the color of yellow orpiment.
The white leśyā (su-kkla-lesā), by way of color, resembles the *saṇa* flower and the *āsana* flower;
it is like a conch shell, the moon, or jasmine (*kunda*), possessing a radiance equal to a flood of milk, and resembling a necklace of silver. (Uttarādhyayana 13.90–91)

Just as the juice of the bitter gourd, the juice of the neem tree, or the juice of the *rohiṇī* plant is bitter, the taste of the black [leaves] should be known as infinitely more bitter than even that. Just as the taste of the three sweets (*trikaṭuka*) is pungent, or like that of elephant-pepper (*hatthipippalī*).
The taste of the blue [earth] should be known as infinitely greater than this;
it is like the juice of a young mango, or like that of a raw wood-apple. The taste of the black [earth] should be known as infinitely greater than this. (Uttarādhyayana 13.93–94)
Just as the juice of a ripe mango, or even that of a ripe jackfruit—
know that the taste in the fire-element is infinitely more [exquisite] than these;
it is like the flavor of excellent *vāruṇī* wine, or like that of various kinds of fermented spirits (*āsava*).
The taste of honey-molasses is surpassed by that of the *pamhā* fruit;

the taste of dates, the juice of grapes, the taste of milk, or the taste of sugar-candy and sugar—each of these is known to be infinitely greater in flavor than the one preceding it, culminating in the taste of the *sukkā* fruit. (Uttarādhyayana 13.96–97)
Just as the odor of a cow’s carcass, or of a dog’s carcass, or of a snake’s carcass,
so too is the odor of the inauspicious *leśyās* infinitely greater than these.
Just as is the fragrance of fragrant flowers when they are being crushed with perfumes and incenses...
The pleasure of the three auspicious *leśyās* is infinitely greater than this. (Utt.
1399) Just as the touch of a goat’s hide is [unpleasant], so too the touch of thorny leaves is; the pleasure of the inauspicious *leśyās* is infinitely greater than this. (Utt. 1400)
Just as the touch of ghee, or the fragrance of butter, or of *śirīṣa* flowers,
so too is the [fragrance] of all three types of commendable *leśyās* infinitely greater than that.
It is of three kinds, or nine kinds, or twenty-seven kinds, or one hundred and eight.
The transformation of the passions (leśyās) becomes either dark or grey. (Utt.

14.02) A man who is negligent regarding the five influxes (āsravas), unrestrained in the three [gates], and lacking self-control in the six [sense objects], who is intent on violent undertakings, is mean and reckless. (Utt. 14.03)
One who is devoid of laziness, free from doubt,
and without envy, being endowed with this yoga, transforms into a black *leśyā*.
Envy, resentment, cruelty, ignorance, deceit, and lack of shame [are its causes].
A householder who is angry, deceitful, negligent, greedy for flavors, and a seeker of pleasure;
a man who is unrestrained in his undertakings, cruel, and prone to violence—being engaged in such activities, he transforms into the blue *leśyā*. (Uttarādhyayana 34.5–6)
Crooked in body, crooked in conduct, deceitful,
dishonest, fraudulent, and hypocritical; holding wrong views, ignoble, a speaker of harsh and wicked words, a thief, and full of envy.
Engaged in this yoga, he transforms himself into the state of kāpotaleśyā.
(Uttarādhyayana 14.08) Living modestly, steady, free from deceit, and devoid of curiosity;
disciplined in humility, self-controlled, possessed of yoga, and observant of spiritual exertion. (Uttarādhyayana 14.09)
One who loves the Dharma, is firm in the Dharma, fears wrongdoing, possesses inner peace, and is devoted to this yoga, should transform into the fiery leśyā;
one whose anger and pride are diminished, and whose deceit and greed are also diminished. (Uttarādhyayana 34.10)
With a tranquil mind, self-controlled, disciplined in yoga, and observant of the vows;
likewise, being soft-spoken, with senses calmed and passions subdued, and fully engaged in the practice of yoga, he transforms his subtle karmic matter (pamhalesa). (Uttarādhyayana 14.11–12)

Avoiding the eightfold obstacles, one whose mind is tranquil and who has subdued the self should meditate on the pure dharmas; being equanimous and guarded in the restraints, whether still possessed of passion or free from passion, one should be peaceful and have conquered the senses. (Uttarādhyayana 14.13)

One who is fully engaged in right yoga transforms into a white leśyā. (Uttarādhyayana 14.14) The number of time-units (*samaya*) in incalculable *avasarpiṇīs* and *utsarpiṇīs*, as well as the worlds (*loka*), constitute the total number of positions for the leśyās. (Uttarādhyayana 14.15)
The minimum duration of the black *leśyā* is half a *muhūrta*, while its maximum duration is known to be thirty-three *sāgaropamas* plus one *muhūrta*.
(Uttarādhyayana 14.16) The minimum duration of the grey *leśyā* is half a *muhūrta*, while its maximum duration is ten *udadhis* (sāgaropamas) plus an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a *palyopama*.

The maximum duration of the blue *leśyā* should be known as this. (Utt. 1417) But the minimum is half a *muhūrta*; the maximum duration of the black *leśyā* should be known as three oceans (*udadhi*) plus an incalculable fraction of a *palya*. (Utt. 1418)
The minimum duration of the fiery leśyā (teulēsa) is half a muhūrta, while the maximum duration should be known as two oceans [of time] plus an incalculable fraction of a palyopama.
The minimum is half a muhūrta, and the maximum is ten sāgaras plus a muhūrta.
The maximum duration of the white leśyā (pure thought-coloration) should be known [as follows]:
the minimum is half a muhūrta, while the maximum duration of the white leśyā should be known as thirty-three sāgaropamas plus one muhūrta. (Uttarādhyayana 14.20–21)
This, indeed, has been described as the duration of the *leśyās* in general across all four states of existence (*gati*). Hereafter, I shall explain the specific duration of the *leśyās*.
The minimum duration for the black (*kāpotā*) *leśyā* is ten thousand years.
Three *palyopamas* and an incalculable fraction (*asaṅkhyabhāga*) is the maximum duration for the Nīla hell.
Three *palyopamas* and an incalculable fraction is the minimum; ten *udadhis* and a *palyopama* and an incalculable fraction is the maximum. (Uttarādhyayana 14.23–24)
The minimum duration of the black *leśyā* is one *asaṃkhyeya* part of ten *udī* and ten *palyopamas*, while the maximum is thirty-three *sāgaropamas*.
This is described as the duration of the *leśyās* for the denizens of hell. (Uttarādhyayana 14.25)

Beyond that, I shall speak of the duration of the *leśyās* for animals, humans, and gods. (Uttarādhyayana 14.26) The duration of the *leśyās* for animals and humans, wherever they may be, is half a *muhūrta*, with the exception of the *kevala* (pure) *leśyā*. (Uttarādhyayana 14.27)
The minimum duration of white-leśyā (śukla-leśyā) is one muhūrta, while the maximum is nine pūrvakoṭīs less nine years;
this should be known as the stated duration of the leśyās for animals and humans. (Uttarādhyayana 14.28)

Beyond that, I shall speak of the duration of the karmic leśyās of the gods. (Uttarādhyayana 14.29) Ten thousand years is the minimum duration for the black leśyā; the maximum duration for the black leśyā is an incalculable part of a palyopama. (Uttarādhyayana 14.30)

That which is indeed the maximum duration of the black state is, at minimum, one moment more than that of the blue state; its maximum is an incalculable *palyopama*. That which is indeed the maximum duration of the blue state is, [at minimum, one moment more than that of the grey state].
At the minimum it is black, and at the maximum it is an incalculable *palya*.
Beyond that, I shall describe the fire-leśyā as it pertains to the hosts of gods:
those of the *bhavanapatis*, *vānamantaras*, *jyotiṣkas*, and *vaimānikas*. (Uttarādhyayana 14.32–33)
The minimum [duration] for wind is a *palyopama*, while for the other two it is more than two *sāgaropamas* increased by an incalculable (*asaṅkhyeya*) number of *palyopamas*.
For fire, it is a fraction [of that]. (Utt.
14.34) The minimum lifespan for fire is ten thousand years.
The maximum lifespan in the fire hell is an incalculable fraction of a *palyopama*.
That which is indeed the maximum lifespan in the fire [hell], that same [measure] increased by one moment is the minimum;
in the *Pamha* [heaven], the maximum is ten *muhūrta*s more. (Utt. 1435–1436)
The maximum duration of the *padma* (pink) leśyā is indeed one *samaya* more than that [of the *tejolesyā*];
the minimum for the *śukla* (white) leśyā is thirty-three *muhūrtas* more [than the maximum of the *padma*].
The black (*kṛṣṇa*), blue (*nīla*), and grey (*kāpota*)—these three are all *adharma-leśyās*.
By means of these three [dark passions], a living being frequently falls into an evil rebirth.
(Uttarādhyayana 14.38) The fiery, the lotus-like, and the white—these three are the auspicious passions (dharma-leśyās).
By means of these three, a living being attains a happy rebirth. (Uttarādhyayana 14.39)

When all the *leśyās* have been transformed in the first moment, there is indeed no rebirth for any living being in a future existence. When all the *leśyās* have been transformed in the final moment... [Uttarādhyayana 14.40]
Indeed, for no living being does rebirth occur in the next life [immediately].
When half a muhūrta has passed and only half a muhūrta remains, beings go to the other world through the transformation of their *leśyās*. (Uttarādhyayana 14.41–42)
Therefore, having understood the power of these dispositions (*leśyās*), the sage should avoid those that are unwholesome and adhere to those that are wholesome.
Thus I say.
[The Path of the Wandering Ascetic] Listen to me with one-pointed minds; this is the path taught by the Buddhas.

By practicing thus, monks shall become those who bring an end to suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 14.44) Having renounced the life of a householder, the sage who has gone forth into homelessness should recognize these attachments by which men become entangled. (Uttarādhyayana 14.45)

In the same way, one who is self-restrained should avoid violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, sensual desire, and greed. [One should also avoid] a captivating house of the mind, scented with the incense of jasmine.
Even with the door closed and the window covered with white cloth, one should not desire [sensual objects] even in one's mind.
For a monk, it is difficult to restrain the senses in such a situation, as they increase passion for sensual pleasures. (Uttarādhyayana 14.47–48)
In a cemetery, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree— solitary and secluded, whether prepared by others— he should take up his residence there, in a place that is pure,
free from danger, and unharmed by women. (Uttarādhyayana 14.49)
In that regard, the monk, possessing supreme self-restraint, should not take up residence through his own intentions.
He should neither himself construct houses nor cause others to do so;
for in the undertaking of house-building, one sees the slaughter of living beings. (Uttarādhyayana 14.50–51)
Therefore, one who is self-restrained should avoid the undertaking of building a house for the sake of mobile and immobile beings, whether they be subtle or gross.
Likewise, [one should avoid] regarding food and drink, as well as cooking and baking.
For the sake of compassion toward living beings, one should neither cook nor cause others to cook. (Utt.

1453) Living beings dependent on water and grain, as well as those dependent on earth and wood, are harmed during the preparation of food and drink; therefore, a monk should not cause them to be cooked. (Utt. 1454)
It spreads and carries [fire] in all directions, destroying many living beings;
there is no weapon equal to fire. Therefore, one should not kindle a fire.
One should not even mentally long for gold or silver.
Monks regard both a clod of earth and gold as equal; they abstain from buying and selling.
One who buys becomes a buyer, and one who sells becomes a merchant.
Engaging in buying and selling, such a person does not become a monk. (Uttarādhyayana 14.56–57)
One should beg for alms and not trade; for a monk who lives by begging, buying and selling are a great fault, whereas the livelihood of a monk brings happiness.
One should seek alms through gathering gleanings, in accordance with the scriptures and beyond reproach.

Content with both gain and loss, the sage should wander for alms. Not greedy, not craving flavors, with tongue restrained and uninfatuated, the great sage should eat not for the sake of taste, but for the sake of sustenance. (Uttarādhyayana 14.59–60)
One should not even mentally long for worship, praise, veneration, offerings, nor for power, honor, and respect.
One should meditate upon the pure meditation (śukla-dhyāna), free from worldly attachment and possessing nothing.
One should dwell with one's body cast off, until the end of time.
Having rejected food, when the law of time has arrived and one has abandoned the human body, the powerful one is liberated from suffering. (Uttarādhyayana 14.62–63)
Free from attachment, free from ego, devoid of passion, and without taints,
he has attained absolute knowledge and reached eternal, final liberation.
Thus I say.
[The Classification of Living Beings and Non-Living Entities] Listen to me with one-pointed mind regarding this classification of living beings and non-living entities.
Having known this, the monk rightly exerts himself in self-restraint.
Living beings and non-living things—this is explained as the world (loka). That which is the region of non-living things and space is explained as the non-world (aloka). (Uttarādhyayana 14.65–66)
The exposition of those [categories], both of living beings (jīvas) and non-living beings (ajīvas), occurs by way of substance, space, time, and likewise by way of state (bhāva).
Non-living beings are of two kinds: those with form (rūpin) and those without form (arūpin).

The formless [substances] are said to be tenfold, and the material ones are fourfold. (Uttarādhyayana 14.68) The substance of motion (dharma-astikāya) is declared to exist in its entirety, as well as in part and in a portion thereof; likewise, the substance of non-motion (adharma) is declared to exist in its entirety, as well as in part and in a portion thereof. (Uttarādhyayana 14.69)
In space, in that region, and in that sub-region,
as well as in time, the formless [substances] are said to be of ten kinds:
Dharma and Adharma are each explained as being coextensive with the world.
In the worlds, the non-worlds, and in space, as well as in time and the spatial field of time—Uttarādhyayana 1471.
Dharma, Adharma, and Ākāśa: these three are indeed beginningless and endless, and are explained as existing for all eternity—Uttarādhyayana 1472.
Even though it is eternal, it is thus described as having a beginning when it attains its manifestation, and it also has an end.
Likewise, there are aggregates, parts of aggregates, and their constituent parts. (Uttarādhyayana 14.73)
And one should understand that matter (*rūpin*) is of four kinds: aggregates (*skandha*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*).

They are to be distinguished according to space as being either in a single part of the world or in the whole world, whether in unity or plurality. [Subtle ones are in the entire world, while gross ones are in a part of the world. From here I shall describe their fourfold division according to time. (Utt. 1474–1475)
Having attained peace, those [beings] are without end; yet, with respect to their duration, they have a beginning and also have an end.
Their maximum duration is an incalculable period of time (asaṅkhya-kāla), and their minimum is one moment (samaya).
This duration has been explained for material non-living entities (*ajīva-rūpī*):
the maximum is infinite time, and the minimum is one moment (*samaya*).
This interval for material non-living entities has also been explained. (Uttarādhyayana 14.77–78)
Transformation is to be understood as fivefold: by color, by smell, by taste, by touch, and likewise by shape.
Those which have undergone transformation by way of color are enumerated as being fivefold.
Black, blue, red, yellow, and likewise white;
those which are transformed by smell are explained as being of two kinds: those transformed into pleasant smells and those that are foul-smelling. (Uttarādhyayana 14.80–81)

Those which have been transformed by taste are declared to be of five kinds: bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, and likewise sweet. Those which have been transformed by touch are declared to be of eight kinds.
Hard and soft, heavy and light;
cold and hot, and likewise smooth and rough—thus have these matter-particles (pudgala), transformed into tactile sensations, been described. (Uttarādhyayana 14.83–84)
Regarding their shape, those that are transformed are declared to be of five kinds:
circular, spherical, triangular, square, and oblong.
As for those that are black in color, they may also be divided according to their smell.
Whether it be blue in color, it is likewise divided by smell, taste, touch, and shape. (Utt.
14.86) Whatever may be blue in color, it is likewise divided by smell, taste, touch, and shape. (Utt. 14.87)

That which is red in color is likewise divided according to its smell, taste, and touch, and it is also divided according to its shape. That which is yellow in color is likewise divided according to its smell... [and so forth].
In terms of taste, touch, and indeed in terms of shape;
that which is white in terms of color is also divided in terms of smell, taste, touch, and indeed in terms of shape. (Uttarādhyayana 14.89–14.90)
Whatever odor may be fragrant, it is likewise composed of color, taste, and touch; and it is also composed of shape. Whatever odor may be foul, it is likewise composed of color... [and so forth].
In terms of taste, it is bitter; and it is likewise divided in terms of color, smell, touch, and shape. (Utt.
14.92) In terms of taste, that which is bitter is likewise divided in terms of color, smell, touch, and shape. (Utt. 14.93)
Whatever is bitter in taste has also arisen [as such] in color, smell, and touch; it has also arisen in shape. Whatever is astringent in taste has also arisen [as such] in color... [and so on].
In terms of taste it is sour; furthermore, it is divided according to color, smell, touch, and shape. (Utt.
14.95) In terms of taste it is sour; furthermore, it is divided according to color, smell, touch, and shape. (Utt. 14.96)
That which is sweet in taste is also produced [as such] in color, smell, and touch; it is likewise produced in shape. That which is hard in touch is also produced [as such] in color...
It is indeed [differentiated] by smell, by taste, and also by shape; that which is soft by touch is likewise differentiated by color, by smell, by taste, and also by shape. (Uttarādhyayana 14.98–99)

Whatever is heavy by way of touch has also arisen [as such] by way of color, smell, and taste; it has also arisen by way of shape. Whatever is light by way of touch has also arisen [as such] by way of color...
It is divided by smell, taste, and also by shape;
that which is cold by touch is likewise divided by color, smell, taste, and also by shape. (Uttarādhyayana 15.01–02)

That which is hot by touch has also arisen [as a transformation] in terms of color, smell, and taste; it has also arisen in terms of shape. That which is smooth by touch has also arisen in terms of color...
That which is dry in terms of touch is also divided according to color, smell, taste, and shape. (Utt.
1504) That which is dry in terms of touch is also divided according to color, smell, taste, and shape. (Utt. 1505)
In its circular shape, it may differ according to color, odor, and taste; it may also differ according to touch. In its shape it may be round, and it may differ according to color.
It may exist as smell, taste, and even touch; it may also exist as shape, specifically as triangular. It may exist as color, smell, taste, and even touch. (Uttarādhyayana 15.07–15.08)
That which is square in shape is also divided according to color, smell, and taste, and it is also divided according to touch.
That which is in the shape of a diamond is also divided according to color... [and so forth].
By smell, by taste, and also by touch;
thus has this classification of non-living beings been explained in brief. Hereafter, I shall describe the classification of living beings in due order. (Uttarādhyayana 15.10–11)
Living beings are declared to be of two kinds: those situated in *saṃsāra* and those who have attained perfection (*siddha*).
The perfected ones are said to be of many kinds; listen as I describe them to you. (Uttarādhyayana 36.12) They are perfected as women, as men, and likewise as neuter beings.
Whether possessing the marks [of a monk], lacking the marks, or likewise possessing the marks of a householder;
whether at the maximum extent of their physical reach, or at the minimum or middle extent; and whether above, below, or across, in the ocean or in the water. (Uttarādhyayana 15.13–14)
Ten among those who are neuter, twenty among women,
and one hundred among men attain perfection at a single moment;
four among those with the lay-robe, and ten among those with other [non-Jaina] robes.
With their own [specific] marks, one hundred attain perfection at once; by many, they attain it simultaneously.
At the maximum height of the body, two attain it together; at the minimum, four; in the middle, one hundred and eight. (Uttarādhyayana 15.16–17)
In the four upper worlds and two oceans, one rests in the water;
likewise, one hundred and eight [yojanas] in the transverse world. In a single moment, one certainly attains perfection.
Where are the perfected ones (siddhas) obstructed? Where are the perfected ones established?
Having cast off the body where? Having gone where does one attain perfection?
The perfected ones (siddhas) have transcended the world; they are established at the summit of the universe.
Having cast off the body here, having gone there, one attains perfection. (Uttarādhyayana 15.19–20)
Twelve *yojanas* above the summit of Sarvārtha, there exists the earth named Īṣatprāgbhārā, shaped like an umbrella;
it is forty-five hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent. (Uttarādhyayana 15.21)
It is just as wide [as the earth], and its circumference is three times greater. It is explained that it is eight yojanas thick in the middle;
it becomes thinner toward the edges, more slender than a fly’s wing.
That earth is composed of Arjuna-gold; by its very nature it is stainless and shaped like an upturned umbrella, as declared by the Supreme Jinas.
It resembles a conch shell or kunda flowers—pale white, immaculate, and beautiful.
One yojana from the Sīyā [river] is explained as the end of the world (loka-anta).
Of that yojana which is there, in the uppermost quarter-krośa (krośa), at one-sixth part of that krośa, is the extent of the penetration (ogāhaṇā) of the Siddhas. (Uttarādhyayana 15.25–26)

The extent of the Siddhas is one-third less than that [of the universe]. (Utt.
1528) In its unity, it is beginningless and also endless; in its plurality, it is likewise beginningless and also endless. (Utt. 1529)
Formless, consisting of pure consciousness, and endowed with knowledge and vision,
they have attained unsurpassed bliss for which there is no comparison in the world;
all of them reside in a single region of the world, endowed with knowledge and vision.

Having crossed to the further shore of saṃsāra, they have attained perfection and the supreme goal. (Uttarādhyayana 15.31) But those living beings who remain in saṃsāra are explained as being of two kinds: the mobile (trasa) and the immobile (sthāvara). Among them, the immobile are of three types. (Uttarādhyayana 15.32)
Earth-living beings, water-living beings, and likewise plant-life—these are the three kinds of stationary beings; hear from me their divisions.
(Uttarādhyayana 15.33) Earth-living beings are of two kinds: subtle and coarse.

They are further divided into two types: those that are developed (paryāpta) and those that are undeveloped (aparyāpta). (Uttarādhyayana 15.34) Furthermore, those which are gross (bādara) when developed are explained as being of two kinds;
they should be known as smooth (saṇha) and rough (khara). Among them, the smooth ones are of seven kinds. (Uttarādhyayana 15.35)
Black, blue, blood-red, yellow, and white; likewise, pale, green, and clay—these are the thirty-six types of hard earth:
earth, gravel, sand, rock, stone, and salt-encrustation.
Copper, tin, lead, silver, gold, and diamond;
yellow orpiment, vermilion, realgar, antimony, and coral;
clouds, hailstones, and coarse sand—these are the varieties of the gross mineral body (*bādarakāya*). (Uttarādhyayana 15.37–38)
Gomedaka and rucaka, aṅka, sphaṭika, and lohitākṣa, as well as marakata, masāragalla, bhujamocaka, and indranīla;
candana, gairika, haṃsagarbha, pulaka, and saugandhika are to be known [as precious stones]. (Uttarādhyayana 15.39)
The moonstone, the beryl, the water-crystal, and the sun-crystal—these are the thirty-six varieties of hard earth, which are explained as being of one kind and without distinction;
therein, the subtle [earth] is also described. (Uttarādhyayana 15.40–41)
The subtle [beings] exist throughout the entire world, while the gross ones exist in a portion of the world.
From this point, I shall describe their fourfold division of time:
having attained a state of existence, they are beginningless and also endless.
With respect to their duration, they have both a beginning and an end. (Utt.
1543) The maximum life-span of the earth-bodied beings is twenty-two thousand years; the minimum is an antarmuhūrta. (Utt. 1544)

The maximum duration of the body-existence of earth-bodied beings is an incalculable period (asaṅkhyakāla), and the minimum is an internal moment (antarmuhūrta); [this refers to] not abandoning that body.
The maximum is an infinite period (anantakāla), and the minimum is an internal moment.
When one's own body is cast off, there is an interval for living beings within the earth.
According to their color, smell, taste, touch, shape, and location, there are thousands of varieties among them. (Uttarādhyayana 15.46–47)

Water-beings are of two kinds: subtle and coarse; likewise, they are further divided into two types, namely, those with complete development (paryāpta) and those without complete development (aparyāpta). Furthermore, those which are coarse and fully developed are enumerated as fivefold.
In pure water, in hot springs, in emeralds, in the earth, and in snow—these are explained there as being of one kind and without distinction, namely subtle.
Subtle [beings] exist throughout the entire world, while coarse ones exist in specific regions of the world. (Uttarādhyayana 15.49–50)
Having attained tranquility, they are beginningless with respect to their state, yet they are both with a beginning and with an end with respect to their duration.
At most, it would be seven thousand years.
The duration of the existence of water-bodied beings is, at its minimum, one antarmuhūrta; at its maximum, it is an incalculable period (asaṅkhya-kāla).
However, the duration of the body itself, as long as one does not abandon that body, is at its minimum one antarmuhūrta. (Uttarādhyayana 15.52–53)
The maximum duration for water-beings (*āujīva*) when they have abandoned their own body is an infinite period of time, while the minimum is a single moment (*antōmuhutta*).
This [duration] is described according to their color, smell, taste, and touch. (Uttarādhyayana 15.54)

Furthermore, there are thousands of varieties according to their configuration and location. (Uttarādhyayana 15.55) The living beings of the vegetable kingdom are of two kinds: subtle and likewise gross; each of these is further divided into two, namely, those with full development and those without. (Uttarādhyayana 15.56)
Those which are gross and fully developed are explained as being of two kinds:
those with common bodies and likewise those with individual bodies.
Those with individual bodies are enumerated as being manifold.
Trees, shrubs, and bushes, as well as creepers, climbing plants, and grasses;

rings, joints, and underground tubers, as well as water-plants, annual herbs, and likewise green bodies—these are explained as the category of single-sensed beings (*patteya*). (Uttarādhyayana 15.58–59)
Those with common bodies are enumerated in many ways: the yam, the radish,
the ginger, and likewise the hirilī,
sirilī, sassirilī, the jāvaī, the kea, and the kandalī.
Onion, garlic bulb, and kandalī, as well as kuhuvvaya;
lōhiṇīhū, thīhū, and likewise kuhagā; kaṇha, vajjakanda, and similarly the sūraṇa bulb. (Uttarādhyayana 15.61–62)
The *assakaṇṇī*, as well as the *sīhakaṇṇī*, the *musuṇḍhī*, and the *haliddā*—these and others such as these are explained there as being of one kind, without distinction, and subtle. (Utt.
Subtle [atoms] exist throughout the entire world, while coarse ones exist in a region of the world.
With respect to their subsistence, they are beginningless; yet with respect to their duration, they are both with a beginning and with an end. (Uttarādhyayana 15.64–65)
The maximum lifespan of forest-dwellers (plants) is ten thousand years,
while the minimum is an antarmuhūrta.
[Uttarādhyayana 36.186] Their maximum is an infinite period of time, and their minimum is an antarmuhūrta.
The duration of the body of fungi (paṇaga) is that very body, not leaving it;
at most for an incalculable period of time, and at least for half a muhūrta—this is the interval for fungi-beings once their own body has been cast off. (Uttarādhyayana 15.67–68)
Their varieties are indeed by way of color, smell, taste, touch, shape, and location; they exist in thousands of types.
Thus, these stationary beings are explained in brief as being of three kinds.
I shall now explain the three types of mobile beings (trasa) in their proper sequence:
fire and wind are to be known as such, and likewise gross (audārika) beings;
thus these mobile beings are of three kinds—listen to me regarding their divisions. (Uttarādhyayana 15.70–71)
Fire-bodied beings are of two kinds: subtle and gross;
likewise, they are further divided into two types, namely, those with complete development (paryāpta) and those with incomplete development (aparyāpta).
Furthermore, those gross fire-bodied beings who possess complete development are explained to be of many kinds.
Embers, glowing coals, and fire, as well as flames and tongues of fire;
meteors and lightning are to be understood—thus, in many ways, these are of one kind yet diverse, and they are explained as being subtle. (Uttarādhyayana 15.73–74)
Subtle [beings] exist throughout the entire world, while coarse beings exist in certain regions of the world.
From this point, I shall describe their fourfold division of time:
they are eternal in terms of their essential nature (*santati*), unoriginated, and indeed endless.
With respect to their duration, they have a beginning and also an end.
The maximum life-span of fire-beings is declared to be three days and nights;
the minimum is an antarmuhūrta.
The duration of the body of fire-beings (*teū*), not abandoning that body, is at most an incalculable period (*asaṅkhakāla*) and at least a moment (*antōmuhutta*).
[In another version: At most an infinite period (*anantakāla*) and at least a moment.
When one's own body has perished, there is an interval for the fire-bodied beings.
Regarding these, there are thousands of varieties according to color, smell, taste, touch, shape, and location. (Uttarādhyayana 15.79–80)
Wind-beings (vāyu-jīvas) are of two kinds: subtle and gross;

likewise, each of these is further divided into two—those that are fully developed (paryāpta) and those that are not (aparyāpta). Furthermore, those which are gross and fully developed are enumerated as being of five types.
The *ukkaliyā*, *maṇḍaliyā*, *ghanaguñjā*, and *suddhavāyā*; the *saṃvaṭṭagavāyā*—thus, by many names, wind is explained as being of one kind, though it is subtle therein. (Uttarādhyayana 15.8–9)
Subtle [beings] exist throughout the entire world, while coarse beings exist in a portion of the world.
From this point, I shall describe their fourfold division of time:
reaching toward the state of quiescence, they are beginningless and indeed endless.
With respect to their duration, they have a beginning and also an end.
The maximum lifespan of the wind-beings (vāyu) would be three thousand years;
the minimum is half a muhūrta. (Uttarādhyayana 15.85–86)
The maximum duration for which the body of air remains without abandoning that body is an incalculable period (asaṅkhyakalpa), and the minimum is less than a moment (antarmuhūrta).
The maximum duration for which the body of fire remains without abandoning that body is an infinite period (anantakāla), and the minimum is less than a moment.
When one's own body has been cast off, there is a distinction between the wind and the living beings (vāyu and jīvas).
Regarding these, there are thousands of varieties according to color, smell, taste, touch, shape, and location. (Uttarādhyayana 15.8–9)
Those which are gross and mobile are classified into four types: those with two sense-faculties, those with three sense-faculties, those with four, and those with five sense-faculties.
Furthermore, those living beings with two sense-faculties are classified into two kinds.
There are those that are fully developed and those that are not; hear from me their distinctions:
the *kimiṇa*, the *somaṅgala*, the *alasā*, the *māivāhaya*, the *vāsīmukha*, the *sippiya*, the *saṅkha*, and likewise the *saṅkhaṇaga*. (Uttarādhyayana 15.91–92)
Pallōyāṇullayas, likewise varāḍagas,
jalūgas, and jālagas, as well as candanas—
these are the various kinds of two-sensed beings, and so forth. (Uttarādhyayana 15.93)
All those [beings] exist in one part of the world, but they are not declared to exist everywhere.
With respect to their existence, they are beginningless; yet with respect to their duration, they are both with a beginning and with an end.
The maximum lifespan of two-sensed beings is explained as twelve years, while the minimum is an antarmuhūrta;
the maximum duration of their existence is a saṃkhyeya period of time, and the minimum is an antarmuhūrta. (Uttarādhyayana 36.196)
The state of existence as a two-sensed being—without abandoning that body—the maximum duration is an infinite time, and the minimum is an antarmuhūrta;
this is declared to be the interval for two-sensed living beings. (Uttarādhyayana 15.97–98)

Their varieties are indeed manifold by the thousands, according to color, odor, taste, touch, shape, and location. (Uttarādhyayana 15.9) As for those living beings with three sense organs, they are declared to be of two kinds.
They are either developed or undeveloped; hear from me their distinctions:
the *kunthu*, ants, mosquitoes, *ukkalas*, earthworms, as well as grass-cutters, wood-gatherers, *mālūgas*, and leaf-gatherers. (Uttarādhyayana 16.00–16.01)
Cotton seeds, *tinduka* stones, *tausa* seeds, *sadāvarī*, and *gummī*—these are to be known as the *indaga* (seed-like) items.
The *indagovasamāiya* (the group beginning with *indaga*) consists of many such types; thus is the category of *maya* (deceit).
All these [beings] exist in one part of the world, but they are not declared to exist everywhere. (Utt.
1603) With respect to their continuity, they are beginningless; and with respect to their duration, they are both with an end and without an end. (Utt. 1604)
The maximum lifespan of three-sensed beings is explained as forty-nine days and nights; the minimum is one muhūrta.
[In the case of hell-beings,] the maximum is a calculable period of time (saṅkhijja-kāla), and the minimum is one muhūrta.
The duration of the state of existence for three-sensed beings is within that body;

not abandoning that body, the maximum is an infinite period of time, while the minimum is an antarmuhūrta—thus has the interval for three-sensed living beings been explained. (Uttarādhyayana 1606–1607)

Their varieties are indeed thousandsfold, according to their color, smell, taste, touch, shape, and location. (Uttarādhyayana 16.08) Those living beings with four sense organs are declared to be of two kinds.
Regarding those that are developed and undeveloped, hear from me their distinctions:
the blind ones, the covered ones, the intoxicated ones, and likewise the mosquitoes, bees, insects, grasshoppers, *ḍhiṅkuṇas*, and *kuṅkaṇas*. (Uttarādhyayana 1609–1610)
The *kukkuḍa*, the *siṅgirīḍī*, the *nandāvatta*, the *vicchu*,
the *ḍōla*, the *bhiṅgirīḍī*, the *virilī*, the *acchivēhaḍa*,
the *acchirē*, the *māhala-acchi*, the *rōḍa*, the *vicitta*, and the *cittapatta*. (Uttarādhyayana 16.11)
The *ōhiñjaliyā*, the *jalakārī*, and the various kinds of *tambavagāiyā*—these are the four-sensed beings (*caürindiyā*).
Thus, in many ways, all of them have been described as existing within one part of the world. (Uttarādhyayana 16.12–13)
Having attained peace, they are beginningless with respect to their duration, yet they are both having a beginning and having an end. At most, however, it is explained as being six months.
The duration of life for four-sensed beings is, at the minimum, one antarmuhūrta; at the maximum, it is a countable period of time.

The duration of the body for four-sensed beings, without relinquishing that body, is likewise from one antarmuhūrta at the minimum to a countable period of time at the maximum. (Uttarādhyayana 16.15–16)
The maximum duration for which it remains bound within one's own body is an infinite period of time, while the minimum is an antarmuhūrta; this is explained as the interval between them.
Furthermore, their description is given according to color, smell, taste, and touch.
Furthermore, according to shape and location, there are thousands of types [of beings].
(Uttarajjhāyā 16.18) As for those living beings who possess five sense-faculties, they are explained as being fourfold:
hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods. (Uttarajjhāyā 16.19)
Hell-beings are of seven kinds; they exist within the seven earths:
the Jewel-Luster, the Rock-Luster, and the Sand-Luster are declared;
then the Mud-Luster, the Smoke-Luster, the Darkness-Luster, and likewise the Utmost Darkness-Luster.
"These are the hell-beings; they have been described in seven ways.
They are all said to exist in one part of the world. Hereafter, I shall describe their fourfold division of time. (Uttarādhyayana 16.21–22)
Having attained peace, they are beginningless; yet, with respect to their duration, they have a beginning and an end.
At the most, it is explained as one *sāgaropama*.
In the first [hell], the minimum [life span] is ten thousand years; the maximum is explained as three *sāgara* ages. In the second [hell], the minimum is one *sāgaropama*. Utt. 1624–1625.
In the third [age], the maximum lifespan is explained as seven *sāgaropamas*,
and the minimum as three *sāgaropamas*. In the fourth [age],
the maximum is explained as ten *sāgaropamas*.
In the fourth [hell], the minimum is seven *sāgaropamas*.
It is explained that in the fifth [hell], the maximum life span is seventeen *sāgaropamas*, while the minimum is ten *sāgaropamas*. (Utt. 1627–1628)

Twenty-two *sāgaropamas* are explained as the maximum lifespan on the sixth [hell], while the minimum is seventeen *sāgaropamas*. Thirty-three *sāgaropamas* are explained as the maximum [lifespan on the seventh hell].

In the seventh [hell], the minimum is twenty-two *sāgaropamas*. Whatever lifespan has been explained for the hell-beings, that constitutes their "body-duration" (*kāya-sthiti*), whether minimum or maximum. (Utt. 1630–1631)
The maximum interval for hell-beings (*nairayika*) in their own body, once it has been cast off, is an infinite period of time, while the minimum is half a moment (*antarmuhūrta*).
Furthermore, [this applies] to them in terms of color, smell, taste, and touch. (Uttarādhyayana 16.32)
Furthermore, according to their configuration and location, there are thousands of types [of beings]. (Utt.
1633) The five-sensed animals are explained as being of two kinds: those born by spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrcchana*) and those born from a womb (*garbhavyutkrāntika*). (Utt. 1634)
These are also of two kinds, yet they are threefold; they should be understood as aquatic, terrestrial, and aerial. Listen to me regarding their divisions:
fish, crocodiles, *gāhas*, and likewise *makaras*.
Crocodiles are also to be understood; these five types are declared to be aquatic creatures.
They are all said to exist in only one part of the world, not everywhere.
From this point on, I shall describe their fourfold division according to time.
The duration of the state of peace (śānti) is beginningless with respect to its nature, yet it is both with a beginning and with an end when considered in terms of its duration.
At most, it is explained as being one *pūrvakoṭī*.
The duration of existence for aquatic beings is, at the minimum, one muhūrta;
at the maximum, it is explained as being up to many millions of years (*pūrvakoṭi*).
The duration of the body for aquatic beings is, at the minimum, one muhūrta. (Uttarādhyayana 1639–1640)
The maximum interval for aquatic beings is an infinite period of time, while the minimum is half a muhūrta, once they have cast off their own bodies.
[This applies] to these [beings] in terms of color, smell, taste, and touch. (Uttarādhyayana 36.197)

Furthermore, according to their shape and location, there are thousands of varieties. (Uttarādhyayana 16.42) Terrestrial animals are of two kinds: quadrupeds and reptiles. Quadrupeds are of four types; listen as I describe them to you. (Uttarādhyayana 16.43)
Single-hoofed and cloven-hoofed animals, those with solid hooves and those with soft pads—
such as horses and oxen, elephants and lions;
reptiles and crawling creatures— crawlers are of two kinds.
The Gohas and the Ahimas each exist in many ways;
all of them are declared to be in one region of the world, not everywhere.
From this point, I shall describe their fourfold division according to time. (Uttarādhyayana 16.45–46)
Having attained tranquility, they are beginningless with respect to their state, yet they are also finite; they are also both with a beginning and with an end.
At most, they are explained to last for three *palyopamas*.
The duration for land-dwelling animals is one *antarmuhūrta* at the minimum;
at the maximum, it is explained as three *palyopamas* plus two *pūrvakoṭis*.
At the minimum, it is one *antarmuhūrta*. (Uttarādhyayana 16.48–49)
The bodily duration of land-dwelling beings is, at most, an infinite period, and at least, half a muhūrta.
When their own body is cast off, such is the interval for land-dwellers. (Uttarādhyayana 16.50)
There are birds with leather wings, birds with feathered wings, thirdly, those with folded wings, and those with outspread wings; these four types of birds are to be known.
All of them are explained as being found only in certain regions of the world, not everywhere.

Having attained tranquility, they are beginningless; yet, with respect to their duration, they are both with a beginning and with an end. A portion of a *palyopama*, specifically an innumerable part, may occur.
The minimum duration of the life-span of the sky-dwellers (birds) is one antarmuhūrta.
At the maximum, it is slightly more than a palyopama in its asaṃkhyeya fraction; at the minimum, it is one antarmuhūrta.
It is also stated as being several pūrvakoṭis at the maximum, with one antarmuhūrta at the minimum. (Uttarādhyayana 16.54–55)
The bodily duration of the sky-dwellers (birds) may be as much as an infinite period of time at the maximum, and a minimum of one antarmuhūrta.
Their [description] by way of color, odor, taste, and touch is as follows. (Uttarādhyayana 16.56)
Furthermore, there are thousands of varieties according to their shapes and locations.
(Uttarādhyayana 1657) Humans are of two types; listen as I describe them:
humans born of spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrchima*) and those born from a womb (*garbhavyutkrāntika*). (Uttarādhyayana 1658)
Regarding the descent into the womb, that is explained as being threefold:
those born in the lands of karma, those born in the lands without karma, and likewise those born in the intermediate islands.
These are further divided into fifteen, thirty, and twenty-two types respectively.
This enumeration of them has been explained in due order. (Utt.
1660) This same classification is declared for those born by spontaneous generation;
they are all said to occupy a single portion of the world. (Utt. 1661)
Having attained tranquility, they are beginningless with respect to their state, yet they are both with a beginning and with an end with respect to that state.
At most, they are explained to last for three *palyopamas*.
The duration of human existence is, at its minimum, one muhūrta;
at its maximum, it is explained as three palyopamas plus two full crores of pūrvas, with a minimum of one muhūrta. (Uttarādhyayana 16.63–64)
The bodily duration of humans may be as much as an infinite period at the maximum, and a single moment (antarmuhūrta) at the minimum. Regarding these [beings],
there is likewise [variation] in terms of color, odor, taste, and touch.
Furthermore, there are thousands of types according to their configuration and location. (Uttarādhyayana 16.66) The gods are said to be of four kinds; listen as I describe them to you:
the Bhavanavāsins, the Vyantaras, the Jyotiṣkas, and likewise the Vaimānikas. (Uttarādhyayana 16.67)
The Bhavanavāsins are of ten kinds, the Vanacārins are of eight kinds, the Jyotiṣkas are of five kinds, and the Vaimānikas are likewise of two kinds.
The Asuras, Nāgas, Suvarṇas, Vidyuts, and Agnis are thus explained.
The wind-gods of the Dīvodahi region, and the thundering ones are the inhabitants of the Bhavana.
Piśācas, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Mahoragas, and Gandharvas constitute the eightfold class of Vānamantara gods. (Uttarādhyayana 1669–1670)

The planets, the suns, the constellations, the celestial bodies, and likewise the stars that move by day— these are the fivefold abodes of the luminaries. Furthermore, those gods who belong to the Vaimānika realm are declared to be of two kinds.
Those who have entered the realm of existence (kalpōvagā) are to be understood, as well as those who have transcended it (kappātītā).

Those who have entered the realm of existence are of twelve kinds: those belonging to the Saudharma and Īśāna [heavens], likewise those of Sanatkumāra and Mahendra, and those of Brahmaloka and Lāntaka. (Uttarādhyayana 16.72–73)
The Mahāsukkas, Sahassāras, Āṇayas, Pāṇayas,
as well as the Āraṇas and Accuyas— these are the gods who dwell within the kalpas.
Furthermore, those gods who transcend the kalpas are explained as being of two kinds.
The Graiveyaka and Anuttara heavens; therein, the Graiveyakas are of nine kinds:

the lowest-of-the-lowest, the lowest-middle, the lowest-highest, the middle-lowest, and likewise [the middle-middle, middle-highest, highest-lowest, highest-middle, and] the highest-of-the-highest. (Utt. 1675–1676)
The middle-middle ones, as well as the middle-higher ones; likewise the higher-lower ones, and the higher-middle ones;
the higher-higher ones—thus are the gods of the Graiveyaka realms.
The Vijayas, Vaijayantas, Jayantas, Aparājitas, and the Sarvārthasiddhas—these five classes of Anuttara gods; thus are the Vaimānika gods of many kinds in this manner. (Utt. 1678–1679)
Within one part of the world, all of them have been described;
now, however, I shall explain their fourfold division of time.
From the perspective of their state of existence (*santati*), they are both beginningless and endless.
With respect to their duration, they have a beginning and also an end.
The maximum duration for the Bhavanapatis would be one ocean (sāgara), and the minimum is ten thousand years. (Uttarādhyayana 36.168–169)
The maximum lifespan of the Vānavyantara gods is one *palyopama*,
while the minimum is ten thousand years. (Uttarādhyayana 16.83) Furthermore, [the next category] is one *palyopama* plus one hundred thousand years.
In the celestial realms, the minimum [life span] is one-eighth of a *palyopama*. (Utt.
1684) In the *Saudharma* heaven, it is explained that the maximum is two *sāgaropamas*, and the minimum is one *palyopama*. (Utt. 1685)
In the realm of Īśāna, the lifespan is explained as being at most two sāgaropamas plus one,
and at its minimum, one sāgaropama plus one. Furthermore, the maximum duration of existence would be seven sāgaropamas.
In Saṇaṅkumāra, the minimum is two *sāgaropamas*;
in Māhinda, the maximum duration would be seven *sāgaropamas* plus one. (Uttarādhyayana 16.87–88)
In the Brahma-world, the maximum lifespan would be ten sāgaras,
while the minimum is seven sāgaropamas. In [the next],
the maximum lifespan would be fourteen sāgaras.
In Lāntaka, the minimum [residence] is ten sāgaropamas;
in Mahāśukra, the maximum residence would be seventeen sāgaras, and the minimum is fourteen sāgaropamas. (Utt. 1690–1691)
In Sahassāra, the maximum lifespan would be eighteen sāgaras,
and the minimum is seventeen sāgaropamas.
In Āṇata, however, the maximum lifespan would be nineteen sāgaras.
In Āṇata, the minimum [residence] is eighteen sāgaropamas;
in Pāṇata, the maximum residence would be twenty sāgaras, and the minimum is nineteen sāgaras. (Utt. 1693–1694)
The maximum lifespan in Āraṇa would be twenty-one sāgaras,
while the minimum is twenty sāgaropamas.
The maximum lifespan [in Acyuta] would be twenty-two sāgaras.
In Accua, the minimum [life span] is twenty-one sāgaras;
in the first [hell], the maximum life span would be twenty-three sāgaras, and the minimum is twenty-two sāgaropamas. (Utt. 1696–1697)
The maximum duration of life in the second [hell] would be twenty-four *sāgaras*,
and the minimum is twenty-three *sāgaropamas*.
The maximum duration of life would be twenty-five *sāgaras*...
In the third [hell], the minimum is twenty-four sāgaropamas;
in the fourth, the duration would be twenty-six sāgaras at the maximum, and twenty-five sāgaras at the minimum. (Utt. 1699–1700)
The maximum duration of stay in the fifth [hell] would be twenty-seven sāgaras, while the minimum is twenty-six sāgaras.
The maximum duration of stay would be twenty-eight sāgaras... [Uttarādhyayana 17.01]
In the sixth [hell], the minimum is twenty-seven sāgaras;
the maximum duration would be twenty-nine sāgaras.
In the seventh [hell], the minimum is twenty-eight sāgaras. (Uttarādhyayana 17.02–03)
In the eighth [hell], the maximum duration of stay would be thirty sāgaras,
and the minimum, twenty-nine sāgaras. In the ninth,
however, the maximum duration of stay would be thirty-one sāgaras.
In the ninth [heaven], the minimum is thirty *sāgaropamas*.
In all four [heavens] beginning with Vijaya, the maximum duration is thirty-three *sāgaropamas*, and the minimum is thirty-one. (Uttarādhyayana 17.05–17.06)
Neither low nor high, thirty-three *sāgarōpamas* is the lifespan in the Mahāvimāna Sarvārtha; this is declared to be the duration of life for the gods.
(Uttarādhyayana 17.07) Indeed, whatever lifespan of the gods has been declared, [that is their measure].
That is their bodily duration, which may be either minimum or maximum. (Utt.
1708) When their own body has been cast off, the interval for the gods is a maximum of infinite time and a minimum of half a muhūrta. (Utt. 1709)
Their varieties are indeed thousandsfold, according to color, smell, taste, touch, shape, and location;
thus are the souls described, both those dwelling in saṃsāra and those who have attained perfection.
"Substantial entities are indeed of two kinds: those with form and those without form.

Thus, having heard and having gained faith in both living beings and non-living beings according to the consensus of all perspectives (nayas), the sage should delight in self-restraint. (Uttarādhyayana 17.11–12)
Having observed the state of a śramaṇa for many years,
the sage should, by means of this application of karma, thoroughly attenuate himself. Indeed, for twelve years, he should remain intent upon self-attenuation.
For one year, the medium [period]; for six months, the lowest.
In the first four-year cycle, one should perform the elimination of the various types of food; in the second four-year cycle, one should practice diverse austerities.
Having practiced for one year with an interval of one month, and then for two years, and then for half a year,
he should practice the non-distinct austerity (nātivigīṭṭha).
Then, for half a year, he should practice the distinct austerity (vigiṭṭha).
In that year, he practiced a limited extent of austerity;
having performed austerities with an extent of ten million [units] during that year, the sage practiced penance by means of food taken every half-month. (Utt. 1717–1718)
Lust, the obsession with pride, the state of being a *kivvisa* (an impure ascetic), delusion, and the demonic state—these lead to miserable rebirths;
they result in failure at the time of death for those who are devoted to false views, who possess the causes of bondage, and who are violent. (Uttarādhyayana 17.19)
For those living beings who die while [in such a state], enlightenment is difficult to attain again. (Utt.

17.20) But for those living beings who die while devoted to right view, free from worldly attachment, and immersed in pure thought-coloration (*śukla-leśyā*), enlightenment will be easy to attain. (Utt. 17.21)
Those living beings who die while intoxicated by false views, possessed of causal attachments, and immersed in dark karmic influx— for them, enlightenment is difficult to attain.
But for those who are devoted to the words of the Jina and who practice the words of the Jina with true feeling...
They are stainless and undefiled, and they become those who have only a limited cycle of existence. (Utt.
1723) Those wretched people who do not know the word of the Jina will die many times over through foolish deaths and likewise through many unwanted deaths. (Utt. 1724)

Possessing extensive knowledge of the scriptures, capable of inducing meditative concentration, and appreciative of virtues— for these reasons, one is worthy to hear the confession. (Uttarādhyayana 17.25) Likewise, [one should avoid] lewdness, mockery, and frivolous talk concerning conduct and character.
One who causes another to wonder and performs the meditation of *kandarpa* [Utt.
1726]; one who, having performed mantras and *yoga*, practices *bhūtikarma* for the sake of the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the ocean, performs the meditation of *abhiyoga* [Utt. 1727].
One who speaks ill of those possessing kevala-knowledge, of the Kevalins, of the Dharma-teacher, or of the Saṅgha and the virtuous monks, cultivates a sinful state of being.
He is one whose outburst of anger is persistent, and likewise, he becomes a practitioner of [prohibited] signs.
By these causes, one cultivates an asuric state of being.
Taking up weapons, consuming poison, entering fire, and entering water—those who indulge in such unrighteous practices bind themselves to further births and deaths. (Uttarādhyayana 17.29–17.30)
Thus have I spoken: the thirty-six *Uttarādhyayanas*, proclaimed by the Buddha, the Knower, the one who has attained final liberation, and established for those destined for emancipation.
Thus I say.
The *Uttarajjhayaṇa*, the root scripture, has been thoroughly edited and prepared by the sage Dīparatnasāgara. It is complete.
